subtopics: Bill Assistance; Cost Shift Prevention (Large Load); Metrics; Monitoring
description: On November 25, 2025, the Office of the People’s Counsel (OPC) DC filed a public petition for the DC Public Service Commission to establish a docket to perform a holistic evaluation of energy affordability for ratepayers and to take affirmative actions to adopt measures to protect and improve energy affordability for ratepayers. Specifically, the OPC requested that the Commission perform an evaluation of affordability in the District, develop an affordability metric, and apply best practices to improve energy assistance programs and consumer protections. The OPC further recommended implementing methodologies from an energy affordability assessment that it commissioned; the report includes an affordability metric that may be used in rate cases and reporting. On January 15, 2026, the Commission granted the petition, opened Formal Case 1186, and invited stakeholders to comment on the petition, as well as provide feedback on topics including the Commission’s authority over affordability, existing programs and proceedings related to affordability, affordability metrics, creation of a specific rate for large loads that impact ratepayer costs, and recommendations such as best practices and new legislation. Several comments were filed in response to the notice. On May 15, 2026, the Commission filed a notice of a legislative-style hearing to be held on June 3, 2026 addressing potential cost mitigation measures for the “generation” portion of customer bills. On June 2, 2026, Commissioner Beverly filed a statement averring that the Commission-approved rate base for Pepco has increased dramatically since 2020, despite a lack of substantive grid modernization investments. The June 3, 2026 hearing hosted speakers from PJM, utilities, advocacy groups, and other industry stakeholders who addressed market structures and challenges, procurement approaches and reforms, DER integration, demand response and virtual power plants.

On October 15, 2025, the Delaware Public Service Commission issued an order opening a docket to require Delmarva Power & Light to promulgate a large load tariff for customers and further requiring the tariff to be in place before interconnecting any large load customers who were not already interconnected by September 3, 2025. On December 19, 2025, the utility proposed a new service class, General Service - Large Demand (GS-LD) for large demand customers. The utility notes the same structure for GS-LD as existing tariff GS-T (General Service - Transmission). The utility also proposed revisions to its Rules and Regulations applicable to large load customers, including a new definition of large load customers as those with projected new load or load additions of at least 50 MW over a 10-year load ramp period. Through a cash deposit for engineering reviews, applicants must pay for the costs of a system impacts analysis and a subsequent detailed engineering analysis. The revisions additionally require a deposit for long lead time equipment, financial assurances for expected distribution extension costs, and a transmission security agreement. Deposits over $2 million must be backed by a letter of credit. On April 28, 2026, Delmarva Power & Light revised the new service classification terms and renamed it General Service - Large Load (GS-LL). Contracts are modified to have an initial period of 10 years, with early termination resulting in exit fees equal to any unrecovered distribution project extension costs, as well as those specified in the transmission service agreement. The revision clarifies that expected distribution extension costs in the rules and regulations may include all associated engineering work and clarifies the company's protocol for returning or releasing delivery revenue and financial assurances.

H.B. 445, as enacted in August 2026, requires large energy use facilities, in order to operate in the state, to produce sufficient power or procure sufficient generation to meet 100% of its annual energy needs from a facility or facilities interconnected in the state or in PJM's Delmarva Power & Light (DPL) transmission zone or a contiguous transmission zone with sufficient transmission to be deliver the additional electricity to the state. A large use energy facility that does not meet such requirements must submit to the relevant utility's regulatory body a plan to increase production or procurement of generation so that it is procuring or producing 100% of its needs within 10 years of operations; facilities choosing this option are curtailable for certain price threshold impacts; facilities may use backup generation systems including at least 50% power met by battery storage or clean energy technology. New energy production generation must be sought out and funded, at least in part, by the large energy use facility. Facilities may not connect to the electric distribution and transmission system until at least 25% of required energy generation consistent with the energy requirements is energized and interconnected, at least 25% of back-up power comes from clean energy technology and is interconnected, and the facility has entered a 15-year binding contract with the relevant utility's regulatory body that contains a guaranteed insurance bond paid into the general fund if the facility fails to meet its obligations to produce or procure energy. If the facility fails to produce or procure sufficient renewable energy for the calendar year, it must also pay a penalty sufficient to cover the costs of producing or procuring the energy or building or procuring the infrastructure the facility failed to produce or procure. Large energy use facilities are defined to include facilities that use or are projected to use a monthly maximum demand of 75 MW or greater at a load factor of 85% or greater, use a monthly maximum instantaneous demand of 100 MW or greater, or use or be able to use a monthly maximum demand of 30 MW or greater and primarily be engaged in providing a service described under code 518210 of the North American Industry Classification System.

categories: Customer Cost Allocation; Customer Cost-Saving Programs
subtopics: Bill Assistance; Cost Shift Prevention (Large Load); LMI Incentives
description: H.B. 233, as enacted in August 2026, requires Delaware Public Service Commission-regulated utilities to establish a service classification and tariff for large energy use facilities, separate from other commercial or industrial customers. Customer Cost Allocation: Large energy use facilities must also get an electric service agreement (ESA) and transmission service agreement approved by the Commission before they can begin operations. Any ESA approved by the Commission directly assign the costs of serving a large energy consumer to the consumer and ensure that the costs of serving the class of large energy use facilities are borne by that class of customers; ESAs must also include minimum contract duration, minimum distribution and supply charges based on 90% of contract capacity, set exit fees, and require financial guarantees to protect other customers in the event that a large load is not able to meet its obligations under the ESA; the tariff must require each large energy use facility to enter into an ESA. The bill further outlines protocols for the ESA and tariff collectively to address assigning infrastructure costs, PJM capacity procurement costs, study costs, and financial security. In determining whether to approve an ESA, the Commission must consider whether the ESA and underlying tariff ensures that all applicable costs attributed to the large energy use facility are directly assigned to the facility and use the incremental cost test outlined in the bill to make this determination. Additionally, the Commission must consider if the ESA and tariff provides protections necessary to ensure that other customers of the utility are not placed at risk for paying stranded costs associated with the utility serving the large energy use facility. Customer Cost-Saving Programs: The tariff must also require large energy use facilities to contribute to the Low-Income Charge at a rate of $0.000190 per kWh; the charge is deposited into the state agency-administered Low-Income Program Fund, which is used for low-income fuel assistance and weatherization programs in Delmarva Power & Light's service territory.

categories: Customer Cost Allocation; Customer Cost-Saving Programs
subtopics: Bill Assistance; Cost Shift Prevention (Large Load); LMI Incentives
description: On August 5, 2026, the Delaware Public Service Commission filed an order approving a Staff request that the Commission conduct workshops to create a large load electric regulations; Staff filed the request in response to the recently passed H.B. 233, which requires the creation of an electric service agreement (ESA) for Commission review and approval and directs the Commission to promulgate regulations to govern tariffs applicable to large energy use facilities under the Commission's jurisdiction. On August 17, 2026, ahead of a planned stakeholder meeting, Staff released draft regulations, outlining that ESA applications must include a minimum contract term of 15 years including the ramp period, estimated dates of service, minimum demand fees, minimum contract capacity, exit procedures and fees, curtailment and interruptibility obligations, estimated system impacts, a study of the impact of the proposed large energy use facility on electricity costs in Delaware, and a surety bond/other financial security to protect other customers in the event of the large load customer being unable to meet its obligations under the ESA. Electric utilities must propose a large load tariff, which must include cost assignment methodology, financial security requirements, and a description of the proposed incremental cost test procedures. The proposed regulations outline further tariff requirements, including direct assignment of costs, cost recovery mechanisms, financial security requirements, incremental cost test procedures, and a contribution to the Low-Income Charge at a rate of $0.000190 per kWh. The Low-Income Charge is deposited into the state agency-administered Low-Income Program Fund, which is used for low-income fuel assistance and weatherization programs in Delmarva Power & Light's service territory.

categories: Customer Cost Allocation; Utility Business Model; Utility Oversight and Cost Recovery
subtopics: Low-Income Discount Rates; Ratemaking; Revenue Decoupling
description: Customer Cost Allocation: On December 9, 2025, Delmarva Power & Light filed an application for an increase in electric base rates. The application includes an income-based rate discount available to ratepayers enrolled in LIHEAP or the Delaware Energy Assistance Program; the rate and associated costs are authorized by H.B. 116 (enacted in 2025). Enrollment in one of the programs qualifies the customer for a 20% discount on the total electric delivery charge. Utility Business Model: The utility also requests approval for a Bill Stabilization Adjustment (BSA) Rider to decouple electricity use and distribution revenue; the BSA would lower customer rates if the company earned above its target revenue distribution revenue per customer and raise rates if the company earned less than the target revenue. The company would seek an annual adjustment to collect or return the balance and propose a revised rate based on forecasted usage. Utility Oversight and Cost Recovery: On July 7, 2026, Delmarva filed revised rates, in accordance with the passage of S.B. 326 on July 1, 2026. Per the new statutory requirements for interim rates, Delmarva will reduce the interim rates it requested; the modified interim rate will be implemented through a Stage 1 with incremental revenues reflecting the 50% of incremental revenue requirement in S.B. 326 and a Stage 2 with incremental revenues reflecting the 75% of incremental revenue requirement in S.B. 326.

On June 4, 2026, Delmarva Power & Light filed an application for its 2027-2029 energy efficiency portfolio. The proposal includes a new dedicated Community Engagement program, which would include pillars of: (1) outreach events for community engagement and energy efficiency program opportunities; (2) energy efficiency kits with easy-to-install energy efficiency measures, and (3) community ambassadors coordinated with Energize Delaware, intended to embed within key communities to directly connect customers to program opportunities and energy education. The community ambassadors pillar is modeled after Energize Delaware's Ambassador Program working with the Southbridge Community Development Corporation. The program is expected to reach 19,500 customers and result in energy savings of 2,615 MWh and peak demand savings of 0.451 MW.

S.B. 321, as enacted in August 2026, requires Delaware Public Service Commission-regulated electric public utilities to offer consolidated billing for all customer classes and requires consolidated billing to be the default billing method for community energy facilities with a final certificate to operate issued by the Commission on or after September 3, 2026. Facilities certified to operate before then can opt-out of consolidated billing; they must submit the opt-out request by October 2028. Utilities may charge an administrative fee (capped at 1% of subscriber bill credits) plus up to 0.25% for an arrearage escrow. The Commission must adopt regulations for consolidated billing protocols by April 1, 2027. For facilities certified to operate after September 3, 2026, the bill also requires a minimum savings rate of 10% for residential community solar participants and 20% for income-qualified participants (accounting for any subscription or other fees charged by the subscribing organization or community-owned energy generating facility); for facilities certified to operate on or before September 2, 2026, the subscription value for residential customers must provide for a net discount. Facilities certified after September 3, 2026 must also dedicate at least 15% of their output to LMI customers whose gross annual income, by family size, is at or below 350% of the federal poverty guidelines, or 80% of the state median household income published by the U.S. Census Bureau, whichever is greater. The Commission must also convene a stakeholder working group to provide recommendations to improve the enrollment and operation of the community energy facility program, with a final report due to the Delaware General Assembly by January 31, 2027.

On December 9, 2025, Delmarva Power & Light filed its application for approval of its 2027-2029 Affordability and Load Flexibility Portfolio. The portfolio includes five programs and two pilots; the total estimated 2027-2029 plan period budget is estimated to be $36.95 million. The new Direct Load Control (DLC) 2.0 program is an update to Delmarva’s legacy A/C control program, supplying utility-provided switches (two-way communication load control devices) that enable direct cycling. Customers can receive annual incentives of $40 for 50% cycling, $60 for 75% cycling, and $80 for 100% cycling. Delmarva claims that DLC 2.0 will focus on affordability and equitable participation for LMI access due to the no-cost, turnkey nature of the program and states plans for outreach in collaboration with community organizations. On June 8, 2026, Delmarva filed a proposed stipulation, which the ALJ approved on the same day. The parties will work together in working groups to potentially redesign the proposed programs. At the end of the process, Delmarva will update, re-file, or withdraw the application.

S.B. 308, as enacted in July 2026, gives the Delaware Public Service Commission the authority and responsibility to review and evaluate load forecasts submitted by Commission-regulated electric distribution companies to PJM, coordinate with PJM and other states to support system-wide planning, and access all relevant materials to review and evaluate load forecasts. The Commission must also open a proceeding to investigate the methodologies used in developing load forecasts, the load forecasts themselves, and individual interconnection requests; it must also submit an annual report to the General Assembly on implementation status.

categories: Planning and Procurement; Utility Business Model
description: H.B. 470, as passed by the House in June 2026, allows Delmarva Power & Light to own and operate utility battery energy storage systems (U-BESS) after appropriate review and approval of the Delaware Public Service Commission. The review must include a determination of cost-effectiveness measured by whether the U-BESS are prudent and provide net value to ratepayers; all costs will be distributed among the entire customer base in a manner prescribed by the Commission if approved. Further, Delmarva must make best efforts to maximize all applicable value streams from BESS, including participating in applicable PJM markets. The bill did not pass both chambers before the session adjourned.

categories: Utility Business Model; Utility Oversight and Cost Recovery
subtopics: Rate Freezes; Return on Equity Rules
description: On June 16, 2026, Delaware Governor Matt Meyer called on several state actors to address energy affordability. First, Governor Meyer called on the Public Advocate to file a petition with the Delaware Public Service Commission asking the Commission to act within the next six months to reset the utility's profit model. The Governor requested that the review examine Delmarva Power's rate of return and consider whether a competitive determination is more appropriate than allowing a set return. Further, the Governor called on the Commission to initiate a review to freeze rates. Finally, the Governor called on the legislature to pass S.B. 326 and H.B. 233. In July 2026, both chambers passed H.B. 233, and the Governor signed S.B. 326.

S.B. 326, as signed by the Governor in July 2026, directs the Delaware Public Service Commission to conduct management audits of Commission-regulated electric distribution companies, which must include an examination of management effectiveness and operating efficiency. Audits would be conducted every five years, unless the Commission finds that a specific management audit is unnecessary. The bill further allows the Commission to require an audit to be performed by independent audit or consulting firms, with stipulations that the firms must be paid by the utility for relevant expenses and that no entity other than the firm will have input or editorial control of the firm's findings and recommendations. The bill also requires each public utility to prepare, maintain, and file with the Commission for approval, a rate summary table for each rate class, showing the total effective rate and itemizing each rate element. Each element will be displayed numerically, using the same units in which the customer is billed and include a schedule that identifies the components of rates that change on a predictable schedule. The Commission may reject or require revisions to the table to align with approved rates. The utility will include the table in its tariff, post the table for each customer class in an easily accessible place on its website, include the table in customer bills, and file the table in the above locations at least 30 days prior to the effective date of any rate change. The bill also outlines a plain language standard in public facing and customer communications and any submissions to the Commission, public utilities, Commission Staff, and Division of the Public Advocate. Pertaining to rate cases, the bill requires that for changes to base rates, notice to the Commission must include the test period and test year applicable. Further, as a part of any base rate filing, a public utility may be subject to a regulatory accounting review of transactions included on the utility's books and records for ratemaking purposes. Current law allows utilities to place their proposed rates into effect if the Commission has not made its decision within seven months after the filing, on the condition that the utility files a bond in a reasonable amount to refund entitled parties the excess if the rate is finally determined to be excessive, provided that the increase does not constitute an increase in excess of 15% of the utility's gross intrastate operating revenues; a utility may put a rate into a bond 60 days after the filing. The bill revises current law to to state that only 50% of the increase may be put into effect, and 75% after 12 months; a utility may put a rate into a bond 90 days after the filing. The bill also stipulates that for any public utility with more than 25,000 customers, the utility will not recover from its customers expenses related to distribution rate cases for attorneys' fees and to engage external expert witnesses incurred after the filing date that exceed the amount spent by Commission Staff and the Division of the Public Advocate on attorneys' fees and fees to engage expert witnesses or consultants. Additionally, the bill stipulates that all orders issued by the Commission must contain adequate support and rationale for any conclusions, including specific facts and factors on which the conclusion is based, and major elements of the settlement when issuing an order accepting or denying certain settlement agreements. Finally, each Commission-regulated utility may not recover in rates annual non-mandatory spending in excess of $70,000,000 for 2026 and 2027, and for year 2028 and continuing thereafter, 5% of its rate base approved in its most recent base rate case.

On April 22, 2026, Duke Energy Florida filed a petition to approve a Large Load Customer Policy (LLCP) and Large Load Customer Agreement (LLCA), following a similar 2025 filing (Docket No. 20250113). The utility plans to propose a new large load rate schedule in its next rate case. The petition reflects changes driven by S.B. 484 of 2026, which requires large load customers to fully cover service costs without shifting risk to other ratepayers. It also prohibits service to foreign entities and prevents load-splitting to avoid classification, while allowing the Florida Public Service Commission to use standard ratemaking tools such as demand charges and financial guarantees. The policy applies to new or expanded facilities with expected demand of at least 50 MW, excluding sites already interconnected as of December 31, 2025. Customers must pay a $150,000 non-refundable system impact study fee (plus $150,000 for updates) and, within three months, execute an LLCA or reimbursement agreement. Service requires a 20-year minimum term and may include a load ramp period (75–85% of contract capacity). Customers must provide financial security and cover all incurred costs if service is not taken or is terminated early, including specified termination fees. Two years’ notice is required for termination, while Duke Energy may terminate for cause with 90 days’ notice. The utility may require upfront payment of extension costs (refundable over five years). Until a new rate is approved, service will be taken under existing GSD-1 or GSADT-1 rates.

On August 26, 2026, the Georgia Public Service Commission Staff and Georgia Power filed a joint letter regarding the approval of a large load contract, which also included an update on the utility's agreement from the 2025 rate case to ensure that revenue from large loads reduces rates for non-large load customers. Georgia Power previously committed to reducing residential bills by $8.50 per month, but the utility now agrees to provide at least $15.00 in monthly savings for residential customers from 2029-2031 given the increased revenue from additional large load contracts.

categories: Customer Cost Allocation; Planning and Procurement
subtopics: Cost Shift Prevention (Large Load); Grid Utilization
description: On July 3, 2024, the Georgia Public Service Commission approved Georgia Power's 2029-2031 All-Source Capacity RFP. After the utility submitted its application for certification under this RFP and selected 14 company-owned proposals on July 30, 2025, the Commission Public Interest Advocacy Staff and Georgia Power filed a stipulation on December 10, 2025, approving the application certification. Within the stipulation, there is language that requires the two parties to investigate the potential benefits of load flexibility, including contract terms and cost saving strategies, and a related report will be released within 120 days of a final order in this proceeding. On June 30, 2026, Georgia Power filed its Load Flexibility Compliance Report, which focused on evaluating the potential role of load flexibility within the utility's programmatic offerings and communications and exploring opportunities to compensate large loads for flexible interconnection and offsetting future generation needs. While Georgia Power acknowledged that there are some gaps in current program offerings for customers over 100 MW, the utility stated that a one-size-fits-all program offering is not feasible and ultimately committed to assessing the role of load flexibility for each new large load contract submitted to the Commission.
sources: Docket No. 55268; Docket No. 56298; Order (July 2024); Load Flexibility Compliance Report (June 2026)

description: Background: Legislation enacted in 2015 established the Community-Based Renewable Energy (CBRE) program. The Hawaii Public Utilities Commission then developed a CBRE program framework and model tariff language. The framework includes island-specific capacity additions, credit rates, project size stipulations, and time-differentiated pricing. The CBRE framework features a phased approach, where future phases will incorporate lessons learned from the first phase. Recent Action: In October 2025, HECO filed its proposed framework for a CBRE Phase 3, which is a utility-resourced model composed entirely of LMI subscribers. In doing so, HECO agreed with a 2024 assessment from the Commission that Phase 2 of the CBRE program has attracted only a fraction of the 235 MW program cap, and most developers working on projects have struggled to meet the program’s complex requirements and schedules. In its proposed model, the utility manages the systems for the program and serves as the subscriber organization. Customers could subscribe directly with the utility and all the fees and credits would be accounted for on one bill. The proposed framework does not propose specific bill credit amounts, but rather identifies that HECO needs to conduct a fresh analysis to determine appropriate subscriber credit rates for each island under a utility-resourced model, as well as a framework for application fees, meter fees, and treatment of unsubscribed energy, reflecting the utility’s new role. It also presents three options for acquiring the projects to support the program, including converting a portion of an existing as-is utility operated renewable generation facility on a leased site to a CBRE project, upgrading and converting existing renewable systems owned by the HECO companies to CBRE projects, and partnering with state government entities to develop new CBRE projects operated by the utility. In May 2026, the Commission denied HECO's proposed CBRE Phase 3 framework, arguing that the application lacked sufficient detail for the Commission to determine whether it is reasonable and in the public interest. The Commission provided a non-exhaustive list of questions to illustrate the type of details that were missing in the proposal when compared to HECO's proposals for other Phases. The order invited HECO to resubmit its application, but cautioned the utility to provide more detail.
sources: Docket No. 2015-0389; CBRE Phase 3 Proposed Framework (Oct. 2025); Order (May 2026)

description: On April 21, 2026, the Hawaii Public Utilities Commission opened a proceeding to design and implement a virtual power plant (VPP) grid-services program to improve upon the Hawaiian Electric Companies' (HECO) existing scheduled dispatch grid services programs. The Commission hopes the new program will expand new customer-sited DER adoption for all customer income levels and ultimately gather nearly all legacy and future DER into a single framework to maximize the benefits of DERs. In opening the proceeding, the Commission presented VPP program design elements it believes are better suited for Hawaii. By listing these design elements up front, the Commission hopes to expedite the development of the VPP program. As part of its proposed design elements, the Commission requires incentive adders for LMI participants; it is open to diverse proposals for appropriate incentive and compensation terms, but prefers performance-based incentives. After a technical conference was held on June 16, 2026, stakeholders submitted straw proposals outlining design parameters for a potential VPP program. Another technical conference was held on September 2, 2026.

subtopics: Performance Incentive Mechanisms; Revenue Adjustment Mechanisms
description: S.B. 2487, as enacted in June 2026, clarifies that performance-based incentives can include revenue adjustment mechanisms, cost control mechanisms, and reward and penalty mechanisms. It also authorizes the Hawaii Public Utilities Commission to adopt alternative ratemaking procedures to establish electricity rates and performance-based incentives, provided that the rates are derived from a performance‑based model for determining utility revenues. The Commission must adopt performance-based incentives by January 1, 2027.

On March 31, 2026, Idaho Power opened a new proceeding to review and determine the appropriate cost of service for new large load customers to ensure that other customer classes are not adversely affected. The petition does not propose tariff changes and does not request any specific class cost of service methodology.

On March 19, 2026, the Illinois Commerce Commission filed a final order adopting Commonwealth Edison’s (ComEd) proposed revisions to its General Terms & Conditions (GT&C), collectively designed to memorialize existing practices and create new ones to ensure that new service requests by large demand applicants and customers, "neither harm, nor unjustly shift costs to, other customers." The revisions include: using deposits or security to ensure recovery of engineering costs of large demand project applications; facilitating the procurement of long-lead materials in ways that do not place cost and risk on other consumers; memorializing utility requirements for applicant letter of credit, as well as utility practices related to transmission revenue requirements and to conducting "cluster" studies for multiple applicants in a joint process. The order adopted the transmission security agreement (TSA) provision with a modification effectively requiring the use of a TSA. On June 12, 2026, Constellation Energy filed a notice of appeal for the Illinois Appellate Court for the Third Judicial District.

On March 19, 2026, the Illinois Commerce Commission filed a final order adopting Commonwealth Edison’s (ComEd) proposed revisions to Rider DE, finding the proposed modifications to Rider DE necessary to strengthen deposit and collateral protections for new large load customers. The revisions clarified requirements and procedures for large load customers' new service requests, requesting an effective date of August 7, 2025. In its filing to the Illinois Commerce Commission, ComEd explained that the revisions were designed to help ensure that such requests, "neither harm, nor unjustly shift costs to, other customers." Revisions included deposits or security to ensure recovery of on-property distribution costs, in addition to off-property extension distribution costs; and revisions to the definition of and conditions for a letter of credit or nonrefundable payment to provide standard electric services. While applicable to all customers seeking new or expanded service, ComEd noted that for customers expected to require 50 MW or more within 10 years, the proposal included a customer deposit for utility facilities on customer premises. Applicable customers with a deposit amount of $2 million or more will be required to provide a qualifying Acceptable Letter of Credit in lieu of a deposit. On June 12, 2026, Constellation Energy filed a notice of appeal for the Illinois Appellate Court for the Third Judicial District.

On March 20, 2026, the Illinois Commerce Commission released a press release stating that the Commission intends to open an investigation into how Commonwealth Edison (ComEd) should address data center issues and cost risks, prompted by consideration of deposit protection in the case of ComEd's newly approved data center tariff. The recent decision requires the Commission to initiate an investigation to (1) examine if data centers warrant a separate tariff structure; (2) the extent to which Rider Nonstandard Service (NS) and Rider Zero Standard Service (ZSS) may need modification to function as companions to, or substitutes for, Rider Distribution System Extension (DE); (3) whether refinements to Rider DE are needed to define standard service, collateral requirements, and methods for assignment of interconnection costs to data centers; and (4) discussion of costs and benefits of infrastructure attributable to large load projects and facilities. On April 8, 2026, a Commission Staff report recommended that the Commission initiate an investigation for the purpose of identifying, examining, and potentially adopting appropriate ratepayer protections and cost recovery mechanisms to mitigate rate base impacts, allocate costs, and address affordability concerns related to large load tariffs. The report further recommended that the proceeding consider topics including cost allocation of infrastructure to serve large load customers and make ComEd a respondent. On April 23, 2026, the Commission concurred in and accepted the recommendations of the Staff report, and initiated the investigation proceeding. Several parties filed testimony between June and August 2026.

On July 10, 2026, Ameren Illinois filed proposed tariffs amending its Customer Terms and Conditions (CT&C) and Standards and Qualifications for Electric Service. Ameren cited the need for a new framework for serving large load customers and outlined goals of establishing clear requirements, ensuring that projects are committed and viable, aligning infrastructure investment with customer readiness and load commitments, and ensuring that costs and risks are appropriately borne by the customers driving those risks. The CT&C amendments define large load customers as a customer with demand greater than 100 MW and that is or will be served by a supply voltage greater than 100 kV; further, the utility outlines a queue process for large load customers and a Transmission System Interconnection Request Study Deposit of $200,0000 specific to large load customers. The utility further adds large load customers to those who may request a revenue test for system expansion and require that transmission system expansions triggered by a large load customer will be subject to provisions of an additional agreement to be filed with the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission, which shall address payment and financial security requirements for the transmission system expansion at a minimum. Additionally, Ameren outlines calculations for large load customer extensions and require that a large load customer or application requesting an extension at a voltage over 100 kV will be subject to a revenue test; large load customers served under Rate DS-4 or otherwise eligible for Rate DS-4 may be required to provide irrevocable letters of credit that last for a minimum of five years.

subtopics: Disconnection Policies; Low-Income Discount Rates; Payment Plans
description: On August 7, 2026, Ameren Illinois filed a petition in response to Public Act 104-0450, which added a new statutory provision requiring any electric or gas utility in the state with more than 100,000 customers that does not have a low-income discount in compliance with the statute to file a new or revised compliant tariff (see H.B. 4456). The new provision also directs the Illinois Commerce Commission to take into consideration the effect of the low-income discount on, and endeavor to maximize, the allocation and receipt of available federal and state energy assistance funds and provides that a utility may fund its low-income discounts through a surcharge. For electric customers, the company proposed amendments to its Rider ESDA -- Electric Service Discount Agreement as approved by the Commission in Docket 25-0083; the amendments comply with the statute and address how the company will maximum the allocation and receipt of state and federal energy assistance funds beginning with the October 2028 billing period. The revised rider states that, beginning with the October 2026 billing period, ESD participants will be placed on the company's rollover budget billing program, with budget billing amounts expected to remain consistent until annual true-up. Participants will remain on the program for 12 billing periods before recertification is required. A participant's portion of the bill is the total charges less the monthly ESD amount; that portion will be provided by the Department of Commerce and Economic Opportunity for each participant with the aim of the final bill being under 3% of the customer's total household income for non-space heating customers and 6% for space heating customers. Customers are still subject to credit collection and disconnection policies, though the company will not assess late payment charges or require new or unpaid deposits for participants in the ESD program. At the time of annual true-up, under-payment will be recovered through the Rider ESDA cost-recovery mechanism and over payment will be credited to the Rider ESDA cost-recovery mechanism up to the amount of the discount provided during the previous year with the remainder credited to the ESD participant. Beginning with the October 2028, billing period, key details remain the same outside of the billing program and true-up protocol. Rather than rollover budget billing, ESD participants with an annual energy burden greater than 3% for non-space heating and 6% for space heating will be placed on a levelized billing amount equal to the respective 3% or 6%, with levelized billing amounts expected to remain consistent until participant recertification or the relevant state agency indicates a new amount. Any overpayment identified during annual true-up will be credited to the participant.

H.B. 4456, as signed by the Governor and enacted as Public Act 104-0540 in July 2026, allows the Illinois Commerce Commission to approve a low-income discount for electric and natural gas residential customers that applies to the entirety of a qualifying customer's bills; a qualifying customer is a residential customer of a utility serving more than 100,000 customers that has a low-income discount program for residential customers (1) who been deemed eligible for assistance under LIHEAP or who receives energy assistance under the Energy Assistance Act and (2) whose household income does not exceed 300% of the federal poverty level. It further allows utilities to fund the discounts through a surcharge on both residential and non-residential customers' bills; any cost recovery mechanisms must be assessed on a fixed, per-customer basis. It further requires any electric or natural gas public utility serving more than 100,000 customers in the state that does not have a low-income discount for residential customers or that chooses to implement a low-income discount that complies with the requirements above on or after the effective date of the bill to to file a new or amended tariff within 30 days of the effective date and for the Commission to issue a final order on the tariff within 90 days of the utility's filing; if the tariff is approved the utility will implement the low-income discount within 12 months and an additional 12 months upon filing a notice with the Commission. The Commission must consider the effect of the low-income discount on, and work to maximize, the allocation and funds under LIHEAP, the Supplemental Low-Income Energy Assistance Fund under the Energy Assistance Act, or other state and federal energy assistance grants. The discount may include, but is not limited to, tiered discounts or a Percentage of Income Payment Plan (PIPP) program. The calculation of the discount will be applied after any federal or state energy assistance funds are applied to a qualifying customer's bill. Additionally, the bill stipulates that in setting the annual eligibility level for the use of state funds from the Supplemental Low-Income Energy Assistance Fund under the Energy Assistance Act, the limit may not be set higher than 300% of the federal non-farm poverty level. Finally, the bill states that beginning January 1, 2027, the Base Energy Assistance Charge will be $0.80 per month for each utility that is required to implement a low-income discount program and $0.40 per month for each utility that is not required to implement a low-income discount program and that contributes to the Supplemental Low-Income Energy Assistance Fund.

description: On March 20, 2026, MidAmerican Energy Illinois filed a proposed increase in electric rates. The proposal contains testimony addressing affordability concerns, including a low-income discount rate. MidAmerican declined to file a low-income discount rate, citing a small customer base and limited customer count, which would result in a disproportionate impact on other customers. However, MidAmerican proposed Rider PI, a phase-in adjustment rider over year one of its rate increase with the rationale of decreasing the customer affordability impacts that would have come from an immediate rate increase. As part of this general rate case, MidAmerican Energy proposed Rider EBA - Electric Balancing Adjustment to separate its revenue from its electricity sales. Rider EBA will allow the company to determine an annual adjustment under the rider, based on the difference in actual revenue and the rate case revenue amounts approved by the Illinois Commerce Commission in the most recent rate case. The EBA factor would be determined through a delivery EBA and a supply EBA, separately calculated for residential and non-residential classes. Rider EBA also includes provisions for revision of factors, annual filing of information and reconciliation sheets, an annual audit, and compliance documents. For the first billing cycle beginning April 2027, Rider EBA will be set at $0 per kWh across classes. Several parties filed testimony between June and August 2026, and a hearing is scheduled for October 13, 2026.

On July 17, 2025, Commonwealth Edison (ComEd) proposed three new tariffs: Rider BYODLR - Bring Your Own Device Load Reduction (BYODLR) Program, Rider VPP - Virtual Power Plant Program, and Rider CSS - Community Solar Plus Storage Program. These tariffs are intended to comply with the requirements of the order from Docket No. 22-0486, ComEd's Multi-Year Grid Plan docket. On November 18, 2025, ComEd filed a motion to withdraw its application. ComEd cited the Illinois legislature passing the Clean and Reliable Grid Affordability (CRGA) Act (S.B. 25) as rationale, since the CRGA Act touches on CSS and VPP program components such as device eligibility, compensation levels, and measurement of participant performance and could be cause for rider revision. ComEd intends to revise its proposals in response to the CGRA Act and additional feedback. On February 17, 2026, in line with the withdrawal order, ComEd filed a new BYODLR program, including enhanced LMI incentives, to allow load response devices while ComEd develops its VPP program, with the intention to eventually incorporate the BYODLR program into the VPP program. The proposal expands eligibility to residential retail customers with a smart thermostat or thermal storage device, and device eligibility may be expanded in the future. The event parameters for smart thermostat load reduction (STLR) include up to 184 events per year between 9 AM and 9 PM lasting no more than four hours. ComEd would provide 24-hour notice for planned events and 30-minute notice for emergency events. The compensation structure for STLR would be $30 for enrollment, with a $50 enhancement for income-eligible customers, and $30/kW for an annual performance incentive. On June 24, 2026, the Illinois Commerce Commission filed an order approving ComEd's rebuttal BYODLR proposal, including the implementation condition of ComEd making a cost-effectiveness evaluation in order for ComEd to determine whether to implement the program.

Public Act 102-0662, also known as the Climate and Equitable Jobs Act, directed the Illinois Commerce Commission to carry out a process to establish "Equitable Energy Upgrade Programs" (EEUP). On September 4, 2025, the Policy Division of the Commission's Public Utilities Bureau filed a draft strawman report on the programs. The programs are intended to provide financial savings to lower-income residents and environmental justice community residents through a Pay As You Save (PAYS) program design. Customers can make fixed monthly payments on their bill to fund projects, which are directed to initially be focused on solar-plus-storage systems in conjunction with Illinois Solar for All and Illinois Shines programs. Other eligible projects include renewable energy generation systems, demand response equipment, or any combination. Projects must pass the "80/20 test," which stipulates that the total cost to the customer for the energy project can be no more than 80% of the estimated annual savings of the project for 80% of the project’s estimated useful life. Additionally, the financial obligation is linked to the customer's electric meter location instead of the individual customer, allowing for transfer of the obligation if the owner or occupant changes. If demand exceeds capital supply, the electric utilities are directed to allocate funds such that 50% of participants are customers in neighborhoods where a majority of households make 150% or less of area median income or residents of environmental justice communities. On September 18, 2025, the Commission filed an order initiating a new proceeding to consider the draft strawman report filed to be approved as guidelines for the new utility-led EEUPs. On July 21, 2026, the ALJ filed a suggested order that would approve revised EEUP Guidelines. The revised guidelines include changes that promote cost-effectiveness screening; affirm that utilities' initial implementation plans should focus on solar and optional storage technologies; modify details on a "safe harbor" mechanism for offering energy efficiency measures; add waiver provisions for braiding funding sources; modify details of the 80/20 test and related cost recovery period details; and clarify other details related to implementers, consumer protection and education, and marketing. The suggested order also addresses eligibility, prohibiting separate income and credit checks for EEUP, and allowing EEUP eligibility for LIHEAP and percentage of income payment plan participants. It further specifies that existing assistance plans would not be applied to the entire customer bill including EEUP participant service charges.

H.B. 4514, as signed by the Governor in June 2026, requires that when any electric public utility proposes a general rate increase, the public utility must notify its customers of their right to request a public forum. A group of customers must make a written request to the Illinois Commerce Commission for the public forum, which the Commission will schedule at its discretion unless staffing or funding is inadequate for a timely convening. The public utility must, to the best of its ability, provide 30 days advance notice of the public forum to any units of local government affected by the rate increase. The day and location of the public forum will be selected to encourage the greatest public participation and reports and comments made during or as a result of the convening must be made available to hearing officials and reviewed when drafting a recommended or tentative decision, finding, or order. However, failure to comply will not affect the validity of any order entered by the Commission in a general rate proceeding.

description: On August 26, 2026, Indiana Michigan Power filed an application for a multi-year rate plan in which the utility requests approval to reduce its rates in 2027 for all customer classes other than the large load customer class. Customer Cost Allocation: Indiana Michigan Power proposed a new Industrial Power Large Load tariff to establish a separate rate class for large load customers. The tariff is the same as the provisions the utility added to its Industrial Power tariff, which the Indiana Utility Regulatory Commission previously approved. Separating large load customers into a separate class, however, will allow the utility to adjust rates specifically for them. Along with the new tariff, Indiana Michigan Power is proposing to remove the large load customer provisions from the existing Industrial Power tariff. Utility Business Model: The application also includes a customer affordability performance metric and a customer affordability performance incentive mechanism (PIM), as well as a service restoration performance metric and a service restoration PIM. The customer affordability PIM will be calculated based on the five-year period of data of 2022 through 2026, and the service restoration PIM will be calculated based on the six-year period of data of 2021 through 2026. Utility Oversight and Cost Recovery: Additionally, the application includes a new Reduce and Freeze (RAF) Mechanism, which will be used to reduce certain rates in 2027 and support rate stabilization for all customers in 2028 and 2029.

S.B. 422, enacted in March 2025, requires the Indiana Utility Regulatory Commission to conduct a study to evaluate the potential use or deployment of advanced transmission technologies (ATTs) by public utilities to enable them to safely, reliably, efficiently, and cost effectively meet electric system demand; and provide safe, reliable, and affordable electric utility service to customers. The Commission should evaluate attributes, functions, costs, and benefits of various ATTs, including grid-enhancing technologies and advanced conductors. The report that includes the Commission's findings is due October 1, 2026. The Commission entered into a contract with Electric Power Engineers, who will be drafting the study report. The Commission provided utilities, stakeholders, and the RTO with a series of questions to inform the study, and requested responses by June 3, 2026. The Commission then held a virtual stakeholder meeting on July 10, 2026.
sources: IURC Advanced Transmission Technologies Study Website; S.B. 422 (2025)

description: On March 24, 2026, the Indiana Utility Regulatory Commission held an investigative inquiry on energy affordability, with the state's five largest investor-owned utilities providing presentations and answering Commission questions. The Commission notes that this is the first phase of a larger strategy that it will lead to better understand the drivers behind energy affordability and identify short- and long-term solutions. The second phase of this process was hearing directly from customers through community listening sessions across the state, which were held during March and April 2026. On July 14, 2026, the Commission released its Energy Affordability Report, including several action items arising from its investigation. The report contains 16 energy affordability action items in total. Four of these action items are for the Commission itself: (1) launch a return on equity investigation; (2) launch an investigation on trackers (periodic rate adjustment mechanisms); (3) develop recommended future performance incentive mechanisms; and (4) provide guidance on transmission, distribution, and storage system improvement charge implementation standards. Five of the actions items are for the state's large investor-owned electric utilities: (1) double the amount of investment in customer assistance programs using shareholder dollars; (2) evaluate energy efficiency program effectiveness and improve coordination with the HOMES and HEAR programs for more impactful investment; (3) meet local economic development needs by improving cost-effective planning; (4) improve customer care by increasing communications and transparency around rates and charges; and (5) communicate ratepayer relief by helping customers understand how utility investments to serve new large customers can provide broader savings. Four of the action items are for the Indiana Office of Energy Development (OED): (1) coordinate all affordability and energy efficiency programs under the OED so that consumers have a single point of contact; (2) expand the use of the Indiana Energy Saver Program; (3) build capacity and enable efficiencies so that the OED can move at the pace of business; and (4) secure federal funding for energy infrastructure, including investing in existing and new generation, transmission, and distribution resources. Additionally, there are three action items for consideration by the Indiana General Assembly: (1) evaluate whether to repeal the sales tax on utility bills; (2) increase oversight on utility ownership by allowing the Commission to oversee utility mergers and acquisitions at the holding company level (currently, their oversight is limited to ownership mergers involving asset purchases by regulated utilities); and (3) mandate RTO participation so that the 0.5% return on equity adder for voluntary participation may be removed.
sources: Investigative Inquiry on Energy Affordability; IURC Energy Affordability Report (July 2026)

description: Executive Order 25-66, issued by the Governor of Indiana in June 2025, creates a Strategic Energy Growth Task Force to oversee development of a State Energy Growth Plan. The plan will focus on energy reliability and affordability to meet power needs. The plan has four objectives: (1) energy development to meet current and future demand; (2) energy affordability for all Hoosiers; (3) energy diversity through an "all-of-the-above" approach to energy policy; and (4) energy collaboration and innovation between state and industry to deploy technology to meet the unique opportunities that lie ahead with unprecedented demand and development. The full plan is due by May 29, 2026. The Task Force provided the Governor with an interim report in December 2025, describing the meetings held by the Task Force in 2025. The Task Force continued to meet in February, March, April, and July 2026. As of September 2026, the final report is not publicly available.

The Commission hosted a technical conference on August 7, 2026, to discuss the specific issues to be addressed in the investigation. Later in the month, parties filed suggestions for the issues to be included in the investigation.

description: On July 15, 2026, the Indiana Utility Regulatory Commission opened a new proceeding to investigate the changes in risks to an electricity supplier and its customers as a result of implementing a multi-year rate plan (MYRP), which will impact the authorized return on equity for the supplier. The Commission hosted a technical conference on August 7, 2026, to discuss the specific issues to be addressed in the investigation. On August 6, 2026, Governor Beshear signed an executive order aimed at protecting ratepayers from cost shifts associated with data center development. Two of the provisions of the order address energy affordability directly. The order requires that data center developers be required to submit energy plans to the Kentucky Energy and Environment Cabinet, with assurances of meeting energy needs now and in the future without imposing additional costs. The order also directs the Kentucky Public Service Commission to reject utility rate increases that would recover costs associated with the development and operation of data centers.

description: Customer Cost Allocation: On May 30, 2025, Kentucky Utilities filed a rate case application including a request for approval of a new Extremely High Load Factor (EHLF) Service tariff for customers with a contract capacity greater than 100 MVA and an expected load factor above 85%. It requires a 15-year contract period, though the initial contract term, load ramp, load ramp period, contract capacity, and other terms of service will be prescribed in the electric service agreement executed between the customer and the utility. The tariff also includes provisions related to financial assurances required of the customer and ways the contract may be modified. Kentucky Utilities and Louisville Gas & Electric filed a stipulation in October 2025, in which the utilities agreed to modify the proposed tariff to reduce the minimum contract capacity to 50 MVA, clarify that it applies only to new customers, and clarify that customers cannot circumvent the minimum capacity threshold by siting multiple smaller facilities. The Kentucky Public Service Commission issued its final order in February 2026, approving the new EHLF tariff as amended by the stipulation. Utility Oversight and Cost Recovery: The October 2025 stipulation also included proposals for two adjustment clauses that Kentucky Utilities and Louisville Gas & Electric claim would benefit consumers, as well as updates to the utilities' return on equity. The mechanisms, a Pilot Generation Recovery adjustment clause (PGR) and a Sharing Mechanism adjustment clause (SM) would, respectively, allow the utility to recover costs associated with specific new generation projects during the next ten month period and allow the utility to recover or distribute additional revenue if its earnings fall outside of a band of 9.4% to 10.15% return on equity. In its February 2026 order, the Commission approved adjustment clause PGR, which would likely increase customer bills but allow the utility to more easily build new generation, but did not approve adjustment clause SM, noting that the utilities did not provide appropriate evidence that the latter adjustment clause would benefit customers. The order also set the utilities' return on equity to 9.775, lower than the requested 9.90. On March 11, 2026, the utilities filed a motion for reconsideration, asking the Commission to consider approval of the adjustment clause SM, changing the cost estimate mechanisms for adjustment clause PGR, and raising the return on equity back to 9.90, but making no requests of changes to the Very High Load Factor tariff. In an August 14, 2026 order, the Commission granted the utilities' request for reconsideration of adjustment clause PGR, but did not for adjustment clause SM or the return on equity.

On August 14, 2026, Duke Energy Kentucky filed an application to amend its demand-side management programs. Specifically, the utility proposed to invest an additional $163,800 in its Income Qualified Neighborhood Energy Saver program, which offers energy efficiency technologies, appliances, upgrades, and retrofits to residential customers in Duke Energy Kentucky's territory.

On August 26, 2026, the Kentucky Public Service Commission opened a proceeding to investigate general electricity and gas affordability issues, to which all regulated electric and gas utilities will be a party. The investigation should consider: (1) the nature and extent of electric and natural gas utility affordability concerns in Kentucky and the appropriate data and measures for evaluating affordability; (2) the factors contributing to affordability challenges, including customer income, electricity and natural gas prices and usage, housing characteristics, rate design and cost allocation, utility investment and operating costs, and other relevant factors; (3) existing Commission regulations, electric and natural gas utility tariff provisions, customer protection measures, utility payment programs and practices, outside assistance programs, and other measures intended to help customers maintain electric and natural gas utility service; (4) strategies to reduce payment delinquencies and disconnections and to promote consistent access to electric and natural gas utility services; (5) disconnection policies, including fees and penalties related to reconnection of service and minimum arrears for disconnection of service; (6) the role of rate design, cost allocation, financial assistance programs, and other regulatory and non-regulatory measures in addressing electric and natural gas utility affordability; (7) the financial and operational impact on jurisdictional electric and gas utilities of affordability measures, and of customer arrearages, debt write-offs, disconnects, and reconnects; (8) differences among electric and natural gas utility business models, geographic areas, customer populations, and other circumstances that may affect the feasibility or effectiveness of potential measures; (9) potential measures that may be implemented by jurisdictional electric and natural gas utilities, legislation, and other policies that may enhance the affordability of utility bills and reduce the number of delinquencies and disconnections; (10) the relative contribution of energy consumption, fixed customer charges, fuel costs, riders and adjustment mechanisms, taxes, and other bill components to overall customer bills; (11) the effectiveness, accessibility, and cost-effectiveness of demand-side management (DSM) programs (e.g., energy efficiency, demand response, and weatherization) in reducing customer energy consumption, lowering utility bills, improving affordability, increasing customers’ ability to manage their energy usage, appropriately incentivizing or compensating customers for actions that provide broader system benefits, and achieving long-term benefits; (12) the impact of housing age, housing condition, home size, existing home energy efficiency, heating fuel type, number of occupants and occupancy status (owner versus renter), and local climate on utility affordability; (13) the relationship between affordability and utility investments is needed to maintain safe, adequate, reliable, and resilient service, including infrastructure replacement and long-term system planning; (14) opportunities for better and enhanced coordination among utilities, state agencies, community action agencies, consumer advocates, and other organizations to improve customer outreach and assistance; (15) whether additional reporting requirements or standardized data collection would improve the Commission's ability to monitor affordability over time, including annual reporting of arrearages, disconnections, payment arrangements, assistance program participation, and customer demographics where appropriate; and (16) the potential effects of renewable energy resources, including solar and wind, and related technologies such as energy storage on long-term affordability, including whether pilot programs or incentives involving customer-sited renewable generation, storage, or time-varying rates could lower customer bills, reduce peak demand, and provide broader system benefits. Interested parties will have until September 30, 2026 to file comments.

On July 2, 2026, the Kentucky Public Service Commission opened an investigation into management and operations at Kentucky Power. The Commission and Attorney General have raised numerous concerns about the judgment of investment, managerial, and operational decisions made by Kentucky Power, including some in its most recent rate case from 2025. The Commission highlights Kentucky Power's failure to provide thorough and rigorous analysis of its large financial decisions, potentially passing on unnecessary cost to consumers.
sources: Docket No. 2026-00159; Order Initiating Management Audit (July 2026)

description: On May 6, 2026, the Louisiana Public Service Commission initiated a repository docket to receive comments regarding its Large Load Additions Non-Binding Guidelines adopted in February 2026. The guidelines illustrate how utilities can seek to add large new loads to their systems to comprehensively address 12 areas of concern. First, utilities should clearly define the load's characteristics -- maximum demand, energy consumption, load factor, and ramp schedule -- and evaluate how it behaves under peak, seasonal, and stress conditions. They should then demonstrate adequate resource capacity and transmission infrastructure to serve the load reliably, ensuring that any interconnection or network costs are borne by the new load rather than shifted to existing customers, and that queue treatment remains fair. The guidelines also include protections against stranded assets if the load departs early, including financial guarantees so ratepayers aren't left covering unused generation. Rate design should fully recover costs attributable to the new load without cross-subsidizing it through existing customers' rates. Utilities need retained operational control, including enforceable curtailment rights during emergencies, and should mitigate the load's effects on power quality, frequency regulation, and voltage support at the load's own expense. Fuel supply adequacy, coordinated load ramp-up with enforceable milestones, and broader impacts on resource adequacy, capacity markets, and system planning should all be assessed. Finally, utilities should address environmental and local impacts with appropriate cost assignment, and commit to ongoing reporting on contract compliance, forecast accuracy, infrastructure status, and cost recovery performance. Parties filed comments in June 2026. SWEPCO stated that protecting existing customers requires large load bills to include minimum billing demands (in MW) -- the greater of the actual rate schedule billing demand or 90 percent of contracted capacity -- and recommended a 75 MW minimum threshold (as used in Texas under its Electric Service Large-Load Contract proposal), longer minimum contract terms, collateral equal to 24 times the customer's previous maximum monthly bill (or at least an exit fee), and a five-year exit notice period. Cleco supported the Commission's approach, noting that the Guidelines appropriately balance the issue with flexibility for case-specific circumstances, including Commission approval where needed. In Cleco's view, subjecting a new customer paying its fair share under an Commission-approved rate schedule to first-to-curtail risk would violate the regulatory compact's non-discrimination obligation and discourage investment, while granting such a customer preferential protection would be equally discriminatory and unfair to existing firm-rate customers. Entergy Louisiana opposed a uniform size threshold for defining a large load, proposing instead a contextual framework considering: (1) load location and system context, which may matter as much as load size; (2) utility size, since what counts as "large" varies by utility given differences in resources and load forecast uncertainty; and (3) the serving utility's current system capacity and ability to dispatch adequate capacity for the new load alongside existing load. The utility cautioned against policies that subject large loads to priority curtailment based on size alone.
sources: Docket No.  X-37921; Large Load Additions Non-Binding Guidelines (Feb. 2026)

description: Executive Order 26-058, signed in late June 2026, directed the Secretary of Louisiana Economic Development (LED) to create a "Ratepayer and Community Protection Framework" that data centers and other large-load, power-intensive projects must satisfy to qualify for -- or continue receiving -- the state's Data Center Sales and Use Tax Exemption and related incentives. Before any project can be approved or continue participating, the Secretary must confirm, in coordination with relevant state agencies, that the project's demands on the state's water, electric generation and transmission capacity, land, and other natural resources have been evaluated and balanced against its benefits to the state, and that contractual agreements include conditions ensuring compliance. The Framework itself must require participating companies to commit to eight areas: (1) fully funding the incremental generation, transmission, and infrastructure investments their projects require, so costs aren't shifted to existing residential and commercial ratepayers; (2) investing upfront in grid resiliency and long-term reliability through infrastructure contributions and coordinated transmission planning; (3) supporting local communities and workforce development through job creation and partnerships with Louisiana universities, community colleges, and workforce programs; (4) contributing meaningfully to local tax bases through property and infrastructure investments that support schools, healthcare, roads, drainage, and public services; (5) operating responsibly with natural resources by applying best-in-class water and energy efficiency standards; (6) advancing broader community investment through support for nonprofits, digital literacy, STEM education, and AI training initiatives; (7) strengthening Louisiana's innovation economy by engaging with the state's startup ecosystem through accelerators, incubators, venture programs, cloud credits, or technical mentorship; and (8) maintaining transparency and accountability through regulatory oversight, construction monitoring, and performance obligations. As a condition of eligibility, each company must submit a formal, detailed attestation to LED outlining how it will comply with these requirements. In developing the Framework, the Secretary and LED must coordinate with a list of named state entities -- including the Public Service Commission, Department of Conservation and Energy, Department of Environmental Quality, Department of Revenue, Louisiana Workforce Commission, Board of Regents, Louisiana Community and Technical College System, Division of Administration, and affected local governments -- following a "Whole-of-Louisiana" approach. The Secretary must present the proposed criteria and Framework to the Governor within 90 days of the order's effective date, and upon approval, must implement, administer, and periodically report on the Framework and the commitments secured from participating companies.

Massachusetts Governor Healey unveiled a Statement of Expectations for Responsible Data Center Development and Operations in Massachusetts for responsible data center development, published June 25, 2026. It sets expectations for data centers -- particularly those seeking state sales and use tax exemptions -- to bring their own clean energy (meeting 100% of demand), avoid shifting infrastructure or grid costs onto other ratepayers, minimize air and water impacts on host communities, follow strong labor practices including project labor agreements, and engage transparently with local communities. The framework covers eight key areas: clean energy supply, grid efficiency, air quality, water use, labor, community benefits, local economic development, and public transparency. While it doesn't replace existing permitting and regulatory requirements, it's meant to guide state agencies, municipalities, and the Massachusetts Department of Public Utilities in evaluating data center proposals -- with the goal of allowing Massachusetts to capture the economic benefits of data center growth without burdening residents, communities, or the energy grid.
sources: Statement of Expectations for Responsible Data Center Development and Operations in MA (June 2026)

description: Background: In January 2024, the Massachusetts Department of Public Utilities (DPU) launched an inquiry into innovative solutions to address energy affordability for residential ratepayers, with a focus on tiered discount rates (TDR) and percentage-of-income payment plans (PIPPs). In September 2024, the DPU issued an interlocutory order outlining areas of consensus from the comment period. These included capping energy burden at 6% of household income, basing eligibility on household income and size, extending the program to both heating and non-heating customers, and ensuring that customers in arrears remain eligible. The order also emphasized outreach to environmental justice communities and extended disconnection protections to periods of extreme heat and poor air quality. Based on these findings, the DPU decided to focus the inquiry on developing tiered discount rates rather than PIPPs, with costs to be recovered through utility-specific residential assistance adjustment factors (RAAF). Several questions remain open, including the specific design of the TDR program, enrollment and verification processes, arrearage management, and disconnection policies for nonpayment. Recent Action: On May 16, 2025, the DPU initiated the Phase II stakeholder working group to discuss the aforementioned areas of inquiry. On February 17, 2026, the DPU issued an order regarding the TDR, establishing a low-income discount rate framework based on its stakeholder inquiry process. In the order, the DPU directed utilities to implement a six-tier rate on a statewide basis to avoid creating separate frameworks for each utility, thereby increasing efficiency and reducing administrative challenges. The rates should include the following tiers: households earning up to 100% of the Federal Poverty Level (FPL); households earning 100-125% of the FPL; households earning 125-150% of the FPL; households earning 150-175% of the FPL; households earning 175-200% of the FPL; and households earning greater than 200% of the FPL and up to 60% of the State Median Income. Each utility must implement the new rate framework by November 1, 2026, and cease charging low-income discount customers for RAAF. The model also assumed a six-tier structure consistent with those used by the state’s Home Energy Assistance Program (HEAP), and the DPU intends to reassess these tiers in the future. In terms of the actual measured discounts, utilities must develop discounts for the lowest tier that achieve a 4% total energy burden and a 2% electric energy burden; the other tiers should achieve a 6% total energy burden and 3% electric energy burden. Recognizing that this approach could result in no discount for some customers in the highest tiers, there would also be a discount floor of 25% for electric customers. In addition, although the DPU has not yet commenced the moderate-income discount rulemaking, the information gathered thus far will inform that proceeding, including determinations regarding how to define eligible moderate-income customers and how to recover the associated revenue shortfall. As part of that rulemaking, the DPU will also consider the appropriate framework for determining discount levels for eligible moderate-income customers. In May 2026, Eversource and Unitil filed revised compliance filings, illustrating their proposed TDR ranges. Eversource proposed a discount range of 25% to 89% for customers within the aforementioned FPL ranges ordered by the DPU, and Unitil proposed a range of 44% to 93%. The Attorney General also released an LDR rate process report on May 14, 2026, highlighting key points of consensus and disagreement related to the TDR design. Misalignment was noted when it came to self-attestation of proof for TDR eligibility from households, automatic enrollment based on state/federal affordable housing addresses, and pairing TDR enrollment periods with HEAP. The DPU filed a Phase II order on June 30, 2026, directing Eversource, National Grid, and Unitil to continue enrolling customers into the income-eligible discount rate who can provide proof of receipt of an eligible benefit, including when the applicable benefit card does include a starting or expiration date. The order details specific implementation requirements for the new rates, which will be put into effect beginning November 1, 2026. The distribution utilities jointly filed a motion for reconsideration (or in the alternative, clarification) on three issues: (1) translation of certain materials, (2) certain changes to the utilities' websites to promote accessibility, and (3) the self-attestation pathway for enrollment in tiered discount rates. The DPU denied the request for reconsideration and affirmed its findings on the importance of language translation and accessibility guidelines to ensure broad uptake. The DPU did, however, suspend the timeline of completing the translation and accessibility upgrades, finding that these do not need to be completed by November 1st so that the utilities can focus on activities essential to implementing the new rates. The DPU also found that further consideration of the self-attestation pathway is necessary and will hold a technical conference to discuss the issue. The marketing, education, and outreach co-chairs filed a report on August 10, 2026, identifying points of consensus, emerging alignment, and opportunities. A workshop was also scheduled for September 16, 2026 to discuss the development of marketing, education, and outreach materials for the income-eligible discount rates.
