description: S. 3166 (the Senate's version of H. 5175, which was passed by the House in February 2026) was passed by the Senate in early July 2026. The bill has been sent to conference committee to reconcile the House and Senate versions of the bill. Customer Cost Allocation: The bill mandates discounted utility rates for low-income customers at or below 200% of the federal poverty level and for moderate-income customers, funded through a non-bypassable charge on non-discount rate eligible customers with proactive outreach and auto-enrollment requirements. It creates an optional statewide energy storage incentive program for distribution-connected storage promoting market stability and ratepayer cost sharing, and allows municipalities by vote to ban third-party competitive electricity suppliers from signing or renewing residential retail contracts, enforceable by the Attorney General. The bill also extends existing winter disconnection protections for hardship customers to summer heat waves (when it is 85 degrees or higher for three days) during May 15 - September 15. Additionally, the bill requires 70% of alternative compliance payments associated with the state's renewable portfolio standard, alternative energy portfolio standard, and clean peak standard to be returned to ratepayers as annual bill credits until July 1, 2029. Beginning July 1, 2029, this will be required in years where fund balances exceed predicted levels by 2% and energy costs are a substantial burden to residents. The bill also makes significant changes to the state's net metering statutes. It removes certain T&D kWh charges from the monthly credit calculations for Class I, II, III, market, and neighborhood net metering, effectively reducing the overall value of credits for those facilities. It establishes a new "supply rate net metering facility" classification for Class I, II, III, and neighborhood net metering systems that file interconnection applications after May 13, 2025, and are authorized to interconnect on or after January 1, 2026. These newer facilities would receive a narrower credit based on the net default service rate minus RPS compliance costs, rather than the broader credit structure available to existing facilities. The bill also extends net metering treatment to low-income multifamily housing projects located in zoning districts compliant for purposes of the single-parcel aggregation rules governing net metering eligibility. The bill changes Mass Save to a statewide building decarbonization and energy efficiency plan run jointly by electric utilities and municipal aggregators, effective January 1, 2028. Administration and planning for the program are capped at 5% of spending and at least 20% of funds would be required to go to low-income customers. Incentives for new equipment utilizing fossil fuels would no longer be allowed, with certain exceptions including low-income households. A new independent board would also review Mass Save's management, budgets, and spending controls until 2031. Customer Cost-Saving Programs: The bill directs the Massachusetts Department of Energy Resources (DOER) to develop a statewide solar incentive program featuring adjustable block incentives or competitive procurement mechanisms. The program would allow the environmental attributes of participating solar PV facilities to be used by retail electric suppliers toward their compliance obligations under the RPS and Clean Peak Standard, as applicable. The bill also specifies that the program administrators of the approved three-year energy efficiency investment plan are not to require household income verification for low-income eligible customers and renters. Income verification will remain in place for moderate-income rebates and incentives. Moreover, to make clean energy upgrades more accessible to residents, the bill directs utilities to develop inclusive utility investment programs providing on-bill financing -- with no upfront cost -- for heat pumps, solar, storage, energy efficiency, and demand response equipment. The programs would be open to both homeowners and renters with landlord permission, must deliver immediate bill savings, and must be accessible to LMI customers. The Massachusetts Department of Public Utilities (DPU) must issue program design parameters by October 2027, utilities must submit proposals by February 2028, the DPU must complete its review by November 2028, and programs must be available to customers by April 2029. The bill also creates a working group tasked with making residential solar more affordable by producing a plain-English comparative analysis of the costs and benefits of different ways consumers can access solar (ownership, power purchase agreements, leasing, and community solar), while also evaluating whether performance guarantees are financially meaningful and enforceable. It will further examine whether consumers should be compensated when systems fail or underperform, how supply chain issues drive up installation and repair costs, and whether existing consumer remedies are adequate -- all aimed at protecting consumers from bearing unexpected costs over a system's lifetime. The group must also assess the financial implications for consumers whose solar systems are folded into virtual power plant operations, with a final report and recommendations due to state leaders by January 31, 2028. Planning and Procurement: The bill authorizes utilities to issue low-cost "rate reduction bonds" to finance grid modernization, gas transition expenses, and storm costs through 2036, as long as the DPU finds that the bonds lower costs for ratepayers. The DOER is also directed to publish resource solicitation plans and competitively procure long-term contracts of up to 30 years for clean energy attributes and energy services, mandating at least 10 GW each of offshore wind and solar capacity by December 31, 2040. To accelerate offshore wind development specifically, the bill creates a state co-investment program enabling DOER to partner with developers on pre-development activities -- including permitting studies, cable route surveys, and engineering work — with a mechanism to recover any state co-investment capital upon a project reaching commercial operation. Complementing these procurement efforts, the bill automatically extends by four years all permits and approvals in effect between January 1, 2025 and January 1, 2029 for large clean transmission infrastructure facilities or offshore wind projects, shielding projects from permit expiration during the current period of federal uncertainty. The bill also updates the definition of "large clean transmission and distribution infrastructure facility" to include offshore wind interconnection and grid reliability upgrades, while explicitly excluding facilities serving only fossil fuel generation after January 1, 2026. Agreements for leasing distribution or transmission asset entitlements between a distribution utility and a non-utility third party may permit the third party to sublease those entitlements to the utility’s projects, provided each lease includes the following protections: a binding commitment to contribute a share of annual after-tax profits derived from ratepayer use of the entitlements to charitable purposes. Finally, the bill creates another working group on sustainable economic development zones, co-chaired by the Secretaries of Environmental Affairs and Economic Development and to be convened within 60 days, tasked with identifying barriers to connecting new electric customers for economic development and housing purposes and developing recommendations for accelerating clean energy infrastructure in target areas -- including affordable housing and life sciences and data center development -- while avoiding fossil fuel infrastructure and cost-shifting to other ratepayers. Recommendations are due to the legislature and the DPU within 10 months, and DPU must act on them within 210 days of receipt. Building on that framework, the bill directs the DPU to establish by July 1, 2028 a comprehensive distribution system planning and cost recovery framework that consolidates rate cases and modernization plans, and requires electric utilities to submit grid utilization metrics and performance assessments by December 2027. By July 1, 2028, the DPU must approve electric grid utilization metrics that, where appropriate, explain how they may inform its review of utility cost recovery requests for capital investments, set a timeline for each electric company to increase grid utilization accordingly, and direct how each company can improve grid performance through virtual power plants (VPPs) and NWAs -- including energy storage, customer-owned and customer-financed capacity resources, VPPs, flexible interconnection, and advanced transmission and grid enhancement technologies. Each year, the DPU's annual report must include its findings on each company's assessment of, and performance against, these metrics, analyze each company's potential to further increase utilization through the same VPPs and NWAs, and may request any information needed from a company to complete that evaluation. Electric companies are directed to propose earnings sharing or other mechanisms that provide companies with a return on investments in load management and reduction, VPPs, and NWAs. Regarding interconnection, the bill requires each distribution company to offer a flexible interconnection program enabling new loads and DERs to connect under agreed curtailment protocols, with DPU issuing implementation guidance within three months, utilities filing proposed tariffs within six months of that guidance, and DPU acting within one year of the act or six months of filing, whichever is later. To further reduce developer burdens, DPU must also open a proceeding within three months to consider whether utilities must accept non-cash financial securities such as surety bonds or letters of credit in lieu of cash deposits for interconnection costs, with a final order due within nine months. Electric utilities and the DOER must additionally develop a single unified application for interconnection, net metering, and solar incentive program participation, with the joint proposal due to DPU within nine months and the common application available within 24 months. The bill also allows government entities to distribute clean energy across public rights-of-way through microgrids serving government properties or critical facilities such as hospitals and emergency shelters, without being classified as a utility. DPU must open an investigation into the microgrid framework within 120 days, issue guidelines within six months, and approve model tariffs within one year, with tariffs taking effect within 14 months of the bill's enactment. The bill separately directs DPU to oversee coordinated gas-electric integrated energy planning to reduce stranded asset risk, avoid unnecessary infrastructure investment, and align utility planning with the state's greenhouse gas limits. Studies and Investigations: The DPU is required to investigate best practices for setting allowed rates of return on common equity for electric and local distribution companies. The DPU is to ensure that rates of return preserve the company's financial integrity and reasonably allow the company to attract capital. The DPU is also to consider how other regulatory mechanisms, such as performance-based mechanisms, can modify return on equity. The DPU is to submit a report and any draft legislation by October 1, 2027. Utility Oversight and Cost Recovery: The bill requires management and operations audits of electric distribution companies once every three years by DPU staff or an independent auditor. Supplemental audits may be ordered on specific aspects of operations and performance as necessary. Audited companies are to submit a plan to to implement the DPU's findings, and the DPU may issue penalties for non-compliance with an approved plan. Upon a request by an electric distribution company for a general rate increase or to make capital improvements, the DPU is to review the company's compliance with the directions and recommendations made previously by the DPU as a result of the most recently completed management and operations audit. The bill would prohibit utilities from charging customers for promotional or political advertising, lobbying, trade association dues, charitable giving, political contributions, or executive travel and aircraft. The bill also requires the DPU to create a real-time online dashboard showing a visual breakdown of the components of residential utility bills, including explanations of each charge. The dashboard is also to quantify the benefits of clean energy, energy efficiency, and demand response programs.

On June 2, 2025, the Massachusetts Department of Public Utilities (DPU) opened an investigation into the use of advanced conductors, grid-enhancing technologies (GETs), and other advanced transmission technologies (ATTs) to improve the performance of the state’s transmission system in areas under federal jurisdiction. On September 25, 2025, the Advanced Transmission Solutions Report was filed, outlining federal and state policies, market trends, and key grid-enhancing technologies (GETs), including dynamic line rating (DLR), advanced power flow control (APFC), advanced conductors, and energy storage. In February 2026, the Hearing Officer filed a memorandum seeking additional information regarding utilities' compliance with a requirement to conduct a cost-effectiveness and timetable analysis of the emerging grid solutions, as well as plans to develop performance incentive mechanisms to deploy ATTs.
sources: Docket No. 25-69; Advanced Transmission Solutions Report (Sept. 2025)

description: On December 15, 2025, the Massachusetts Department of Public Utilities (DPU) opened an investigation to conduct a comprehensive review of gas and electric delivery rates and charges, aiming to contain customer costs, reduce bill volatility, and increase bill transparency. Specifically, through Phase I of the proceeding, the DPU is focusing on: (1) identifying electric and gas reconciling mechanisms that can be eliminated or included in base distribution rates going forward, (2) determining whether certain electric and gas reconciling mechanism costs should be collected from customers through fixed charges rather than volumetric charges, (3) determining whether certain electric reconciling mechanisms should be included in utilities' annual retail rate filings fore review and approval rather than filed in separate dockets, (4) determining how the value of net metering credits and bill impacts to electric customers in the state compare to similar programs in other jurisdictions and whether the value of these credits should be adjusted, and (5) determining the feasibility of creating a maximum threshold for the amount that charges assessed to customers may change from one month to another. Phase II of the proceeding will focus on utility bill redesign to improve customer knowledge, agency, and responsiveness to price and policy signals. The DPU requested that utilities file reports with specific information related to the Phase I topics. The DPU also accepted comments through March 31, 2026 and held a technical conference in early April 2026. On June 26, 2026, the Hearing Officer issued a memorandum providing an update and next steps for the investigation. The Hearing Officer noted that further guidance reconciling mechanisms will be provided at a future date, the DPU will seek additional input on the net metering issues, and the DPU will investigate in a later phase of the proceeding the feasibility of creating a maximum threshold for the amount that charges assessed to customers may change from month to month. The memorandum requests that electric distribution companies submit proposals for a reporting template for rate changes by July 15, 2026. The DPU later scheduled a technical conference on the net metering credit issues for October 15, 2026.

In June 2026, the Maryland Public Service Commission filed a notice convening a public conference to implement the Utility RELIEF Act's (H.B. 1532) requirement that $1,000,000 from the Strategic Energy Investment Fund be credited or funded to residential electric customers via their electric companies to offset charges associated with EmPOWER Maryland, the state's utility energy efficiency program. The Commission directed utilities to file proposed implementation plans for the credit or refund. The Act further requires that the Commission determine which commercial companies use a master meter for multi-occupancy residences, the estimated energy use by those customers, and the number of multi-occupancy residential dwelling units served by each master meter. If such information is available, the Commission may require that the master meter customers receive a pro rata share of certain residential grant funds authorized by the Act for the master meter customers to then distribute to residential accounts behind their master meter. On August 14, 2026, the utilities filed their credit implementation plans. Potomac Edison planned to take the amount allocated to the company and apply it based on a projection of 2027 residential customer numbers as an equal monthly bill credit from January 1, 2027 through December 31, 2027 and to establish a true-up mechanism. Baltimore Gas & Electric, Delmarva Power & Light, and Pepco (collectively, the Exelon utilities) planned to apply the funds as a reduction to the Operations & Management (O&M) expense in their existing EmPOWER surcharge with an existing true-up process; the Exelon utilities recommended against an equal monthly bill credit approach.

On June 26, 2025, in compliance with the "Next Generation Energy Act" or H.B. 1035 of 2025, the Maryland Public Service Commission initiated a new public conference and formed a work group to investigate regulations regarding large load customers and utility tariffs. The Commission is required to adopt regulations which will (1) establish notice requirements, deadlines, and contract requirements related to large load customer study requests; (2) if necessary, specify common forms of acceptable financial surety or collateral to meet requirements; and (3) establish study deadlines and fees. Final regulations must be adopted by June 1, 2026. Further, investor-owned utilities and cooperatives are required to submit to the Commission a rate schedule for electric large loads by September 1, 2026. On December 8, 2025, the Commission Technical Staff filed a request that the Commission open a rulemaking to consider the proposed regulations required as outlined above. On December 9, 2025, the Commission initiated Rulemaking 93 to consider the proposed regulations. On February 4, 2026, the Commission moved to publish the subtitle 20.96 Large Load Customers in the Maryland Register for comment. The regulations were published for comment in the Maryland Register on June 26, 2026; in an August 18, 2026 rulemaking session, the Commission moved to adopt the new chapter and regulations as published. They outline a load study request, load study agreement and payment, contract terms that largely defer to the relevant electric utility, a minimum notice of one year for contract termination or modification, and forms of collateral that utilities may require. On July 13, 2026, the Commission filed a request for comments surrounding capacity procurement for large loads and corresponding cost allocation. The Commission anticipates that PJM will hold a backstop capacity procurement coming out of its Reliability Backstop Procurement Critical Issue Fast Path proposal and expressed concern that the anticipated auction and other PJM auctions may occur before the tariffs under development are resolved. Accordingly, the Commission directed utilities to provide information identifying risks and assurances that load will materialize; how capacity procured through PJM auctions will be allocated among customer classes, how procurement costs will be allocated, and how they will ensure that large loads pay for capacity procurement costs; and recommended measures the Commission may take surrounding capacity procurement before the tariffs are resolved. On August 20, 2026, the Commission filed a request for utilities to provide further data surrounding large load projects and collateral. On September 1, 2026, the electric utilities, Baltimore Gas & Electric (BGE), Delmarva Power & Light (Delmarva), Potomac Electric Power Company (Pepco), and Potomac Edison (PE) filed their proposed large load tariffs in alignment with H.B. 1035 (2025) and H.B. 1532 (2026); statute defines large load customers to have a demand of 25 MW or greater and load factor of 60% or greater. BGE, Delmarva, and Pepco jointly filed their proposals as the Exelon utilities, proposing substantially similar new service classifications and service rules for large load customers. Across the Exelon utilities, tariffs require a ramp period of ten years and a minimum initial contract term of five years; a minimum billing demand of 75% of contract capacity for customers 25 MW-49 MW and 85% for customers 49 MW+; financial assurances such as instruments to cover study costs and costs for long lead time equipment, distribution service agreements, transmission service agreements, and contribution in aid of construction; and exit notices and fees. PE's tariff requires a minimum contract term of ten years and a load ramp of up to four years; a minimum bill of 85% of contract capacity; financial assurances including collateral requirements for the cost of new facilities and study costs; and exit notices and fees.
sources: Public Conference No. 72; Rulemaking No. 93; H.B. 1035 (2025); Regulations (Maryland Register June 2026)

description: On October 1, 2025, Public Conference 59's Work Group on Energy Burdens filed a report on a proposed Limited Income Mechanism (LIM) for Utility Customers. On February 12, 2026, the Maryland Public Service Commission filed an order approving utilities' ability to develop systems to provide discounted rates to limited-income customers, approving the general design of the proposed LIM, and approving Phase II of the Work Group; utilities will need to update their billing systems, marketing materials, and tariffs accordingly by January 1, 2027. The Commission also approved the tiered discount mechanism program design, which will categorize customers based on the Office of Home Energy Programs' (OHEP) poverty level identification standards, as well as the customer's heating source; customers at Poverty Level 6 and below would be eligible for the LIM year-round. The credit would be calculated by subtracting the Target Energy Burden Threshold (Average Income multiplied by the Energy Burden Percentage) from the Applicable Bill Net of OHEP assistance; customers will receive the credit as a rider or surcharge. The Commission approved a percent-of-rate discount mechanisms for all utilities except for Southern Maryland Electric Cooperative, which will employ a flat bill credit. The Commission did not make a final determination on the target energy burden, stating that the Commission would return to this determination when the utilities file their updated proposals and tariffs, and that such proposals should be developed with the 6% goal recommended by the Work Group in mind. Further, the Commission approved the application of the LIM to both supply and distribution charges. On May 26, 2026, the Commission approved a proposal from the Work Group to extend the 12-month LIM enrollment period to address concerns about gaps in coverage while applicants re-apply for financial assistance with OHEP; the Commission ultimately approved an 18-month enrollment period. On July 1, 2026, Baltimore Gas & Electric (BGE) filed its Limited Income Discount (LID) proposal, with customers in OHEP Poverty Levels 1 through 5 being eligible except for master-metered customers and the discount applying for 18 months. For each category of benefit level and heating source, the LID rate will be calculated as the difference between the calculated annual energy burden and the average annual electric billings, after considering average OHEP benefits for that category, divided by the average annual usage for customers in that category. On July 8, 2026, to implement a provision of the Utility RELIEF Act that allocated $38 million of the Strategic Energy Investment Fund (SEIF) to offset residential electric customer costs associated with LIMs for Fiscal Year 2027, the Commission filed an order directing utilities to report metrics for Fiscal Year 2026 surrounding the number of residential customer accounts they serve in state, residential customers' total electricity use, the number of residential customers who received Electric Universal Service Program or Maryland Energy Assistance Program benefits, total arrears for customers enrolled in those programs, and any other information useful for determining proper allocation of the funds. The Commission also directed the utilities to file a proposed plan for how the funds should be allocated and used to offset residential electric customer costs. On July 28, 2026, the Commission found BGE's proposal to be premature, due to its reliance on Fiscal Year 2025 data, the lack of discussion of ratepayer impacts of the proposed deferred cost recovery, and the lack of a determination regarding funding allocated by the General Assembly as outlined above, and referred the tariffs back to the Public Conference 59 Work Group. On August 7, 2026, Pepco, Delmarva Power & Light, and BGE (collectively, the Exelon Utilities) proposed that the SEIF funds be allocated among the utilities based on each utility's share of total residential usage and that the funding allocations be used to offset LIM costs that would otherwise be incurred through the LIM surcharge. Potomac Edison proposed that SEIF funds be allocated based on the average number of total residential accounts served and that the funding allocations be used to offset the recovery of the LIM discounts in the LIM surcharge. The utilities additionally proposed reporting and verification plans.

description: Utility Oversight and Cost Recovery: On July 1, 2026, Baltimore Gas & Electric (BGE) requested an increase to its base rates. H.B. 1532 disallowed the use of forecasted test years in rate plans; therefore, the rate case is based on an adjusted historical test year ending in March 2026. The application further stated that H.B. 1532's prohibition against forecast test years increases investors’ exposure to regulatory lag and attrition and undermines support for BGE’s financial strength and credit standing and recommended a return on equity of 10.4% for BGE. Additionally, the filing reported on BGE’s implementation of the Next Generation Energy Act by removing certain costs through operating income adjustments, including corporate jet costs, and industry trade association membership dues, as well as reconciliation amounts sought after January 1, 2025. Customer Cost Allocation: As a part of the filing, the company proposed a new voluntary prepaid service program, BGE FlexPay. The program will allow customers to prepay for their anticipated energy consumption, track usage in relation to prepayment, and add to their prepaid account as necessary. The program modifies a previous Prepaid Pilot by removing the maximum enrollment of 1,000 customers and revising eligibility to be limited to those who have an arrearage balance of $1,000 or less at time of enrollment. Participants must also have advanced metering infrastructure installed. Further, participants are not eligible for vehicle charging time of use, net energy metering, or community solar programs; the company cited difficulties in accounting for these programs prior to billing. Customers carrying and arrearage can defer payment of those accounts through a coupled payment plan; BGE would apply 75% of each new payment to replenish the account and 25% to reduce the deferred arrearage balance balance and customers would have the option to make additional payments towards the deferred arrearage balance. Customers would also have the option to register for automatic payments that would be triggered if their balance reaches a remaining balance that is enough to cover two days’ worth of service. If an account balance reaches zero, customers would typically be disconnected the next business day with the option to restore service quickly by making a payment that brings their balance to at least $15; they may also request a five day extension to make a payment. The program excludes security deposits, late fees, or reconnection fees. If approved, the program would be implemented in 17 to 20 months, with ~$4.5 million in initial project costs. Testimony noted that participants in the previous pilot experienced a greater number of disconnections than non-participants but that their disconnection durations were shorter; the company claimed that prepay helped participants avoid accruing new arrears and that they typically owed little after disconnection. The company also noted that it was awaiting Commision approval of its limited income mechanism tariff; therefore, it was not included in the rate case.

The Maryland Public Service Commission adopted regulations for a statewide community solar garden pilot program in June 2016; since then, the Commission has made regular changes to the program. The Commission adopted rules for the permanent Community Solar Energy Generation Systems (CSEGS) program in February 2025 and rules for consolidated billing in September 2025. On June 5, 2026, the Net Metering Working Group submitted a suite of draft regulations for the Commission's consideration as a proposed rulemaking. For certain areas where the Working Group did not reach consensus, several proposals per area were submitted. There are three versions of LMI Regulations concerning tracking, banking, and enforcing compliance for projects with minimum LMI subscriber requirements; three versions of Net Metering Transition Deadline criteria to determine how customer-generators qualify for standard net metering ahead of the program transition; and two Master Metering for Community Solar proposals. The Working Group also submitted community solar local government participation regulations, net excess generation revisions, bonding regulations, and proposed changes to regulation for subscription contract assignment. On August 11, 2026, the Commission held a rulemaking session; the Commission addressed requests from the Working Group to select preferred regulation out of proposed options and moved to post the regulations as amended in the Maryland Register. The regulations address the LMI subscription compliance, with the Commission selecting Office of Peoples' Counsel's proposal, which stipulates that subscriber organizations must submit compliance filings for LMI requirements; organizations that do not meet LMI allocation requirements during a billing period must submit a corrective action plan, and those who do not meet their LMI requirements for two years must appear at an administrative meeting or other hearing to discuss remedial measures and financial penalties. The Commission also moved to adopt new regulations to allow master-metered facilities to participate in the community solar program, including tenant protections from higher fees or rents as a result of participation.

description: On July 1, 2025, Maryland's Public Service Commission-regulated electric utilities filed proposals for virtual power plant (VPP) programs, as required by the 2025 Distributed Renewable Integration and Vehicle Electrification (DRIVE) Act. The DRIVE Act stipulates that it is reasonable to provide additional incentives and protections to LMI participants. On October 21, 2025, the Commission filed an order in response to the utilities' proposed VPP programs, denying the proposals and ordering the utilities to re-file with various modifications. On January 29, 2026, the utilities filed their revised VPP proposals. Pepco and Delmarva Power & Light's proposal mentioned the possibility of providing enhanced incentives to LMI customers, but did not specify any enhanced incentives. Potomac Edison's (PE) Bring Your Own Device pathway provides that for qualified batteries and bidirectional electric vehicles, customers will be paid a connectivity incentive of up to $150/connected year (with a $50/year LMI adder) and a performance incentive up to $300/kW-year based on event participation (full compensation for participation in at least 75% of events) and estimations of device performance. For its Energy Savings Rewards Smart Thermostat program, the utility proposed that customers receive $25 for summer or $50 for year-round, plus a $25 bonus in targeted locations where peak loading is nearing distribution limits, as well as one-time enrollment bonuses of $50 for summer (plus a $25 enhancement for LMI) or $100 for year round (plus a $25 LMI enhancement). On June 29, 2026, the Commission filed a second order on the DRIVE Act program proposals. First, the order acknowledged statutory changes effectuated by the Utility RELIEF Act, enacted in May 2026. Any DRIVE Act incentives must come from the Maryland Energy Administration (MEA), and utility cost recovery is no longer allowed for DRIVE Act incentives; effectively, utilities can no longer offer incentives for participation, and incentives must instead come from the Maryland Strategic Energy Investment Fund. The Commission outlined a determination that a payment for participating in the DRIVE act is a payment for providing grid service in response to a utility dispatch order, including locational adders, not an incentive. However, an incentive is direct or indirect compensation designed to promote participation in DRIVE Act program offerings by reducing cost barriers to entry. Accordingly, Potomac Edison's LMI incentives cannot be funded through utility rates. All investor-owned electric companies are directed to coordinate their incentive funding needs with MEA. Regarding cost recovery, DRIVE Act costs shall be recovered by the utilities within the calendar year in which those costs were incurred; if it is not feasible to recover these costs in a single year, a regulatory asset for non-capital costs may be used with the intent to bill these costs through a surcharge when available. Cost recovery for VPPs used to defer or avoid distribution upgrades in the pilots is still subject to the one-year timeline; Baltimore Gas & Electric (BGE’s) argument that a VPP used to defer or avoid distribution upgrades should be treated as a non-wires solution and afforded cost recovery consistent with traditional infrastructure investments will be further considered when the pilots are transitioned to permanent programs. On July 1, 2026, PE, BGE, Delmarva, and Pepco filed compliance documents evaluating the potential to avoid or defer electric system capital projects through the use of TOU rates, demand response and demand-side programs, and renewable on-site generating systems. The utilities' reports include peak load production potential, cost, and other performance considerations metrics for each applicable program. PE stated that such solutions remain nascent in terms of performance record and are most appropriate to provide incremental or localized system benefits.

On June 12, 2026, the Maryland Energy Administration submitted proposed standard siting and design requirements and proposed standard licensing conditions for Distributed Generation Certificates of Public Convenience and Necessity (DGCPCN) pursuant to statutory requirements. A DGCPCN is defined to cover community solar energy generating systems that would be otherwise required to obtain a CPCN, have a capacity of 2-5 MW-AC, and are not located within a municipal corporation. The DGCPCN proposal provides for replacing the CPCN with an expedited, administrative review for well-sited community solar systems; the proposals include standard siting and design requirements, standard conditions, and a voluntary pre-DGCPCN application. On July 22, 2026, the Maryland Public Service Commission initiated Rulemaking 97 to address the proposals and scheduled a rulemaking session for August 19, 2026.

description: In June 2021, the Maryland Public Service Commission launched a new work group process in Public Conference 44 to conduct a comprehensive examination of distribution system planning in Maryland. On March 16, 2026, the Distribution System Planning Work Group filed a report pertaining to incorporating certain metrics, including DER enablement, into system planning ahead of a new statutory requirement for utilities to file Annual Electric System Plan Updates. The report included two metrics adoption approaches for the Commission to mix and match: (1) adoption a "short-list" set of metrics reflecting broad Work Group consensus, which requires utilities to report the number/description of system constraints for which non-wires solutions (NWS) were identified and to report DER interconnections by reference; and (2) adoption of a consolidated list of metrics supported by the Office of People's Counsel, Commission Staff, and the Maryland Energy Administration that would incorporate expanded NWS planning information. On April 27, 2026, the Commission filed an order agreeing to adoption of the updated "short-list" for the upcoming Electric System Plan Updates, and on June 12, 2026, the utilities reported the metrics in their Electric System Plan Updates accordingly. On July 10, 2026, the Commission filed an order responding to the Maryland Energy Administration's (MEA's) June 30, 2026 mail log petition. MEA's petition focused on Executive Order 01.01.2025.27's directives surrounding customer affordability metrics, which MEA interprets as a performance incentive mechanism framework for DER integration and grid utilization, and a non-wires solution/grid utilization framework. The Commission agreed with MEA's petition to further explore proposals for a unified cost control and grid optimization regulatory strategy and stated that MEA's petition should be considered in the Electric System Planning and Interconnection Work Groups. Further, the Commission directed electric companies and other interested parties to respond to a list of questions in Appendix I of MEA's petition pertaining to cost containment.

description: Utility Oversight and Cost Recovery: On October 14, 2025, Pepco filed an application for approval of distribution rates using a fully forecasted test year. On April 14, 2026, Pepco withdrew its forecasted test year request and proceeded with a traditional historic test year case; the company cited the imminent passage of H.B. 1532, which prohibits the Maryland Public Service Commission from approving utility rate increases based on fully forecasted test years while the Commission considers the merits of forecasted versus historic models. On August 28, 2026, the Commission filed an order on Pepco's application, citing residential customer concerns surrounding rate increases and stating that adjustments that utilize regulatory lag need to be carefully scrutinized. The Commission further declined to approve a new open-ended regulatory asset to account for any new legislative, regulatory, or changes in accounting rules that have an impact on cost of service. Prompted by testimony from the Office of Peoples' Counsel (OPC) arguing that ratepayers should receive a benefit from volume-based rebates that suppliers provide the company when it purchases above a certain threshold, the Commission directed Pepco to work with interested parties to determine the appropriate accounting treatment of such rebates to be included in its next rate case. The Commission also initiated a Phase II of the proceeding, responding to an OPC proposal to schedule a Phase II to ensure compliance with the rate provisions in the recently enacted H.B. 1532, such as capping rate recovery for supervisory compensation over 110% of the Commission Chair's salary. Planning and Procurement: The Commission also responded to a request by the Maryland Energy Administration that cost recovery and grid modernization investments be contingent on Pepco's delivery of a DER roadmap within one year of the rate case's final order to prevent siloed investment, that Pepco provide certain data for DER integration and utilization, and that Pepco provide a non-wires solutions screening framework and other analyses for the ongoing Electric System Planning Process. The Commission declined to adopt the requirements since they would rate recovery on future filings, but stated that MEA can and should raise these concerns in the relevant dockets and work groups.
sources: Docket No. 9820; MD PSC Press Release (Aug. 2026)

description: On October 2, 2023, the Maryland Public Service Commission issued an order initiating a workgroup to develop an energy storage program for Maryland. In November 2025, the Commission-regulated electric utilities filed their proposals for energy storage projects. On April 8, 2026, the Commission filed an order on the energy storage plan proposals. Regarding procurement model, the Commission directs the utilities to utilize an RFP model for this first tranche of distribution-connected energy storage projects. The Commission will also hold pre-award confidential conferences for the sake of procurement transparency. The Commission also noted that more standardization of benefit-cost analysis (BCA) methodology is necessary before these conferences; it stated that Potomac Edison's BCA methodology was not acceptable. Bill impacts must be re-analyzed following RFPs, and cost recovery decisions are deferred pending new bill impact analyses. On April 9, 2026, a memo reviewing the BCAs was submitted; a meeting with the goal of achieving consensus on a standardized BCA approach was scheduled for April 23, 2026. On May 11, 2026, Pepco and Baltimore Gas & Electric jointly requested that the Commission approve their request for a regulatory asset for a limited amount of pre-award development and launch costs for the projects. On July 22, 2026, the Commission conditionally approved the request for a regulatory asset with the requirements that the utilities issue RFPs for their distribution-connected programs within 30 days of the order, that the utilities prepare analyses sufficient to facilitate productive pre-award conferences, and that the utilities cap their program development costs in the asset and provide cost tracking.

H.B. 270 and S.B. 116, enacted in December 2025, require an analysis from the Department of the Environment, the Maryland Energy Administration, and the University of Maryland School of Business, in conjunction with the Department of Legislative Services, of the likely environmental, energy, and economic impacts of data center development in the state. The analysis must include an assessment by the Maryland Energy Administration of the potential energy impacts of the data center industry, including an evaluation of ratepayer impacts. By September 1, 2026, the Department of Legislative Services will submit the report to the Governor. According to recent news coverage, the study will be delayed beyond the September 1, 2026 deadline.

Executive Order 01.01.2025.27, issued on December 19, 2025, creates an Energy Subcabinet to coordinate interagency actions and align energy policy with state policy goals, including affordability. The bill also creates a Maryland Energy Advisory Council to provide external stakeholder input to the Subcabinet. The Council must identify barriers to the deployment of generation facilities and affordability and provide recommendations to the Subcabinet. Within 180 days of the order, the Council must submit a memorandum to the Subcabinet identifying the most urgent challenges to energy affordability and reliability. As of June 2026, the Council had posted slides outlining challenges and solutions for topics of (1) Supply and Demand Challenges, (2) Insufficient Transmission and Distribution, (3) Energy Burden, (4) Disconnect Among Policy Goals, and (5) Financing and Market Design. The slides outline common themes, areas of disagreement, particularly interesting points, and potential solutions identified by working group participants in a survey. The Energy Burden group identified potential solutions of creating a low-income rate class, targeted energy efficiency program deployments, and value-added products like incentives for smart home investments. The Financing and Market Design group identified solutions related to rate classes and cost allocation for high-demand users.
sources: Executive Order 01.01.2025.27; MD Energy Advisory Council Website

description: On January 9, 2026, the Cost Recovery Work Group filed its status report regarding decisions on Baltimore Gas & Electric and the PHI Utilities' (Pepco and Delmarva Power & Light) alternative performance incentive mechanism (PIM) proposal. The original proposal was a shared savings proposal, which raised stakeholder concerns about evaluation, measurement, and verification, along with potentially contentious decisions about incentive amount. The alternate proposal also uses a shared savings mechanism, but with pre-defined incentives that utilities may earn at the start of the 2027 to 2029 EmPOWER Maryland program cycle, calculated as a percentage of the net benefits over the prior three years on a rolling basis. The status report refers to the alternate proposal in its discussion. The parties have not come to a consensus about performance levels, thresholds of savings, incentive/penalty amounts, or total expenditures. On February 6, 2026, the Maryland Public Service Commission filed an order in response to EmPOWER Semi-Annual and Work Group reports, where it decided to table discussion of PIMs in the Cost Recovery Work Group. On April 15, 2026, the Future Programming Work Group filed a status report contemplating several EmPOWER topics. Regarding whether a single third-party administrator would be more effective than utility-led programs, non-utility parties largely supported a third-party administrator to increase cost-effectiveness and program effectiveness. On May 22, 2026, the Future Programming Work Group filed revised EmPOWER Goals for 2027 to 2029 in response to the Utility RELIEF Act, outlining party perspectives on methodologies for calculating savings goals and their potential bill impacts. In the vein of program review and reducing customer surcharges, the Act changes the minimum EmPOWER goal specified to be based on a percentage of baseline 2016 electricity sales from 2.5% to 1.75% for the 2027-2029 EmPOWER cycle. The parties disagreed on the methodology to translate the 1.75% goal into a lifecycle greenhouse gas emission reduction metric and the resulting customer impacts from the program. Commission Staff advocated for an estimated useful life bin methodology and major utilities supporting a statewide weighted average metric resulting in lower savings goals. The utilities provided estimates of surcharge reductions for the revised goal using their methodology and Staff's methodology, compared to the 2026 EmPOWER surcharge, claiming that their methodology would yield greater surcharge savings and thus greater affordability. The Maryland Energy Administration noted that the utilities failed to discuss any of the lost customer benefits and fewer opportunities to reduce energy consumption resulting from the smaller goals they advocated for, which were not calculated using the already approved estimated useful life bin methodology. On July 10, 2026, the Commission filed its order in response to the utilities' EmPOWER Semi-Annual and Work Group Reports. Regarding 2027-2029 EmPOWER goals, the Commission directed the utilities to develop an EmPOWER portfolio based on the methodology proposed by Staff and Maryland Department of Environment, as well as a sensitivity plan more aligned with the utilities' proposed methodology for cost consideration purposes, and further outlined specific calculation parameters.

On July 2, 2026, Maryland's Governor announced that the Maryland Energy Administration (MEA), Public Service Commission, and Office of People's Counsel filed a complaint with FERC to end a surcharge that the Utility RELIEF Act (H.B. 1532) aimed to eliminate. FERC allows utilities to collect a surcharge as an incentive to voluntarily join RTOs; however, the Utility RELIEF Act made membership mandatory. In their complaint, the parties alleged that the RTO Adder is only available to utilities that voluntarily participate in a transmission organization, cited past cases of denial due to involuntary participation, and asserted that the continuation of the adder in the Maryland utilities' return on equity (ROE) is unjust and unreasonable. On August 5, 2026, the Exelon Utilities (Baltimore Gas & Electric, Pepco, and Delmarva Power & Light) filed a motion to dismiss MEA's complaint because (1) the utilities remain entitled to the adder regardless of interpretation of the Maryland Act and federal statute; (2) MEA did not show that the Exelon utilities' company-wide ROE rates are unreasonable; (3) the Maryland Act is unconstitutional; (4) it would be unjust and unreasonable, unduly discriminatory, and an unlawful subdelegation to deny the RTO adder whenever a state enacts an RTO mandate; and (5) FERC's reading of the RTO adder statute is wrong and the statute does not contain a voluntariness requirement. Potomac Edison filed a motion to dismiss on the same day, making similar arguments and siting the terms of a previous settlement agreement it entered.
sources: FERC Docket No. EL26-87; MD PSC Press Release (July 2026); Complaint (July 2026)

description: On July 20, 2026, the Maine Public Utilities Commission opened a docket to examine the state's winter disconnection procedures contained in Chapter 815 and determine whether changes should be made to ensure that arrearages are minimized and customers are receiving available assistance during the winter disconnection prohibition period.

On June 25, 2025, the Maine Public Utilities Commission opened a proceeding to inquire about opt-in programs to reduce net energy billing (NEB) costs. The Commission filed a notice of inquiry on April 13, 2026, with a request for comment by May 13, 2026, for the following questions: what kinds of long-term financial mechanisms and buy-down arrangements would encourage a DG project sponsor to voluntarily leave its existing NEB agreement; and what potential mechanisms can create savings for low-income customers that could provide savings to other ratepayers. Central Maine Power filed comments on May 13, 2026, stating that it supports savings initiatives for low-income customers as long as they are cost-neutral or beneficial for other customers. On August 24, 2026, the Commission filed a procedural order, which declined the option to initiate rulemaking for opt-in programs to reduce net energy billing costs and closed the docket.

On May 27, 2026, the Maine Public Utilities Commission initiated an informal investigation into large data center development. A notice was filed on June 5, 2026, to identify and implement strategies to: (1) safeguard customers against increased energy supply costs, including the risks associated with overbuilding new generation; (2) safeguard customers against increased transmission and distribution costs, including by mitigating the risk of stranded utility assets; and (3) promote the development of market and regulatory mechanisms to ensure that costs attributable to data center development are fully borne by the entities responsible for creating those costs.

On August 20, 2026, the Maine Public Utilities Commission opened a docket concerning renewable energy procurement for LMI consumer-owned projects. On September 1, 2026, the Commission issued an RFP for up to 4 MW of energy from one or more eligible DG resources, which is defined in L.D. 1966 (2026) as projects placed into service on or after August 1, 2026 that have a nameplate capacity of no more than 200 kW, serve only LMI households, are wholly owned by its customers or a cooperative, provide discounts similar to net energy billing to offset customer electricity bills, and are connected to the grid.

subtopics: Advanced Transmission Technologies; Grid Utilization; Non-Wires Alternatives
description: The Maine State Legislature enacted L.D. 1959 in 2022, which directs investor-owned transmission and distribution utilities to submit integrated grid plans every 10 years to the Maine Public Utilities Commission. As a result, the Commission directed Central Maine Power (CMP) and Versant Power to file integrated grid plans by January 12, 2026, which must include utilities' near-term and long-term grid investments and metrics to measure grid planning effectiveness. CMP and Versant Power filed inaugural integrated grid plans on December 15, 2025, and January 12, 2026, respectively, both of which discussed ways to improve grid utilization. In particular, CMP's plan lists several pilot project concepts in the early development phase, including a dynamic line rating pilot and a flexibility marketplace pilot for NWAs and DER flexibility, and commits to reporting on the status of a pilot to improve grid utilization in the next integrated grid plan. Versant Power's plan mostly focused on distribution and transmission upgrade solutions that favor traditional utility investments, but it did mention the growing potential to leverage NWAs like grid-enhancing technologies when resolving transmission violations moving forward. The Commission filed an order approving the plans on July 31, 2026.

On October 17, 2025, the Maine Public Utilities Commission opened an inquiry regarding a review of the NWA investigation and recommendation process, as a result of a requirement in L.D. 1726 (2025). The Commission requested comments on several questions, including whether regulatory or legislative changes or clarifications could improve the NWA process; how the NWA process should be incorporated into, or better integrated with, the integrated grid planning process; whether utilities should review cost-effective NWAs to implement DER interconnection to avoid system upgrade costs; and whether there are areas in the state that may be best suited to NWAs in relation to reliability and resiliency needs. After first submitting it to the Joint Standing Committee on Energy, Utilities, and Technology on February 27, 2026, the Commission filed the final report on August 13, 2026. In the final report, the Commission recommends varying statutory changes, including requiring five-year planning studies to be submitted to the Commission and giving the Commission authority to adopt routine technical rules for the NWA investigation, recommendation, and procurement process. Together, these changes would let the Commission formalize the NWA process by standardizing deadlines for planning studies and data requests, standardizing utility reporting requirements, using integrated grid plans to inform five-year studies, and formalizing the NWA benefit-cost analysis methodology. The Commission recommends further study -- with findings reported back to the Legislature -- on whether current NWA exclusion criteria for certain projects should be expanded or narrowed, and whether additional changes are warranted, including possibly raising the cost threshold for project review. The Commission also flags issues for either legislative consideration or further Commission proceedings, including the statutory definition of NWA and evaluating whether utility incentives are needed to encourage better NWA outcomes.

On July 30, 2026, the Maine Public Utilities Commission filed a notice of inquiry into potential requirements for municipal community choice aggregation (CCA) programs to support aggregating the load of residential and small commercial customers to procure electricity. The proceeding was developed to implement the provisions in L.D. 2112 (2026), which allows municipalities to form CCA programs by January 1, 2027. The Commission seeks input on what terms need defining (especially "residential" and "small commercial" customers); approval standards and timelines for aggregation plans; customer notice, opt-out, and opt-in procedures; protecting default service and coordinating with procurement cycles; when customers can be denied service or dropped for non-payment; data exchange standards between utilities and program suppliers; adapting the standard provider contract for CCA use; tribal program provisions; consumer protections; and keeping implementation costs off utilities.

description: On April 17, 2026, Central Maine Power filed a general rate case, including a request to eliminate a cap on recovery of costs incurred for shared services from Avangrid service companies. In its application, the utility requested the possibility of a potential phase 2 filing to establish a multi-year rate filing, which may include performance mechanisms and earnings sharing, in addition to the one-year filing.

On May 30, 2025, the Maine Public Utilities Commission opened a formal investigation into the operation and management practices of Versant Power due to a recent external audit, which identified four primary deficiencies: (1) a lack of a strategic plan or corporate planning process, (2) difficult collecting billed revenues resulting a high bad debt rate, (3) mismanagement of the interconnection process, and (4) a failure to improve service quality and reliability to justify significant rate increases and capital investments. The Commission held several technical conferences in 2025 and early 2026, and ultimately Versant Power, the Office of the Public Advocate, and additional parties reached a settlement. On September 3, 2026, the Commission issued an order approving this settlement, which includes requirements for the utility to generate quarterly reporting and adhere to recommendations in the initial audit through a Performance Improvement Plan (PIP), create a strategic plan specific to Versant, develop a benchmarking action plan, establish department-level performance tracking and reporting, establish capital planning and execution tracking and reporting, increase accountability for executive compensation through more closely tying compensation to overall performance, and providing Versant's parent company's internal audit report of compliance with the PIP.

On July 16, 2026, the Maine Public Utilities Commission opened a docket to collect stakeholder feedback on the development of an affordability metric in compliance with L.D. 1949 (2026). As outlined in L.D. 1949, this affordability metric must assess the impact of electricity bills on the overall energy burden for residential customers of investor-owned transmission and distribution utilities. The Commission must submit an interim report on its progress to the joint standing committee having jurisdiction over energy matters by January 15, 2027, and a final report by December 15, 2027, including any recommendations or proposed legislation. The Commission scheduled a workshop for October 8, 2026 and provided an opportunity for written comments.

On April 17, 2026, the Michigan Public Service Commission filed an order increasing the Low-Income Energy Assistance Fund (LIEAF) funding factor from $1.00 to $1.50 per meter per month for the September 2026 through August 2027 billing months. The LIEAF funding factor (funding factor) is a nonbypassable surcharge to be added to each retail billing meter (but not charged on more than one residential meter per residential site), payable monthly by every customer that receives retail distribution service. An electric utility, municipally owned electric utility, or cooperative electric utility shall remit the LIEAF payments to the Michigan State Treasurer for deposit in the LIEAF on a monthly basis no later than 30 days after the last day of each calendar month. Each utility identified in this order as opting out of the funding factor shall establish and fund an energy assistance program consistent with the Michigan energy assistance program year October 1, 2026 through September 30, 2027, for their eligible residential customers that provides assistance to their residential customers for both their electric and home heating needs consistent with the eligibility requirements of the Michigan energy assistance program. The increased funding surcharge is expected to raise about $90 million for the year beginning with the September 2026 billing month, estimated to provide energy security for a year for about 90,000 Michigan households. On May 1, 2026, the Commission issued an RFP for non-profits, units of local or state government, and Tribal governments for the administration of funding and provision of services for assisting income-qualified households in the reduction of home energy insecurity and the resolution of energy crisis situations. The deadline for submitting a grant proposal is June 12, 2026, with grant awards expected to be announced in July 2026. The grant period is expected to begin October 1, 2026, and end no later than September 30, 2027. The amount available is estimated to be $93,000,000, consisting of an estimated amount of $88,000,000 from the LIEAF and $5,000,000 from federal LIHEAP Assurance 16 funds. Projects should have the following goals: (1) reduce energy insecurity by assisting eligible low-income households in meeting their home energy costs; (2) develop household plans to reduce energy insecurity and enable participants to become self-sufficient; (3) prioritize vulnerable populations for energy assistance including certain low-income households; (4) collaborate with relevant state agencies and energy providers to ensure statewide access and that all funds collected from a geographic region are prioritized for that geographic region; and (5) promote education and outreach on availability of assistance programs and funding.
sources: Docket No. U-17377; MI PSC Press Release on Increase to Funding Factor (Apr. 2026); MI PSC Press Release on LIEAF RFP (May 2026); MI Energy Assistance Program RFP (May 2026)

description: On October 17, 2025, Indiana Michigan Power (I&M) filed an application to modify its Large Power tariffs to incorporate specific terms and conditions to accommodate large load customers whose contract demands equal or exceed 50 MW. I&M seeks to balance the obligation to serve these customers with the risk they pose to the utility's system and other customers. I&M proposes a contract term of 15 years with a five-year load ramp period, an exit fee that would apply if the customer permanently closes, takes service from an alternate electric supplier, or reduces contract capacity by more than 20%, provisions that allow the customer to reduce its contract capacity by up to 20% with 60 months notice, a 90% monthly minimum billing demand, a 65% monthly minimum energy, and an increased amount of minimum collateral. On May 19, 2026, the ALJs filed a proposal for decision (PFD) on I&M's modifications to its Large Power tariffs. The PFD found four uncontested issues that should be adopted by the Michigan Public Service Commission. Of those, requirements for paying all costs during temporary service; and minimum monthly billing demand are most applicable to cost allocation. There were a number of contested issues. On the matter of customer protection vs. economic development, the ALJs declined to adopt Commission Staff's arguments that I&M should prioritize customer protection over economic development, and agrees that I&M strikes an appropriate balance between the two. On the topic of cost-shifting, the ALJs agree with the Attorney General and other intervenors that large loads pose a serious cost-shifting risk and those must be abated in the tariff; new large load customers must fully pay for the costs needed to serve them and adequate guardrails are needed to avoid cross-subsidization. However, the PFD does not make a recommendation on the appropriate method for preventing cost-shift. The PFD declines proposals for a standalone data center tariff. The PFD also ruled on exit fees, adopting Staff’s and the Attorney General’s recommendation that the exit fee should be based on the large load customer’s full contract capacity and should not be offset by any allowed capacity reduction; and that reducing contracted capacity and permanently departing are discrete and distinct events. The ALJs also found that Staff’s recommended modifications to I&M’s proposed collateral requirement provisions are reasonable, including that: (1) the default collateral amount is equal to 50% of the exit fee; (2) a standby irrevocable letter of credit or cash, which would earn interest, is acceptable; and (3) I&M may require a different collateral amount or accept a form of collateral other than the default provisions, subject to Commission review and approval. The ALJs agree with Staff that the collection of an administrative fee is advisable given the unique size of large load customers and the requirement of studies and adopt I&M’s tiered fee of $50,000 for large loads of 50 MW up to 99 MW and $100,000 for loads of 100 MW of more. The ALJ recommended that I&M should be required to file six cost allocation and rate design proposals to illustrate the impact on test year costs, including surcharges, for existing customers and large load customers. On August 27, 2026, the Commission filed an order approving changes to Tariff LP, accepting the ALJ's recommendations.

On March 27, 2026, the Michigan Public Service Commission Staff filed a report, in response to an order issued in August 2025. The report makes recommendations for improvements to the critical care shutoff protection rule, which prohibits utilities from shutting off electric service to patients for whom a loss of power would be life threatening and provides other protections and transparency requirements around electricity shut-off for medically vulnerable customers. The recommendation amends the existing rule: (1) by removing the stipulation that this rule only applies due to inability to pay and by requiring critical care customers to identify themselves to the utility annually; (2) by prohibiting a utility from requiring payment of an after-hours reconnect fee or a deposit as a condition of restoring service; (3) and making other changes to how the customer and utility enroll in and operate the program. On May 14, 2026, the Commission filed an order inviting comments on the proposed rule change.
sources: Docket No. U-21939; Report on Critical Care Shutoff Protection Rule (Mar. 2026); MI PSC Press Release (May 2026)
