description: On July 16, 2026, the Michigan Public Service Commission responded to a request from Governor Whitmer detailing recommended legislative approaches to addressing energy affordability. In particular, the Commission recommended that the legislature: (1) address utilities' capital bias and realign utility incentives with cost efficiency and improved performance outcomes for customers; (2) rein in unnecessary costs; and (3) increase opportunities for competition to drive down costs within the current regulatory framework. To address utilities' capital bias, the Commission recommended that the legislature: (1) amend existing law to authorize the Commission to establish multi-year rate plans that couple utility earnings to performance on core reliability and affordability metrics; (2) require transmission utilities to demonstrate that they are making efficient use of the existing grid, require distribution utilities to increase their use of the existing grid, allow the Commission to incorporate utilization metrics into utility cost recovery, and require the demonstration that new builds are more cost effective than utilization of existing resources; and (3) authorize the Commission to develop a process for scaling the deployment of cost-effective DERs. To rein in unnecessary costs, the Commission recommended that the legislature: (1) modify the financial compensation mechanism, a tool by which utilities are rewarded for engaging in lower cost contracts or PPAs, to ensure that it does not apply to situations where a utility is obligated to enter into a PPA; (2) require securitization of retiring assets; (3) codify the requirement that customers be shielded from paying costs associated with serving data center customers and that large load tariffs contain certain provisions designed to prevent cost shifts, and directly assign costs of transmission upgrades needed to serve data center customers to those customers; and (4) direct the Commission to develop rate design approaches that reflect cost causation principles in a modern electric system. To increase competition, the Commission recommended that the legislature: (1) grant the Commission licensing authority for third-party aggregators of DERs and demand response; (2) empower customer participation through VPPs, energy waste reduction, DERs, flexibility, and plug-in resources; (3) grant the Commission authority to require competitive procurement and re-establish minimum percentages of projects that must be procured under PPAs; and (4) strengthen integrated resource planning to require greater consideration of transmission, require that utilities show that generation and transmission investments have been optimized, explore opportunities to improve the cost effectiveness of transmission projects, and direct the Commission to submit a transmission report every three years. The Commission also recommended new and improved affordability assistance programs. The Commission suggested: (1) aligning low-income rate eligibility with increased eligibility for the Michigan Energy Assistance Program (MEAP), to 60% of the state median income; (2) align programs funded by LIHEAP to 60% of the state median income; (3) redesigning the Home Heating Credit (HHC) to complement existing assistance programs; (4) allow the Commission to take over implementation of the MEAP; (5) increase program funding for MEAP, State Emergency Relief, and HHC; (6) increase funding for low-income weatherization and pre-weatherization programs; (7) create a new assistance program for further weatherization; and (8) create a permanent funding source for Michigan Saves, Michigan's non-profit green bank.
sources: Letter from MI PSC to Governor Whitmer (July 2026)

description: On May 8, 2026, DTE Electric submitted an application for authority to securitize the costs of converting two coal plants to natural gas plants and for cost recovery for vegetation management. The Michigan Public Service Commission previously approved securitization of the coal handling costs at the Belle River generating facility in Docket No. U-21193 and the securitization of unrecovered balances from the company operating Belle River in Docket Nos. U-21543 and U-21860. The Commission approved securitization of the costs of tree trimming as a regulatory asset in Docket No. U-20162. Securitization has been found to be the least cost method of financing these infrastructure projects. Customers will initially receive bill credits that go into effect coincident with the securitization charges. The bill credits will reflect the current revenue requirement associated with the portions of the above-identified costs that are included in DTE Electric’s retail electric rates, and will remain in effect until such time as the company’s rates are reset. The residential bill credits range from 0.0371 cents to 0.0704 cents per kWh. On July 6, 2026, DTE Electric and the Commission Staff filed a settlement agreement in which Staff found that DTE's proposed securitization was appropriate and recommended that the Commission approve the proposal. On August 4, 2026, the Commission approved the settlement agreement, allowing DTE to move forward with its securitization of its coal plant assets as proposed. The order also includes a directive that DTE must, after all of the costs and interest is paid on the securitized assets, return any excess revenue to its customers as a bill credit, to be determined through the normal ratemaking process. Additionally, the Commission directed DTE Electric to file updated tariffs including information about the cost savings this process would provide, including details on the securitization charge and the removal of charges for Belle River site costs.
sources: Docket No. U-22109; Settlement Agreement (July 2026); Order (Aug. 2026)

categories: Planning and Procurement; Utility Oversight and Cost Recovery
description: H.B. 5710, passed by the House in May 2026, requires energy utilities in Michigan to remit specified amounts to the utility consumer representation fund before filing energy cost recovery proceedings, with amounts varying based on customer count. Companies serving at least 100,000 customers pay proportional shares of $2,500,000 adjusted annually, while smaller companies pay proportional shares of $150,000 adjusted annually. The bill also requires the Michigan Public Service Commission to consider affordability and net cost to ratepayers when evaluating utilities' IRPs, including the relationship between affordability and factors like reliability and diversity of generation and whether peak load reduction is cost-effective. In evaluating affordability, the Commission should consider capital, fuel, operation and maintenance, and decommissioning costs, levelized cost of energy or capacity, projected impacts on customer bills and overall rate stability, and long-term cost escalations, contingencies, and revenue requirements. The bill defines "affordability" as the capacity of a generation resource or portfolio to deliver electricity at a cost that minimizes the total financial burden on ratepayers over the resource's expected operational life.

H.B. 5879, as passed by the House in May 2026, requires utilities to provide the Michigan Public Service Commission with property tax exemption savings amounts within 60 days of the bill's effective date. Within 30 days of receiving this information, the Commission is to begin reconciliation proceedings. The bill requires that the Commission issue orders decreasing residential utility rates by the amount of property tax exemption savings and utilities cannot file rate increase applications for two years after such orders.

subtopics: Bill Assistance; Disconnection Policies; Payment Plans
description: An ALJ filed recommendations in Xcel Energy's ongoing rate case on April 29, 2026. The ALJ summarized an ongoing dispute over a disconnection moratorium and rate study alternative, but did not provide recommendations on the issue. Intervenors in this case have recommended that the Minnesota Public Utilities Commission implement an indefinite moratorium on disconnections for all customers based on the claim that disconnections do not serve any purpose. Instead, the intervenors recommend that the Commission authorize a randomized control trial to test the impact of disconnection practices by testing different ramifications for real customers that are otherwise subject to disconnection. The moratorium would exist until Xcel Energy could demonstrate that the benefits of disconnection outweigh the costs. Xcel argued that such a moratorium would negatively impact arrearages and customers in the long run by eliminating opportunities for the utility to connect with customers and make them aware of affordability programs and payment plans, in addition to making some customers eligible for some forms of crisis assistance that require a disconnection notice. Additionally, the ALJ recommended approving a proposal to expand the utility's existing PowerOn assistance program by implementing an auto-enrollment provision that would apply to the utility's LIHEAP-enrolled electric-only customers. The PowerOn program is currently tailored to households that have received federal LIHEAP funding but are still paying more than 3% of income towards electricity bills. The program offers assistance in the form of monthly payments as a percentage of household income and past-due bill forgiveness. On July 31, 2026, the Commission issued an order approving the PowerOn auto-enrollment program, but denying the proposed disconnection moratorium and randomized control trial.

On July 16, 2025, Xcel Energy filed a proposal for a new tariff, the Large General Time of Day Service tariff. The tariff would serve customers that meet the demand threshold of at least 100 MW and be open to all industries. Qualifying demand would be determined by an interconnection agreement and will be inclusive of any load ramp-up period, which is limited to five years and a contract term length of at least 15 years. Early termination would require at least 24 months' notice and require the customer to pay an exit fee based on a calculation of the current effective demand charges, times 75%, times the lesser period of ten years or the remainder of the term. The pricing of this tariff would shift more cost recover through demand charges and less from energy costs. The utility also proposes a Form Electric Service Agreement that details the specific terms and conditions governing service to the customer. On June 12, 2026, the Commission issued an order approving the tariffs with several modifications. These modifications include: creating a standalone customer class for large load customers, rather than housing the tariffs under the existing Commercial and Industrial class; requiring all transmission and distribution upgrades needed to serve very large customers be paid directly by these customers; and requiring that for each new customer, Xcel Energy must demonstrate that the electricity provided will meet the state's renewable and carbon free energy benchmarks without delaying statewide progress.

On February 18, 2026, Minnesota Power filed a proposal to accommodate very large customers within its existing Large Power Service Schedule (LP Tariff). Under the revised tariff, large industrial customers with identified new load growth of at least 10 MW would enter into a negotiated energy service agreement (ESA) with the utility. Each ESA is subject to the applicable regulatory review process and approval by the Minnesota Public Utilities Commission and will be tailored to the specific customer, defining the full scope of commitments. A large power surcharge applies to new customers whose Firm Demand exceeds 50 MW within any 24-month period, or to existing customers whose Firm Demand increases by more than 50 MW within any 24-month period. On April 14, 2026, Minnesota Power filed an updated proposal which changed the provisions of the large power surcharge to a charge that could be applied to any eligible customers with load growth in excess of 50 MW. Minnesota Power will assess the surcharge tied to the load addition by calculating a margin contribution analysis approximately six months before reaching load growth of 50 MW. On May 19, 2026, Minnesota Power filed a petition to withdraw its application without prejudice. The utility stated that due to the lack of support received, it will submit a new petition with a proposal to create a new Very Large Power Customer Class and associated Service Tariff by mid-summer 2026. On July 15, 2026, Minnesota Power filed a petition for a new Very Large Power (VLP) Customer Class and associated service schedules. VLP customers would be customers with new load growth of 100 MW or more and would enter into a negotiated ESA with the utility under the VLP tariff. VLP customers seeking to connect directly to the transmission system are required to follow an open-access transmission interconnection process and cover all costs associated with necessary studies and upgrades. Customers would be billed on a base rate, as well as any applicable riders and customer-specific provisions included in the individual ESA. Contracts would be for a minimum of 15 years with a multi-year termination notice and required exit fee. On July 23, 2026, the Minnesota Public Utilities Commission approved the petition for withdrawal on the retroactive condition that the utility file its new proposal by July 15, 2026.
sources: Docket No. 26-126; Revised Application (Apr. 2026); Petition for Withdrawal (May 2026); Order (July 2026)

description: On May 18, 2026, Otter Tail Power filed an application for approval of a new class for very large customers, generally, for customers above 25 MW. The new class would be designated as Large General Service - Tier II - Time of Day. Customers under this service must have a demand of at least 25 MW within the most recent 12 months and will have the option to select this rate schedule for an optional trial service. The tariff is designed to protect all non-participating customers from cross-subsidy and stranded cost risk.

On July 30, 2026, in an ongoing docket surrounding Xcel Energy's Integrated Distribution Plan (IDP), the Minnesota Public Utilities Commission ordered the creation of an IDP Improvement Working Group. The working group will evaluate changes to the planning process and develop a metric for grid utilization. This order was made at a meeting and, as of mid-September 2026, the official order has not yet been filed.

On September 23, 2026, the Minnesota Public Utilities Commission opened an investigation into rate-regulated electric and natural gas utility service affordability. The purpose of the proceeding is to collect public and stakeholder input and develop recommendations for utilities, the Commission, the Governor, the legislature, and the federal government. The initial topic of the investigation will focus on how Minnesota customers experience electric and natural gas costs, how affordability should be defined and measured, the principal sources of affordability concern, and potential improvements. The investigation will also examine the costs, benefits, and trade-offs of potential reforms. The investigation will begin with three informational sessions held on October 13, 2026, November 2, 2026, and December 8, 2026.

On September 11, 2026, Liberty Utilities filed an application for approval of its Schedule Transmission Service Large Load (Schedule TS-LL), designed to establish a standardized framework for service large load customers. Schedule TS-LL requires each large load customer to enter into an electric service agreement (ESA) for a minimum of 15 years with an optional 5-year load ramp up period. Customers taking service under this schedule are responsible for the costs of incremental generation, transmission, network upgrades, and related facilities required to serve their load.

Executive Order 2, signed by the Governor in January 2026, directs the Missouri Department of Natural Resources, in collaboration with the Missouri Public Service Commission, to initiate an investigation and review of energy regulations and infrastructure planning in light of the growing demand for power from data centers supporting AI. The Department is directed to review the current regulations and practices to ensure the construction and operation of large power users do not result in higher energy rates for residential and small business customers and project the current and future energy needs of the state, including the impact of large power customers, and develop strategies to address these needs. Findings must be completed by November 30, 2026.
sources: Executive Order 26-02; MO DNR Data Center Investigation

description: On March 31, 2026, NorthWestern Energy filed a proposals for a Large Load Service Tariff Rule (Rule No. 24) to establish minimum terms for each electric service agreement. The rule will apply to customers who will take new or expanded service with an expected average monthly demand of at least 5 MW and provide a tiered approach for very large customers, those whose average monthly demand is at least 50 MW. The rule will include a development deposit to pay for any study costs in addressing the ability to serve the customer, a five-year minimum contract, a load ramp-up period not to exceed five years, a minimum demand and load factor, a minimum termination cost, and a curtailment provision. The tiered approach for very large customers will include stricter guardrails such as a 15-year minimum contact length and a minimum demand payment of 75%.

On July 15, 2026, Dominion Energy North Carolina and NextEra Energy filed a joint application with the North Carolina Utilities Commission requesting approval for NextEra to acquire Dominion. The application proposes merger commitments from the utilities, including $2.25 billion in shareholder-funded bill credits for Dominion's customers across Virginia, North Carolina, and South Carolina. For North Carolina, Dominion and NextEra assert that this would result in $74 million in benefits over a two-year period.
sources: Docket No. E-22 Sub 791; Joint Application (July 2026)

description: S.B. 730, as passed by the House in June 2026 and under consideration by the Senate, establishes certain requirements for electric service agreements (ESAs) entered into between utilities and data centers (defined as those with a peak monthly electricity demand of 100 MW or greater). Each contract must (1) include terms and conditions designed to protect residential, other retail, and wholesale electricity customers from costs incurred or reasonably anticipated to be incurred by the utility to provide service to the data center, and (2) prevent, to the maximum extent reasonably feasible, the subsidization of data center electric service costs by other retail customers. Contracts must include minimum billing requirements, a contract term sufficient to recover all of the utility’s incremental costs, performance and credit provisions designed to protect retail customers in the event of contract default, and termination provisions. Additionally, the bill directs the North Carolina Collaboratory to issue an RFP for a study to be conducted that examines the current and projected impacts to customer bills of the 2050 carbon neutrality goal and whether any changes to this policy or other policies are advisable to improve customer affordability. The study also must provide recommendations for effective policies to prevent adverse rate impacts from large load customers on other customer classes. The study would be due by May 1, 2027. The bill also institutes a cooling-off period for North Carolina Utilities Commissioners and Commission Staff, prohibiting these individuals from intending to influence on behalf of an employer or client, any communication to or appearance before the Commission within a period of six months following the end of their service or employment with the Commission.

subtopics: Cost Shift Prevention (Large Load); Earnings Sharing Mechanisms; Performance Incentive Mechanisms; Revenue Decoupling
description: In its November 2025 multi-year rate plan (MYRP) application, Duke Energy Progress (DEP) proposed an earnings sharing mechanism (ESM) by which the utility pays customers back any revenues that exceed 0.5% over the utility's return on equity. Returned revenues will appear as a rider or credit on customers' bills. The MYRP also proposes a residential decoupling mechanism (RDM), which would distribute to or collect from residential customers funds based on the difference between actual and target revenues. The RDM includes net lost revenues due to DEP's demand side management and energy efficiency programs; as a result, this kind of mechanism encourages continued investment in these programs. DEP is also proposing a set of performance incentive mechanisms (PIMs): time differentiated and dynamic rate enrollment, reliability, renewables integration, and customer service. Notably, the time differentiated and dynamic rate enrollment PIM is identical to DEP's existing PIM, with changes to the incentive amounts. The PIM is designed to reduce peak load and is based on winter peak load reductions from customer enrollments in time differentiated rates. The changes increase the potential reward from $5 to $10 per enrolled customer and decreases the customer enrollment cap from 250,000 to 50,000. On July 24, 2026, in rebuttal testimony, DEP proposed a new Large Load Tariff. The tariff would apply to customers with either a total contract demand of 50 MW or more and an expected load factor of 80% of more, or a total contract demand of 100 MW or more and any load factor. The minimum initial contract term for customers below 100 MW would be the greater of 10 years or 5 years, plus the load ramp period. The minimum initial contract term for customers 100 MW or more would be the greater of 15 years or 10 years plus the load ramp period. On August 5, 2026, DEP filed settlement agreements related to the revenue requirement and proposed PIMs and tracking metrics with multiple parties. The settlement related to the revenue requirement lays out a few parameters related to the ESM and RDM, most notably requiring separate ESMs for DEP and Duke Energy Carolinas in the second year of this performance-based regulation (PBR) rate case. In the settlement related to PIMs and tracking metrics, the parties support the time-differentiated and dynamic rate enrollment PIM with minor modifications, a facilities study PIM proposed by the Public Staff, a vegetation management PIM, and a slightly modified reliability PIM. The settlement also supports Duke Energy maintaining its existing beneficial electrification from EV load tracking metric, removing the existing Circuit Performance Report as a tracking metric and instead submitting the Circuit Performance Report quarterly to the Public Staff, and maintaining its existing Call Center answer rate tracking metric. Duke Energy will also host a PIMs workshop to be completed prior to the filing of the next PBR rate case.
sources: Docket No. E-2 Sub 1380; Revenue Requirement Settlement Agreement (Aug. 2026); PIMs Settlement Agreement (Aug. 2026)
