description: In July 2025, Duke Energy Carolinas (DEC) and Duke Energy Progress (DEP) filed a joint application to merge their operations into one entity called Duke Energy Carolinas. The utilities entered into an agreement and stipulation of settlement with other parties in February 2026 resolving all the issues within the proceeding. One condition in the settlement is that the utilities commit to engaging with Google to receive and consider in good faith a more detailed proposal related to a new customer clean energy program structured similarly to the Clean Transition Tariff in Nevada cited by Google in its direct testimony. The settlement also includes plans by DEC and DEP to provide around $286 million in customer benefits to North Carolina. If this benefit to the state is not achieved, DEC’s and DEP's shareholders will fund the resulting shortfall, unless the shortfall is due to some other unforeseen economic circumstances, subject to North Carolina Utilities Commission approval. The settlement also commits the utilities and the Public Staff to developing a tracking methodology to measure benefits to North Carolina from the merger. In May 2026, the Commission filed an order approving the merger and the settlement agreement in its entirety. On July 31, 2026, DEC and DEP jointly filed the benefits tracking methodology, which outlines methods for calculating each of the four benefit categories: (1) reduced reliability purchases, (2) reduced operating reserves, (3) reduced online contingency reserves, and (4) fuel savings. Additionally, the utilities proposed a deadline of March 31 for the annual report detailing the measurables benefits of the merger for North Carolina and South Carolina.
sources: Docket No. E-2 Sub 1383; Docket E-7 Sub 1332; Settlement Agreement (Feb. 2026); Order (May 2026)

description: On August 26, 2025, the Governor of North Carolina created the NC Energy Policy Task Force, an advisory body made up of legislators, state officials, electricity customers, investor-owned utilities, municipal and cooperative utilities, research organizations, and advocacy organizations. The Task Force's goal is to provide policy recommendations to the Governor, General Assembly, Utilities Commission, and other policymakers on pressing energy issues. Its first issue to address is load growth in North Carolina. On February 15, 2026, the Task Force published its interim report, in which it made a number of recommendations for further investigation. Specifically, the Task Force recommended further development of policy options for large load tariffs in order to address the potential for cost shift from large load additions in the state. Most recently, the Task Force held a meeting on July 9, 2026, to hear presentations on different aspects of load growth and discuss updates from working groups on policy mechanisms under consideration such as large load tariffs, bring your own capacity, and load flexibility.
sources: Executive Order No. 23; Interim Report (Feb. 2026); NC Energy Policy Task Force Website

categories: Customer Cost Allocation; Utility Business Model
description: In its 2025 multi-year rate plan, Unitil proposed modifications to its revenue decoupling mechanism (RDM) and implementation of an arrearage management program. In a February 25, 2026 settlement agreement, Unitil agreed to transition from the Revenue-Per-Customer (“RPC”) methodology to a total revenue methodology that is calculated based on the total authorized base revenue for each customer group. The RDM has also been expanded to include the company’s electric vehicle customer classes as well as outdoor lighting. The settlement lays out a methodology for computing a new revenue decoupling adjustment factor, based on monthly variances from expected revenues per customer class. The factor is a charge or credit applied to the bills of each customer class. The utility must cap the adjustment at 3.0% of authorized base revenues; any adjustments needed in excess of 3.0% will be deferred to the next billing cycle. The settlement also includes implementation of the arrearage management program (AMP). The AMP will be open to all customers coded as “Financial Hardship.” Those financial hardship customers are eligible for the AMP if they have past due balances of $200 or greater, 60 days or more past due. Financial Hardship customers will be offered enrollment in a budget billing payment plan to pay their average bill each month. For customers enrolled in, and complying with, the AMP, the company will forgive up to $400 per month, for a maximum annual arrearage of $4,800. The utility’s base rates can include $449,000 in annual revenue attributable to the implementation of the AMP. On May 28, 2026, the New Hampshire Public Utilities Commission approved the settlement in its entirety, paving the way for implementation of the AMP. On June 2, 2026, and in response to the order filed in Docket No. DE-25-025, Unitil filed an application for approval of its Revenue Decoupling Adjustment Factor (RDAF), which proposes reducing its RDAF charge from $0.00216 to $0.00108 per kWh for residential customers. The Commission filed a procedural order noting its approval of Unitil's proposed rates at the end of July 2026, then later filed a final order on September 11, 2026, fully approving the RDAF and other proposed rates.
sources: Docket No. DE 25-025; Settlement Agreement (Feb. 2026); Order (May 2026); Order (Sept. 2026)

description: S.B. 538, as enacted in July 2026, lays out long-term eligibility for net metering customers, which includes groups of one or more customers who are political divisions or LMI community solar projects. In line with a June 2017 order from the New Hampshire Public Utilities Commission, this bill allows LMI community solar projects designated for the Electric Assistance Program to lock in their net metering term for 20 years or until 2040, whichever is longer. If the Commission adopts a new tariff, then these systems can either stay on their existing tariff or enroll in the new tariff for 20 years, as long as they submitted an interconnection application before 2032; if a system transfers to the new tariff, it cannot revert back to the previous tariff.

A.B. 5327, as enacted in June 2026, appropriates $10,675,000 from the Global Warming Solutions Fund to the New Jersey Board of Public Utilities and directs the President of the Board or a designee to distribute the funds to electric public utilities that had a base rate case adjudicated between January 1, 2026 and July 1, 2026 solely to provide bill credits to their residential customers.

On August 4, 2026, the New Jersey Board of Public Utilities filed a notice of funding opportunity for a new round of Payment Assistance for Gas and Electric (PAGE) grants. Money from the Unclaimed Utility Deposits Trust Fund will be made available to a non-profit energy assistance organization to administer a program that provides assistance for payment of overdue electric or gas bills. Eligible recipients are New Jersey households with zero-to-moderate income and facing a financial hardship that includes a recent notice of overdue payment for gas or electric service on the electric bill for which assistance is being sought. Further, where practicable, recipients eligible for New Jersey's LIHEAP or Universal Service Fund (USF) should be directed to apply for those programs first. Recipients may only receive assistance once in a year, and priority is given to customers in danger of disconnection. All proposals must be received by September 4, 2026, and awards will be announced by November 1, 2026.

On June 30, 2026, the New Jersey Board of Public Utilities filed an order providing customers eligible for the Board's Winter Termination Program (WTP) with bill credits through the third iteration of Residential Energy Assistance Program (REAP). Staff recommended funding bill credits using available funds from the Regional Greenhouse Gas Initiative (RGGI); the most recent Strategic Funding Plan for the funds stated that the Board may utilize all or a portion of RGGI funds to support direct ratepayer relief that helps to lower costs for LMI residents. The Board approved a third round of bill credits through REAP, with residents receiving three $50 monthly bill credits over August, September, and October 2026 for a total of $150 in bill credits. The Board ordered that the third iteration will maintain the methodology of determining REAP eligibility by way of categorical WTP eligibility; however, the order outlines additional criteria to ensure that customers served by both gas and electric utilities receive REAP bill credits for either their gas or electric account, not for both. The Board further ordered public utilities to file a certification form of accounts deemed eligible to allow Staff to transmit funding. The order also includes procedures for the utilities to report the total customers who received credits and to return any unused funds.

On June 30, 2026, the New Jersey Board of Public Utilities issued an order in response to Executive Order 1, which required that the Board issue an additional iteration of Residential Universal Bill Credits (RUBCs) by July 1, 2026. Board Staff recommended an additional round of RUBCs funded by both Solar Alternative Compliance Payments (SACP) collected through the state's RPS and Clean Energy Program funds collected through the state's Societal Benefits Charge on electric bills. Between the remaining SACP funds and the Clean Energy Program RUBC line item, the state has a combined $170,800,978 available for RUBCs. The Board ordered that all residential households with an existing electric account with the state's electric distribution companies are eligible for RUBCs and that each eligible customer will receive one flat $25 credit during the month of August. The Board further made findings and modifications to procedure to allow for timely distribution of RUBCs and further required reporting by the companies of RUBC distribution by October 16, 2026.

A.B. 796, as enacted in July 2026, requires the New Jersey Board of Public Utilities to establish standards for the provision of electricity to large data center customers by electric public utilities within 12 months of the bill's effective date. The standards must (1) be designed to identify the defining characteristics of a large data center and large data center customer, including but not limited to minimum MW size, which will not be greater than 50 MW aggregate for data centers under common control; (2) ensure that other utility customers do not subsidize large data center customers, and costs incurred specifically to serve a large data center -- including infrastructure investments in generation, transmission, distribution, or substations -- must be allocated to that customer; (3) shield other customers from stranded costs if the data center later leaves or reduces its load; (4) incentivize large data center customers to bring their own new clean generation or energy storage to meet their energy needs; and (6) develop a framework for the tariff treatment of customers served in whole or in part by "co-located generation" (on-site power facilities serving a data center), ensuring those customers still pay their fair share of transmission, distribution, capacity, reliability, and public benefit costs tied to their use of the grid, among other requirements. Within 180 days of the Board order establishing the standards, each utility will file a petition with the Board for approval of a rate class and tariff for the provision of electricity to large data center customers. Financially, the tariff must require large data center customers to commit to paying for at least 85% of their requested electricity supply over a 10-year period, backed by deposits, financial security, or (for high-credit customers) financial commitments -- with the Board authorized to establish a stranded-cost recovery mechanism that applies only to this customer class. It must also provide large data center customers whose load or procured capacity is to be included in a large load adjustment, peak shaving adjustment, or successor form of submittal to the RTO and an opportunity to correct the data prior to submission; it must also include provisions to ensure that payment by the customer is proportionate to its share of the costs allocated by the RTO to the utility from a reliability backstop procurement auction; the share of costs will be reduced with the customer procurement of capacity resources. Data centers already approved for service before the law takes effect are exempt from the 85% payment guarantee, deposit requirements, and study cost requirement, though they remain subject to the tariff's other provisions, and this exemption doesn't extend to any future expansion. Finally, any service agreement with a large data center customer, however authorized, must meet these same substantive cost-protection standards, and the Board cannot approve any agreement that weakens them.
On August 10, 2026, the New Jersey Board of Public Utilities opened a docket in the matter of the implementation of the data center fair share act (A.B. 796).

On June 24, 2026, the New Jersey Board of Public Utilities, in collaboration with the New Jersey Department of Community Affairs (NJCDA), announced a Summer Termination Program (STP). The STP ran from June 15 through August 31st and prevented electric utility service disconnection for qualifying residential customers. Customers who qualified for LIHEAP or any other NJCDA assistance programs were eligible. Other individuals unable to pay their utility bills due to circumstances beyond their control, such as unemployment, illness, medically related expenses, recent death of a family member, or other circumstances resulting in financial hardship may have qualified.

categories: Customer Cost Allocation; Customer Cost-Saving Programs
description: S.B. 4373 requires the Division of Housing and Community Resources in the Department of Community Affairs to enter into a memorandum of understanding with each state agency and statewide non-profit energy assistance organization that is not currently on the Department's consolidated application portal and that administers a utility assistance program to be included in the Department's website. Each relevant organization and agency must enter into the memorandum of understanding, assist the Department in updating the consolidated application, and alert the Department to temporary programs that provide financial assistance for utility bill payments and energy efficiency measures to be incorporated into the form. Current law only requires a memorandum of understanding to be between the Department and a statewide non-profit agency that administers its own program. The Senate passed the bill in June 2026.

categories: Customer Cost Allocation; Utility Oversight and Cost Recovery
description: On June 10, 2026, the New Jersey Board of Public Utilities (BPU) filed an order approving BPU Staff's recommended changes to the state's Universal Service Fund (USF) program, citing the need to address energy affordability for LMI customers. The BPU approved Staff's recommendations to authorize and direct the utilities to approve payments resulting from USF applications for the remainder of the program year and to move the program administration from the Department of Community Affairs to the BPU for the following program year. Staff also recommended that utility performance targets be amended to scale up rather than scale down to address increased workload. The USF enrollment targets would be a 2% increase over program year one (October 2025-September 2026) compared to the base year, 3% in year two compared to the prior program year, and 5% in year three compared to the prior program year. The BPU approved the recommendations, reasoning that they would improve application times and increase enrollment access due to sufficient utility resources; the BPU also noted that the utilities' costs would remain subject to audit. The Board further found that employing the utilities' resources would ultimately benefit customers and utilities by reducing utility uncollectibles, reducing disconnections, and subsequently increasing energy affordability.

A.B. 1072, as passed by the Assembly in June 2026, requires the New Jersey Board of Public Utilities to establish a distributed energy storage incentive program within 180 days. In general, the program should, in conjunction with existing incentive programs, incentivize 3,000 MW of customer-sited and front-of-the-meter energy storage by 2032; however, the Board may reduce the procurement goal to no less than 2,000 MW if the original target’s costs will likely outweigh the benefits to ratepayers. The Board must provide incentives in blocks: up to 350 MW by 2028, at least 1,000 MW by 2030 (inclusive of the previous 350 MW), at least 2,000 MW by 2032, and at least 2,000 MW in subsequent blocks. The incentives should be administratively-determined and fixed, paid out annually for 15 years based on capacity; incentive levels must be differentiated by project characteristics, cannot exceed 40% of a project's total cost, and may include adders for certain attributes. Further, the Board must reserve at least one quarter of the incentives provided to customer classes or deployment scenarios that face greater economic hurdles, including but not limited to LMI customers and customers located in or serving overburdened communities; however the Board may reduce this goal if it finds that it will materially interfere with the procurement goals above.

subtopics: Advanced Transmission Technologies; Grid Utilization; Non-Wires Alternatives
description: A.B. 5188, as enacted in July 2026, requires that before constructing a supplemental transmission project, an electric public utility must explain in its application whether the project will deploy ATTs in addition to or in lieu of traditional transmission investments and benefits thereof. If the utility elects not to deploy ATTs, the application must include an explanation for the decision and a third-party analysis of the cost-effectiveness of the project. The New Jersey Board of Public Utilities must develop grid performance benchmarks based on criteria such as reliability, cost effectiveness, and reduced transmission congestion to evaluate the proposed projects. The bill further includes two sets of criteria for the Board to use to evaluate applications and the circumstances under which each set of criteria should be applied.

subtopics: Grid Utilization; Planning Rules; Streamlining Interconnection
description: On June 5, 2024, the New Jersey Board of Public Utilities (BPU) filed a notice that the first Grid Modernization Forum Workgroup was formed with the working title "Integrated Distribution and DER System Planning (IDDER)." The IDDER workgroup is tasked with advancing formal requirements for electric distribution companies to file proactive plans to outline their intentions to evolve more adaptive and flexible distribution systems with increased hosting capacities. On February 3, 2026, BPU Staff filed an RFI in response to the Governor's Executive Order 2 (January 20, 2026). The RFI requests that Atlantic City Electric, Jersey Central Power & Light, Public Service Electric & Gas, and Rockland Electric Company provide feedback within 30 days on topics including (1) how the utility is working to comply with the BPU's Interconnection of Class I Renewable Energy Systems regulations; (2) opportunities for the Board to modify or waive existing regulations to improve efficiency and speed of interconnecting new projects; (3) how the utility can improve hosting capacity maps and ensure projects can connect to 34.5 kV distribution lines; (4) constrained circuits in the utility territory that should be upgraded to expedite and support interconnection of DERs; and (5) other means of supporting interconnection of DERs on constrained circuits. On April 20, 2026, the Board filed an order expanding the opportunity for all interested parties to provide written response. On April 29, 2026, the Integrated Distribution of DERs (IDDER) Workgroup under the Board's Grid Modernization Forum filed its workgroup summary. The summary outlined its past meetings under its purpose of advancing a formal requirement that the utilities file Proactive System Upgrade Plans (PSUP). The PSUPs are designed to move segments of the distribution grid towards being more adaptive and flexible and having higher DER hosting capacities. On May 8, 2026, the Workgroup published its straw proposal for PSUPs. PSUPs will qualitatively describe cost-effective three- and ten-year distribution system strategies to achieve goals including (1) affordably increase generation hosting and load serving capacity to prepare for increased DERs and load growth and (2) utilize DERMS and non-traditional distribution solutions to better oversee the distribution system and increase grid utilization. The straw proposal outlines filing requirements, baseline distribution system assessment, load and DG forecasting, and solution identification.
sources: Docket No. QO24030199; Order (Feb. 2026); Straw Proposal (May 2026)

description: A.B. 4881, or the Power NJ Act, as enacted in July 2026, requires the New Jersey Board of Public Utilities to promote construction of affordable advanced nuclear energy projects in the state. Within 180 days of the effective date, the Board will issue a request for expression of interest for construction of advanced nuclear projects in the state. The expressions of interest must include: (1) a Class IV cost estimate (a cost estimate prepared in accordance with certain specified practice and an expected accuracy range of approximately -30% to 50%) or better; (2) the proposed capital structure and financing plan, including evidence that the project is pursuing available federal financing; (3) the proposed output to be made available to the state and any PJM procurement program; (4) any proposed offtake agreements and their role in financing the project with a description of the anticipated ratepayer benefits and any commitment by the parties to share in capital costs and any potential cost overruns; (5) the proposed price structure for the reliable capacity certificates (RCC); (6) a projection of the anticipated monthly bill impact on ratepayers resulting from the proposed RCC price structure; (7) a proposal for returning to state ratepayers some or all revenues earned from sales in the PJM market during the RCC term; and (8) an economic analysis of the project, including consideration of potential downward pressure on PJM wholesale market prices. The Board must begin a preliminary evaluation of all proposed projects and provisionally qualify or deny each proposed project no more than 90 days after receipt of a complete expression of interest. The bill further requires that no later than 18 months after first issuing an order approving a project, the Board will establish a reliable capacity certificate (RCC) program to require that a proportional number of MWh sold in the state by each electric power supplier and basic generation service provider be from nuclear energy generated by qualified projects; the program will be designed to support at least 1,100 MW of capacity from qualified projects. The Board will approve projects contingent on requirements including a net benefit to ratepayers as a result of the project and offtaker risk mitigation provisions.

categories: Planning and Procurement; Utility Business Model
description: Planning and Procurement: On July 24, 2026, Atlantic City Electric (ACE) filed a petition to develop a battery energy storage system (BESS) up to 500 MW on company-owned property, with a projected operational date in late 2030. ACE outlined its case that the New Jersey Board of Public Utilities has the authority to approve a BESS owned by ACE. The company claimed that the Board has broad authority to take steps to support energy affordability and reliability and argued that the BESS will provide necessary capacity to support these objectives. It further claimed that statutes permitting utilities to invest in energy efficiency and conservation may also apply to BESS because such facilities conserve energy and improve overall grid efficiency. It further stated that it was pursuing the BESS project in the name of affordability and in alignment with Governor Sherrill's Executive Orders No. 1 and No. 2. The company intends to sell the services associated with the project into the PJM market and use them to offset customer costs. ACE clarified that it will not seek cost recovery until the project is in-service, but it is expecting to recover through base rates. Utility Business Model: Separately, ACE claimed that the project would not run afoul of statute that prevents utilities from providing electric generation service, since BESS are not generation technologies. On September 4, 2026, Board Staff issued a letter finding that ACE's petition was administratively deficient and directed the company to cure the deficiencies. On September 9, 2026, the Board filed an order determining that the petition should be retained for hearing if and when ACE cures the deficiencies.

subtopics: Study (Large Load Cost Shift Prevention; Procurement Rules)
description: On August 13, 2026, the New Jersey Board of Public Utilities released a report outlining the state of the current PJM market, noting high Base Residual Auction prices and capacity market outcomes becoming an increasingly large driver of retail electricity rates. The report recommends that since the data center customer class is the primary driver of current resource adequacy risks, reforms should aim to allocate the costs and risks associated with providing service to it. Specifically, the recommendations include (1) requiring data center projects to bring their own new capacity, (2) state level priority curtailments that may force data centers to pay for their own new supply or accept curtailment, and (3) regional interim resource adequacy service (IRAS), which would be implemented at the PJM level, requiring large loads that wish to receive the same level of firm service as other load to bring sufficient new capacity or otherwise take service under the IRAS. The report further states that New Jersey will largely operationalize these reforms through implementing the recently passed Data Center Fair Share Act (A.B. 796). Related to broader concerns about high capacity market prices, the report also recommended the PJM implement market reforms to improve the capacity market and that states direct long-term procurements for new resource development.
sources: An Investigation of PJM's Capacity Market (Aug. 2026); NJ BPU Press Release (Aug. 2026)

description: On April 9, 2026, the New Jersey Board of Public Utilities (BPU) initiated a proceeding on the electric utility business model study being conducted pursuant to Executive Order 1. On April 16, 2026, the BPU filed a notice of a public stakeholder meeting to address issues in the executive order pertaining to the study. The stakeholder meeting will cover the relationship between the traditional business model and recent trends affecting electricity affordability and opportunities including making utility revenue models less dependent on capital spending on infrastructure, expansion of performance based ratemaking, multi-year rate plans, lowering return on equity, least cost resource testing requirements, greater use of asset securitization, and amendments to regulations governing infrastructure investment programs. On July 15, 2026, Energy and Environmental Economics (E3) submitted their Phase 1 Report on Modernizing New Jersey's Electric Utility Business Model for the BPU. Phase 1 focuses on how electricity bills in New Jersey are currently determined, evaluating the implications of the current utility business model on customer costs, and assessing potential utility business model reforms. Specifically, the study assesses how potential utility business model modernization can influence the distribution portion of the customer bill that the BPU can directly influence. The report states that utility business model reform at the state regulation level can act mostly on the distribution and programmatic portion of the bill, that no one reform or modernization is a clear solution, that the most reliable near-term gains could come from "cost-discipline," and that other financing, incentive, and performance-based reforms could follow with more mature data, baselines, and customer data.
sources: Docket No. EO26040117; Phase 1 Utility Business Model Report (July 2026)

description: On August 6, 2026, Jersey Center Power & Light (JCP&L) filed a request to increase its distribution base rates, citing storm recovery costs, program costs, and other capital costs. Testimony in the request responded to recommendations from a previous Management Audit Order. The recommendations included (1) providing testimony showing that ratepayers have not been adversely impacted by FirstEnergy's actions related to the Ohio H.B. 6 investigation or any costs for resolving related investigations, (2) addressing the recommendation that the company consider holding the depreciation and carrying charges associated with FirstEnergy Service Corporation previously charged to FirstEnergy Solutions Corp and First Energy Nuclear Operating Company at the parent company, rather than increasing the allocation to the regulated entities, and (3) provide testimony addressing the recommendation that the company restructure the basis for allocating Directors and Officers (“D&O”) insurance costs to JCP&L to avoid charging it amounts arising from risks to which it does not contribute. JCP&L stated in its testimony that it believes its customers were shielded from any costs as a result of FirstEnergy’s actions related to its federal investigation or any costs associated with related investigations and that the company believed that the allocations to JCP&L after the loss of FirstEnergy Solutions Corp. and FirstEnergy Nuclear Operating Company were appropriate. JCP&L further stated that the third recommendation's implementation plan had not yet been addressed and will be considered in a future forensic audit. An additional recommendation from the previous audit included recognizing compensation of the FirstEnergy chair and executive director as a shareowner cost, rather than customer cost. Testimony stated that these positions were temporary and that allocations from FirstEnergy being sought for recovery would not include any compensation associated with the role. The rate increase is proposed to go into effect on May 6, 2027; however, to delay the impact on customer's the company proposed Rider TXA, which will provide a one-to-one offset of the increase to the customer charge and volumetric rate to all residential customers through a bill credit from May 6, 2027 to December 31, 2027. Instead of increasing rates, the company will flow through deferred tax savings and an refund of an overcollection balance of $26.8 million in spent nuclear fuel costs. Deferred taxes will need to be collected in the future, which will result in a higher tax expense in future rate cases.

On March 13, 2026, the New Jersey Board of Public Utilities (BPU) scheduled an informational session and invited comments on a BPU Staff straw proposal for a one-year extension of New Jersey's second energy efficiency and peak demand reduction program, known as "Triennium 2.5," which would extend Triennium 2 through the period of July 1, 2027 to June 30, 2028. The straw proposal focuses on promoting affordability and cites Executive Orders No. 1 and No. 2 as part of the motivation. The proposal would use gross savings (total reduction in energy consumption directly resulting from measures installed through the program), rather than net savings (gross savings adjusted to account for what would have occurred without the programs) to comply with Clean Energy Act requirements at a lower cost. BPU Staff also proposed setting the upcoming Program Year 7 (PY7)/FY2028 targets equal to that of PY6. The same total electric target of 2% savings would be adjusted for compliance based on gross savings. The document further directs each utility to apply its approved weighted average net-to-gross at the Triennium 2 portfolio level to their PY6 budget to determine its maximum Triennium 2.5 budget.
sources: Docket No. QO25050300; Triennium 2.5 Straw Proposal (Mar. 2026)

description: A.B. 2757, as enacted in July 2026, requires any transmission owner located in New Jersey to be a member of, and transfer control of any electric transmission facilities that it operates to, an RTO. Because current utility participation is voluntary, utilities are eligible for a 0.5% adder on their return on equity for transmission assets. By mandating participation, utilities are no longer eligible for the adder.

subtopics: Bill Assistance; Cost Shift Prevention (Large Load)
description: As part of a general rate case stipulation filed on June 22, 2026, Xcel Energy agreed to develop a new large load tariff within six months. The tariff should be designed to ensure that all costs attributable to large load customers are assigned to that customer class and do not shift costs or risks to other customers. The utility also agreed to changes for its Electric Affordability Program (EAP). Xcel will evaluate whether the proposed $750,000/year budget is sufficient; it must also make a one-time shareholder contribution of $750,000 to improve program reach, supplement benefits, or support outreach and administration. It must convene an EAP workgroup to evaluate the program, and the workgroup must provide recommendations in the utility's next rate case. Xcel must coordinate its EAP with other low-income programs, including energy efficiency, weatherization, LIHEAP, and customer outreach resources.

subtopics: Cost Shift Prevention (Large Load); Low-Income Discount Rates
description: As part of a general rate case filed on March 27, 2026, El Paso Electric (EPE) proposed a new Low Income Rider to waive the monthly fixed charge for low-income residential customers enrolled in SNAP or LIHEAP. The utility already offers a Low Income Rider in its Texas jurisdiction, and this proposal mirrors the Texas offering. EPE will identify customers using the New Mexico Human Services Department Health Care Authority Client Database, and customers would receive the discount for 12 months or the length of their enrollment in the identified program, whichever is less. The current fixed charge is $7, and EPE has a proposed an increase to $14.36 in Phase 1 and $18.89 in Phase 2. EPE also proposed two new large load tariffs. The new High Load Factor Power Service rate would apply to facilities 30 MW or higher with average monthly load factors 85% or higher. The tariff includes a minimum bill, minimum 20-year contract term, financial security requirements, exit fees, and a facility charge. The new Large Load Power Service rate would apply to facilities 10 MW or higher with monthly load factors that can vary from month to month. This tariff also includes a minimum bill, minimum 20-year contract term, and financial security requirements. EPE also proposed changes to its line extension policy to address large load requests. First, any customer requesting an alternate primary voltage line must either make a customer contribution equal to the estimated cost of the extension or pay a monthly facilities charge equal to the utility's fixed charges on the extension. Second, if the alternate extension requires a reservation of distribution capacity, then the customer must pay a Reserved Distribution Capacity Charge. Third, if a customer requires a transformer over 750 kVA, EPE will request verification from the customer's electrician. If the customer does not verify its planned connected load, then EPE will provide a transformer sized to the verified load and reserve distribution capacity for up to one year after transformer installation; if the customer still does not verify, then it will bill the Distribution Capacity Reservation Charge to any customer that requests to hold the reservation past the one-year period. Fourth, any customer interconnection 30 MW or more at the distribution level would be responsible for the costs of any unplanned substation and transmission line upgrades. If EPE installs and operates the facilities, then the customer must pay an Infrastructure Capacity Charge to recover the costs.

On March 16, 2026, the New Mexico Public Regulation Commission opened a docket to investigate El Paso Electric's and Xcel Energy's treatment of community solar credits for budget-billed customers. Under statute, utilities must apply community solar credits "to subscriber bills within one billing cycle following the cycle during which the energy was generated" for all subscribers, but RFI responses from both utilities implied that the crediting process for budget-billed customers is different than the crediting process for non-budget-billed customers; the RFI response from Public Service Company of New Mexico explicitly stated that the process is the same for budget-billed and non-budget billed. Commission Staff held an educational session regarding the issue on April 1, 2026. In early July 2026, Xcel Energy notified the Commission that it had fixed its process to comply with statute; El Paso Electric notified the Commission in mid-August 2026.

On April 20, 2026, El Paso Electric (EPE) filed an application to implement a demand response and DER pilot, originally proposed in its 2025 IRP. The pilot would, at each home, install a 20 kW / 57.6 kWh front-of-the-meter solar-plus-storage system, a smart panel for full home automation and control (including HVAC, hot water heaters, electric vehicle charging, and all switched loads), and an inverter that can correct power factor and provide overall DER control. By aggregating solar, storage, demand response, and energy efficiency, the systems could be controlled to support phase balance correction for the distribution feeder for the benefit of all customers. Systems would be installed at up to 250 new homes, plus up to 10 existing low-income homes. The systems would be installed, owned, and operated by a third party; EPE would communicate dispatch and scheduling needs to the program administrator, who would then implement the dispatch instructions. The pilot has a proposed budget of $1.64 million in the first year, increasing by 2% per year thereafter, and an expected nominal budget of $66.5 million over 30 years, in addition to $350,000 for a demonstration site and $47,000 for a value stream analysis. Cost recovery would be deferred to a future ratemaking proceeding.

On September 10, 2026, the New Mexico Public Regulation Commission issued an order establishing a volunteer working group to develop and propose amendments to the Commission's IRP rule, with a focus on responding to increased demand from large load customers. Rule amendments will be intended to reduce excessive delay and regulatory uncertainty in the planning and resource procurement process, while maintaining appropriate Commission oversight, stakeholder engagement, and ratepayer protections.

Executive Order 2026-023, signed in April 2026, creates the New Mexico Energy Affordability and Reliability Council. The Council must: (1) recommend strategies that ensure residential, rural, tribal, and small business customers are not disproportionately burdened by the cost of capital investments to meet growing electricity demand; (2) recommend affordable utility rate designs that protect consumers while ensuring investment in grid modernization, reliability, and resilience; (3) assess financing strategies, alternative project delivery methods, and rate design approaches that minimize long-term rate escalation, avoided stranded costs, and prevent regressive cost impacts on frontline communities and vulnerable populations; (4) recommend strategies that advance progress to net-zero emissions by supporting affordable access to zero-carbon electricity; (5) balance cost containment with other issues when assessing strategies that preserve environmental, tribal, transparency, and quality assurance safeguards; (6) recommend measures that enhance transparency in infrastructure planning, including providing stakeholders with visibility into projected investments and associated cost impacts; (7) recommend streamlining for state and local permitting review timelines; (8) design a framework to appropriately adjust permitting to accelerate low-carbon impact projects and prioritize state resources on projects that require deeper review or coordination; and (9) ensure alignment with applicable innovation, infrastructure, and economic development funding. The Council must submit its final report, including recommendations, by November 1, 2026.

On April 16, 2026, Public Service Company of New Mexico (PNM) filed its 2027-2029 Energy Efficiency and Load Management Program Plan, continuing its sliding scale profit incentive, allowing PNM to earn 7.10% of annual program costs if it achieves 81 GWh in annual savings. For each GWh above 81 GWh, it would earn an additional 0.125% up to 86 GWh. For each GWh above 86 GWh, it would earn an additional 0.175% up to 91 GWh. For each GWh above 91 GWh, it would earn an additional 0.225% up to 100 GWh, for a maximum incentive of 10.54% of annual program costs.

On April 20, 2026, in an ongoing proceeding to investigate resource adequacy and planning to ensure that electric utilities' supply of energy is sufficient to satisfy demands and maintain reliable, continuous service, the Public Utilities Commission of Nevada filed a procedural order. This order directs comments to be submitted on the topic of specific challenges or concerns presented by large load self-generation. On May 21, 2026, Microsoft Corporation filed comments requesting that the Commission consider a proposed Ratepayer Protection Tariff (RPT). The RPT is a rate design model that prioritizes ratepayer protections above all else by holding large load customers accountable for paying both the costs they cause and their share of existing costs associated with the provision of safe and reliable service. Under this tariff, large load customers would pay all of the new costs caused by the large load customer and otherwise applicable rates that recover the new customer's fair share of existing system costs. Ratepayers are protected from cost shifts from large customers because these costs are separated and directly allocated to the cost-causing customer.

In December 2025, Nevada Power and Sierra Pacific Power filed applications to implement a new tariff, Net Metering Rider-Solar Powered Affordable Housing Systems (Schedule No. NMR-SPAHS) that allows for qualifying multifamily affordable housing properties to operate solar-powered affordable housing systems, as required by A.B. 458 of 2025. A.B. 458 established virtual net metering for low-income multifamily housing with renewable energy systems no larger than 1 MW. Virtual net metering will function the same as traditional net metering currently approved for the utilities, however, net metering credits associated with the system will be allocated to the individual tenants according to the allocation schedule provided by the owner of the energy system, without requiring the energy system to be physically interconnected with the meter of each tenant. The aggregate capacity limit for each utility's tariff is 50 MW until the limit expires on December 31, 2029. NV Energy and Commission Staff filed a stipulation in June 2026, and the Public Utilities Commission of Nevada issued an order on July 1, 2026, accepting the stipulation and approving the new Net Metering Rider-Solar Powered Affordable Housing Systems tariff.
sources: Docket No. 25-12029 (Nevada Power); Docket No. 25-12030 (Sierra Pacific Power); A.B. 458 (2025)

description: On April 17, 2026, Nevada Power submitted a report evaluating the existing programs in the state that provide energy and energy-related assistance to the state's ratepayers. The report includes information on three government and customer funded programs, three NV Energy Foundation-Funded programs, and two other programs to aid customers.

On May 1, 2026, NV Energy filed a petition with the Public Utilities Commission of Nevada for adoption of alternative ratemaking goals and outcomes, in line with new regulations. NV Energy's proposed goals and outcomes focus on providing smaller but more frequent and predictable changes in rates; enhancing efficiency at the utility; and aiming to reduce administrative burdens for the Commission, stakeholders and the utility. The petition presents four goals: (1) balancing interests while ensuing an economically viable utility model, (2) enhanced customer engagement, (3) enhanced safety and reliability screening, and (4) balanced customer interests with utility predictability. Each goal has a series of outcomes associated with it. The outcomes for Goal 1 are rates that are more predictable and feature gradual changes that reflect major capital projects; rate changes that are determined reasonable based on identified cost drivers over a specified period such as a multi-year rate plan; large customer load growth that is reflected in rate changes, ideally benefiting households, small businesses and existing industrial customers; and administrative cost reductions that are measured to determine if more regulatory efficiency is captured with alternative ratemaking. The outcomes for Goal 2 are greater customer rate awareness through better customer education and the development of new customer awareness tools. Goal 3 has one outcome, which is tracking reliability, safety, and risk reduction related to projects that are not part of the Natural Disaster Protection Plan. The outcomes for Goal 4 are rates that support utility financial stability and dampen rate impacts when compared to traditional ratemaking; and balancing regulatory lag between customers and the utility. On September 17, 2026, NV Energy, the Regulatory Operations Staff of the Commission, and additional parties filed a stipulation recommending that the Commission does not adopt a list of alternative ratemaking goals and outcomes within this docket given that the specifics of alternative ratemaking mechanism utility proposals in future rate cases are inherently uncertain and will impact any goals and outcomes generated from this docket. Further, the stipulating parties support vacating the remainder of this docket's procedural schedule.

A.B. 10160, as passed by the Assembly and Senate in June 2026, requires gas or electric corporations to accept and credit any public assistance payment tendered on behalf of a residential customer by a social services district or the office of temporary and disability assistance, including but not limited to payments made pursuant to the home energy assistance program, and emergency funding from social services programs. Upon receipt of such payment or notice that such payment has been authorized or issued, a gas or electric corporation shall treat the payment as made for all purposes under this section, including restoration of residential utility service, and satisfaction of other forms of collections activity, regardless of the status of the customer's account.

As part of an ongoing case considering energy affordability for low-income residents of New York, the New York Public Service Commission filed an order on February 12, 2026 that permanently paused customer disenrollments in utility energy affordability programs and ensures utilities will continue to provide assistance to low-income customers during federal government shutdowns and continued uncertainty around federally-funded programs. Additionally, the Commission filed an order on February 17, 2026 allowing Central Hudson Gas & Electric, Consolidated Edison, New York State Electric & Gas, National Grid, Orange & Rockland, and Rochester Gas & Electric to carry out their cost recovery plans for implementation of the low-income energy assistance pilots in their next base rate proceedings. On June 30, 2026, Orange & Rockland filed a petition seeking an emergency increase to its Energy Assistance Program (EAP), raising the program cap to 3.0% of its total revenue across both gas and electric service. Without the budget cap increase, Orange & Rockland's electric customers' energy burden is estimated to be 6.77%, meaning EAP customers are paying $20 more than they should be. An increase of the program cap to 3.0% reduced energy burden to 6.0%, and saves customers that $20.

A.B. 11560, as passed by both chambers in June 2026, requires utilities to file with the New York Public Service Commission an independent classification of service for large data centers (those with a peak demand of 20 MW or more) that is distinct from other classifications of service. The service classification should assign all costs (including those associated with infrastructure upgrades, administrative expenses, operational costs, and rate of return) to serve these large data centers entirely to this classification. The classification should also mitigate risks and impacts to other service classifications from large data centers, ensuring there are no increases to surcharges, basic service, or other fixed charges not directly related to energy usage.

On February 12, 2026, the New York Public Service Commission issued an order initiating a proceeding to review the planning and interconnection processes, cost allocation mechanisms, and tariff structures relating to the integration of large loads within the state’s transmission and distribution systems. Interested stakeholders were directed to file comments by May 13, 2026. On July 14, 2026, the Commission filed a press release highlighting Governor Hochul's statewide moratorium on data center permits.

On July 14, 2026, the Governor of New York signed an executive order imposing a moratorium on permitting for data centers pending a generic environmental impact statement. The executive order includes a number of energy-related provisions, including: (1) directing the New York Department of Public Service (DPS) to consider a grid acceleration fund, which would require data centers to make upfront contributions to grid upgrades, participate in demand response, fund procurement of new clean energy and DERs, and contribute to a stranded asset insurance pool; (2) requiring DPS to stand up a data center interconnection working group and convene transmission owners to review system impacts from large loads, and allowing DPS to create new service classes for data centers; (3) allowing DPS to require data centers to fund new clean generation or battery storage dedicated to their own operations, including customer sited DERs; and (4) directing DPS to provide guidance on setting up and maintaining a fund that data center developers and operators pay into, usable for energy affordability efforts.

S.B. 1327, as passed by both chambers in June 2026, requires the New York Public Service Commission to establish standard payment plans for eligible customers' utility bills. Those standards include consideration of household income, ability to pay, payment history, bill size, and other factors; a grace period of 21 days to pay the bill; prorating a rate increase across a payment plan; and prohibiting disconnections while on a payment plan. Eligible customers include those households enrolled in income-based assistance programs.

categories: Utility Business Model; Utility Oversight and Cost Recovery
description: In August 2026, the New York Public Service Commission opened a docket to address the affordability index and other affordability measures required by budget bills A.B. 10008 and S.B. 9008, enacted in May 2026. The Commission plans to discuss the matter at its September 17, 2026 meeting. On September 17, 2026, the Commission filed an order formally initiating this proceeding. Utility Business Model: The budget bill included requirements that the Commission create performance-based targets around affordability. The Commission directed Staff to include proposals for those targets in the Energy Affordability Index. Utility Oversight and Cost Recovery: New York Department of Public Service Staff will, with an external energy affordability consultant, develop an energy affordability index. Large electric utilities in the state will assist by providing data on their number of customers served, mean and median annual bill, and mean and median annual energy consumption. These data will be broken down by ZIP code, electric vs. gas service, and heat vs. power service. According to the law, in each major rate filing, the utilities must include the Energy Affordability Index. Additionally, the order directed Staff to conduct a review of the energy burden of the utilities’ residential customers and file a report with findings by July 1, 2027. Finally, the order provided interim guidance while the Energy Affordability Index is finalized. The utilities will submit separate energy burden calculations for all electric, gas, and combined electric and gas residential customers by dividing the utility’s actual annual median residential household costs for gas or electric service by the corresponding annual median household income.
sources: Docket No. 26-M-0547; NY PSC Press Release (Sept. 2026); Order Initiating Proceeding (Sept. 2026)

description: At a recent utility collections conference attended by multiple New York utilities, an employee from one of the utilities allegedly joked that “people think much better in the dark” when discussing service shutoffs. The New York Public Service Commission opened an investigation into these comments requesting a range of information from New York utilities, including: (1) identification of any programs or incentive structures utilized with third-party revenue or arrears collection vendors; (2) providing all documents, including but not limited to any policy, standard operation procedure, manual(s), or employee training materials, and a detailed description of all existing practices and policies related to arrears and revenue collection; (3) providing all documents including but not limited to any policy, standard operation procedure, manual(s), or employee training materials, and a detailed description for the qualification and termination of service for Life Saving Equipment (LSE) customers, senior citizens, and medically impaired individuals; (4) providing a detailed breakdown of the process and timeline for customer notifications issued in pursuit of termination for arrears; and (5) confirming the use of Deferred Payment Agreements (DPAs) as a mechanism to help customers avoid service shut-offs and provide all documents including but not limited to any policy, standard operation procedure, manual(s), or employee training materials, and a detailed description of the utility’s process to implement DPAs.

On July 16, 2026, the New York Public Service Commission initiated a proceeding to examine all regulated utilities' estimated billing practices. The Commission directs New York Department of Public Service Staff to conduct an examination of the procedures, methodologies, and practices of Central Hudson Gas & Electric, Consolidated Edison (Con Ed), New York State Electric & Gas (NYSEG), National Grid, Orange & Rockland Utilities (O&R), and Rochester Gas & Electric (RGE), with respect to estimated billing. Staff will file a report and any resulting recommendations for public comment within 180 days of utility responses to this order. The information requested is: (1) an examination of the utilities’ policies and procedures for obtaining actual meter readings and relying on estimates of customer usage for billing; (2) an examination of the barriers to obtaining actual meter reads and how the utilities and municipalities currently address such barriers; (3) an analysis of the frequency of estimated billing and the root causes for it; (4) an examination of how the utilities ensure the accuracy of their records of the reason for failing to obtain an actual meter reading; (5) a review of the prevalence of AMI or AMR in utility service territories and the impact of using such technology on the frequency of estimated billing; (6) an examination of the adequacy and reasonableness of the methodologies the utilities use to calculate estimated bills; (7) recommendations for Commission consideration to improve the utilities policies, procedures, methodologies, and practices regarding obtaining actual meter readings and estimated billing; and (8) an assessment of whether additional actions, limitations, consequences, refunds, or penalties are needed to address estimated billing. The utilities must also provide: (1) current procedures for obtaining an actual meter reading and any other procedures related to estimated billing; (2) the number of estimated bills issued as a total number and as the percentage of total bills for each year for the past 10 years; and (3) the number of AMI and/or AMR meters (specifying each separately) as a total number and as a percentage of the total number of meters throughout the service territory each year for the previous 10 years.

On May 22, 2026, FirstEnergy's three Ohio electric companies - Ohio Edison, Cleveland Electric Illuminating, and Toledo Edison - filed an application for three-year electric distribution rates. The companies proposed a new Energy Assistance Fund program for customers at or below 300% of the Federal Poverty Level, which would provide grants to restore customer service up to $500 per customer per year, with a total program cost of $ 4 million; the companies do not plan to recover the costs of this program from ratepayers. The companies also proposed a new Emergency Energy Support Fund for customers at or below 200% of the Federal Poverty Level, which would provide grants up to $250 per customer per year to help customers avoid disconnection or restore service, with a forecasted cost of $1 million. The programs are intended to run from June 1, 2029 to June 30, 2030.

On July 21, 2026, AES Ohio filed a stipulation and settlement in its ongoing three-year rate case, where it proposed a new Data Center Tariff for data center customers with a maximum monthly aggregate demand of 25 MW. A customer may take generation service from AES Ohio only if the customer certifies it is unable to secure generation service from an alternate generation supplier, and customers have a monthly billing demand of 85% of contract capacity. Upon requesting service, a customer must pay for the cost of facilities studies; based on the company’s studies, a customer must pay the costs of facilities necessary to provide service to the customer. The company may divide its facilities construction into phases, and the customer is allowed a maximum load ramp of two years per phase of construction. Following the ramp period, the customer must enter a contract for a minimum of 10 years; a customer may terminate the contract with 36 months of notice and pay an exit fee equal to the minimum charge for at least 75% of the service term or the actual costs of facilities built to serve the customer multiplied by the percentage of the service term remaining. To cover the above obligations, the customer must provide a collateral requirement equal to the sum of (1) the minimum charges during the ramp period, (2) three years of minimum charges during the service term, and (3) the exit fee in the form of a parent guaranty, a letter of credit, or cash.

On January 15, 2026, FirstEnergy filed an application and compliance tariffs in the matter of the review of the non-market-based services rider (Rider NMB). On March 11, 2026, Public Utilities Commission of Ohio (PUCO) Staff filed its review, recommending approval of the application for rates effective April 1, 2026, subject to a recommendation that due to the large projected growth of data centers in Ohio, the utility will be required to provide updated data center load growth information semi-annually to PUCO Staff and that any data center not participating in the Rider NMB Pilot Program is not be eligible to the added to the Rider NMB Pilot Program after April 1, 2026. On April 17, 2026, the Ohio Consumer's Council filed a request for rehearing. On May 13, 2026, PUCO denied the request for rehearing and directed FirstEnergy to file an application within 30 days for approval of a tariff creating a separate class for data centers to assure that future costs are properly allocated to these customers. On June 12, 2026, the FirstEnergy Ohio companies proposed a new Schedule Data Center Tariff (DCT) after PUCO directed the utility to file for a separate customer class for data centers. The tariff applies to any customer operating a data center or mobile data center, with no minimum load threshold, and requires a minimum monthly billing demand equal to the higher of 85% of contracted capacity or actual usage. New data center loads must sign contracts with an initial term equal to the load ramp period (up to 4 years) plus 10 years, though customers may exit after the seventh year following the ramp period by paying an exit fee equal to 36 months of minimum charges. New customers must also post collateral covering dedicated transmission and distribution infrastructure costs, scaled to creditworthiness. Customers must procure generation from a competitive retail supplier rather than standard service.

On March 30, 2026, as a part of its general rate case pre-filing, Duke Energy Ohio modified its electric service regulations and Rider X line extension policy to include provisions applicable to individual or aggregate customers with large service demands. For both the regulations and Rider X, customers seeking service of 40 MW or greater at one or more aggregated premises, or whose demand is reasonably expected to grow to this level, or require significant transmission and/or distribution investments by the utility for the provision of service may be required to provide the utility appropriate financial and/or performance and credit assurance at the utility's discretion.

On February 6, 2026, AEP Ohio filed an application to commence a collaborative process before it finalizes its proposed tariff for the generation-related costs of data centers. Additionally, AEP Ohio requested interim protocols for standard service offer (SSO) price volatility and magnitude mitigation, should data centers return to the SSO. These include: (1) If for some reason the reliability backstop auction (RBA) price does not follow the data center customer MWs when they return to the SSO, a separate procurement or auction product should be acquired for data center load being served by the SSO (i.e., so that the data centers can pay the full price of their procurement without impacting the regular SSO price); (2) Data center customers should provide 180 days advance notice to AEP Ohio prior to returning to the SSO, in order to implement solutions being provided in a timely manner; and (3) If the data center does not provide sufficient advance notice before returning to the SSO, spot market purchases will be made during any period that a separate SSO auction/product can be conducted to serve data center load. On August 5, 2026, the Public Utilities Commission of Ohio granted AEP Ohio's interim request protocols and directed the company to modify its data center tariff, Schedule DCT, accordingly.

On July 27, 2026, Duke Energy Ohio proposed a new Data Center Tariff (Rate DC) that creates a new classification for data center customers, with similar provisions to those proposed in the FirstEnergy Companies' Schedule DCT. Data center customers are defined as those that use 25 MW or greater or that require transmission and/or distribution investment of $10 million or more; they must enter an electric service agreement (ESA) and arrange generation service through a competitive retail electric supplier to take service under Rate DC. Minimum demand is set no lower than 60% and no higher than 85%. The tariff further requires customers to pay 100% of non-network transmission costs for infrastructure to provide service to the customer in accordance with Rider X and requires customers to pay for the costs of company engineering studies. It directs security and credit requirements to be included in the ESA; the amount will be tiered based on project risk. It further sets an initial contract term equal to the load ramp period (up to 4 years) plus 10 years, though customers could exit after the seventh year following the ramp period by paying an exit fee equal to 36 months of minimum charges, and directs contract modification and termination requirements and charges to be outlined in the ESA.

In Docket 26-0035-EL-RDR, on January 15, 2026, FirstEnergy filed an application and compliance tariffs in the matter of the review of the non-market-based services rider (Rider NMB). On March 11, 2026, Commission Staff filed its review and recommendation. Staff recommended approval of the Application for rates effective April 1, 2026, subject to the following to a recommendation that due to the large projected growth of data centers in Ohio, the Companies be required to provide updated data center load growth information semi-annually to Staff and that any data center not participating in the Rider NMB Pilot Program not be eligible to the added to the Rider NMB Pilot Program after April 1, 2026. On April 17, the Ohio Consumer's Counsel filed a request for rehearing. On May 13, 2026, the Commission filed an entry on rehearing denying the request for rehearing and directing FirstEnergy to file an application for tariff approval creating a separate class for data centers within 30 days. In Docket 26-0697-EL-ATA, in June 12, 2026, FirstEnergy's three Ohio operating companies (the Illuminating Company, also known as the Cleveland Electric Illuminating Company; Ohio Edison; and Toledo Edison) proposed a new separate class of data center customers, to be served under a new Schedule Data Center Tariff (Schedule DCT). The tariff would apply to any customer operating a data center or mobile data center, with no minimum load threshold, and would require a minimum monthly billing demand equal to the higher of 85% of contracted capacity or actual usage including retail transmission and distribution. If a facility operates one or more data centers and also has non-data center load at the same single location, Schedule DCT would apply to all electric distribution service to that customer, unless the customer separately meters its data center and non-data center loads where technically feasible and pays for them through separate accounts. New data center loads would sign contracts with an initial term equal to the load ramp period (up to 4 years) plus 10 years, though customers could exit after the seventh year following the ramp period by paying an exit fee equal to 36 months of minimum charges. New customers would be required to post collateral covering dedicated transmission and distribution infrastructure costs, scaled to creditworthiness. Customers would need to procure generation from a competitive retail supplier rather than standard service, and mobile data center operators would need to attest they are not affiliated with any foreign adversary. Schedule DCT would require the data center to enter into a contract with the electric distribution utility and its transmission affiliate. The contract, which would be filed with FERC, would set an 85% minimum demand for allocation of wholesale transmission costs based on single coincident peak. The contract would further include a true-up to recover any shortfall at wholesale.

subtopics: Cost Shift Prevention (Large Load); Performance Incentive Mechanisms
description: On July 21, 2026, AES Ohio filed a stipulation and recommendation in its ongoing three-year rate case for Public Utilities Commission of Ohio review, including new stipulated rate base and performance incentive mechanisms (PIMs). The company claims that these rate base increases reflect recommendations in a Commission Staff report to include the portion of the company's prepaid pension asset that is projected to generate savings for customers. Customer Cost Allocation: Further, the stipulation includes data center protections by adopting a Data Center Tariff that establishes data centers, defined to have a minimum monthly demand of 25 MW or greater, as a separate customer class. A customer may take generation service from AES Ohio only if the customer certifies it is unable to secure generation service from an alternate generation supplier, and customers have a monthly billing demand of 85% of contract capacity. Upon requesting service, a customer must pay for the cost of facilities studies; based on the company’s studies, a customer must pay the costs of facilities necessary to provide service to the customer. The company may divide its facilities construction into phases, and the customer is allowed a maximum load ramp of two years per phase of construction. Following the ramp period, the customer must enter a contract for a minimum of 10 years; a customer may terminate the contract with 36 months of notice and pay an exit fee equal to the minimum charge for at least 75% of the service term or the actual costs of facilities built to serve the customer multiplied by the percentage of the service term remaining. To cover the above obligations, the customer must provide a collateral requirement equal to the sum of (1) the minimum charges during the ramp period, (2) three years of minimum charges during the service term, and (3) the exit fee in the form of a parent guaranty, a letter of credit, or cash. Further, the company plans to continue its Weatherization and Bill Payment Assistance Program and Disadvantaged Communities Energy Initiative at current funding levels, with $2 million included in the forecast for each test year. Utility Business Model: The stipulated PIMs include an operating expense PIM, rate base PIM, reliability PIM, and billing efficiency PIM. Pertaining to cost containment, the operating expense PIM results in a 5 basis point upward adjustment if the test year's operating expenses are less than 1.25% more than the previous year's operating expenses and a 5 basis point downward adjustment if test year operating expenses are more than 6.50% more than the previous year's operating expenses. The rate base PIM results in a 5 basis point upward adjustment if the test year's average rate base is less than 4.00% more than the previous year's average rate base and a 5 basis point downward adjustment if test year's average rate base is more than 12.50% more than the previous year's average rate base.
