description: H.B. 1667, as amended in conference committee in July 2026, outlines new return on equity (ROE) requirements for utilities. Unless an authorized ROE is established under the auction process proposed in the bill, the Pennsylvania Public Utility Commission will set the authorized return on a covered utility’s common equity equal to the sum of the 10-year treasury and 2%. The default authorized return will reset annually (as of January 1 each year) to reflect the average of the 10-year treasury rate on the 60 business days prior to January 1 of that year. Further, the burden of proof for demonstrating that the default ROE is insufficient to attract capital will be with the covered utility; the default will be presumed just and reasonable unless rebutted through the auction process. The ROE provisions do not preclude performance-based ratemaking, but the performance-based ratemaking plan may not permit the aggregate effect of performance-based adjustments to increase the utility's realized ROE by more than 2% above the authorized ROE. The default authorized ROE will apply to covered utilities immediately upon the effective date, regardless of if a current rate case is pending or when the most recent rate case was completed. Further, a rate component reflecting or permitting a ROE rate higher than the default or auction rate will not be considered just and reasonable. Within 60 days of the effective date, the Commission must issue an order for each covered utility setting the authorized ROE, and within 120 days it must implement corresponding adjustments to customer rates to reflect the new authorized ROE. For the period between the bill effective date and the date the adjusted rates take effect, the Commission must also implement a true-up adjustment for the difference between the revenue actually collected by the utility and revenue that would have been collected under the authorized return set by the bill. In accordance with the implementation timeline above, the Commission will also determine a corresponding rate base for determining the authorized ROE. Rate base reductions will only be allowed for capital which is not supplied by investors; additionally, the Commission may not exclude an asset on the basis that it has not yet been placed in service if the investment has been deemed prudent and is being undertaken for the benefit of regulated service. The bill further outlines the new auction process. If a utility determines that its cost of equity exceeds the default authorized return, it may petition the Commission for an auction within 30 days of the effective date of the bill or the last reset of the default authorized return. The auction process includes an analogous true-up adjustment and adjustment to customer rates for rates collected between the petition and the effective dates of the adjusted rate. The bill also outlines a Commission-initiated auction process for cases where the authorized return materially exceeds the cost of equity, including true-up mechanisms and penalties for utility non-compliance. The bill further outlines protocols for the case of multiple auctions where different equity interests bear different authorized rates of return. The Commission must adopt and promulgate rules and regulations to implement the competitive equity auction procedures, including process and eligibility, disclosure obligations, guidelines for independent auction administration, and consumer protection standards. Finally, the bill includes extensive protocols for auction participants, misconduct and risk attribution, the formation of regulated service corporations and LLCs, and annual reporting and transparency requirements.

categories: Utility Business Model; Utility Oversight and Cost Recovery
description: H.B. 2224, as passed by the House in June 2026, outlines new return on equity (ROE) requirements for investor-owned utilities regulated by the Pennsylvania Public Utility Commission (“covered utilities”), set either by a competitive auction or at the authorized return on a covered utility's common equity equal to the sum of the 10-year treasury and 2%. The default authorized ROE rate will apply to each regulated service of a covered utility immediately on the effective date, regardless of whether a rate proceeding related to voluntary changes in rates is pending and when a rate proceeding was last concluded. A rate component reflecting or permitting an authorized return may no longer be considered just and reasonable, except to the extent established through a competitive equity auction. Within 60 days of the effective date, the Commission must issue an order for each covered utility setting the authorized ROE. Within 120 days, the Commission must implement corresponding adjustments to customer rates through the Commission’s most expedient mechanism, including a surcharge or credit. The Commission must also implement a true-up adjustment for the period between the effective date of the bill and the date that the adjusted rates take effect. A covered utility that believes the default authorized return is insufficient to attract capital may petition the Commission for a competitive equity auction. The ROE provisions do not preclude performance-based ratemaking, but the performance-based ratemaking plan may not permit the aggregate effect of performance-based adjustments to increase the utility's realized ROE by more than 2% above the authorized ROE. The bill also requires annual report outlining each utility’s requested ROE, rate of return, and capitalization mix in the most recent rate case, the approved ROE, the results of any competitive ROE auctions, an analysis of the impact on average customer rates resulting from implementation, and a description of how returns on equity have changed.

On August 27, 2026, the Pennsylvania Public Utility Commission (PUC) voted to publish its Fiscal Year 2025-2026 annual report on PUC management audits and management efficiency investigations. Across management audits, PUC Staff provided recommendations in its final audit reports to companies, and companies subsequently filed implementation plans. In its July 2025 management audit of Pike County Light & Power Company, the PUC recommended improvements including those related to cost allocation, affiliated interests, and financial management. Specific examples include establishing internal controls over intercompany transactions and cost allocation processes and complying with all aspects of approved affiliated interest agreements, as well as improving the customer experience by expanding payment options and eliminating the manual process for budget billing. In its implementation plan, the company accepted 23 of the PUC's 25 recommendations, partially accepting one recommendation and rejecting another. In its June 2026 management audit of Duquesne Light Company, PUC Staff provided 17 recommendations; the company's implementation plan indicated acceptance of all recommendations. The recommendations included those related to affiliated interests and cost allocation, as well as financial management. Specific examples include implementing measures to reduce outstanding pole attachment fees and developing procedures to review stock inventory and remove obsolete materials to minimize excessive carrying costs. In September 2025, the PUC released its management efficiency investigation of FirstEnergy Pennsylvania, examining the company's progress in implementing 15 recommendations made in a June 2022 management audit. FirstEnergy effectively or substantially implemented 7 of 15 recommendations, including realizing $41 million in operations and maintenance savings specific to FirstEnergy Pennsylvania, due to FirstEnergy's strategic planning initiatives and implementing new internal controls over financial reporting. PUC auditors also identified 15 follow-up recommendations, including disclosing and explaining increases in operating costs attributed to executive misconduct in future base rate filings, and evaluating processes to increase pole attachment fee collection and reduce write-offs. In March 2026, the PUC released its management efficiency investigation of PECO's progress implementing recommendations from its August 2022 management and operations audit. PECO effectively or substantially implemented 9 of the 19 prior audit recommendations and has taken some action on the remaining 10. These include establishing a surcharge credit to return amounts collected for use of its fiber assets to distribution ratepayers through 2025 and filing a money pool agreement, which was subsequently approved by the PUC. The money pool, administered by Exelon BSC, had been used as one of the company's major sources for short-term borrowing, helping to reduce banking costs and overall need for financing; the company had received approval of the agreement with FERC, but not the PUC. The investigation also outlined 18 follow-up recommendations, including completing distribution of the fiber affiliate revenue surcharge to ratepayers.
sources: Docket No. D-2026-3063674; PA PUC Press Release (Aug. 2026); PA PUC FY 2026-2026 Annual Report (Aug. 2026)

description: On April 10, 2026, the Puerto Rico Energy Bureau (NEPR) re-started the rulemaking process for this docket, which was originally opened to develop a community solar pilot with a carve-out requiring at least 50% of a project's subscribed capacity to be reserved for LMI customers, but was delayed indefinitely in August 2025 after the federal grant funding the pilot was canceled. The focus of this docket is pivoting to a facilitated conversation about alternative methods of implementing community solar, but there is still discussion regarding potential set-asides for service to low-income or disadvantaged customers. On June 9, 2026, NEPR held a community solar stakeholder workshop, which included a presentation on LUMA's recommended program design that advocated for a minimum level of LMI participation through targeted benefits for customers who cannot install rooftop solar.

On March 2, 2026, PREPA filed its Energy Efficiency and Demand Response Three Year Plan, covering FY2027 and FY2028. On March 24, 2026, the Puerto Rico Energy Bureau (NEPR) ordered PREPA to file proposed performance incentive mechanisms (PIMs) and associated targets for its plan. On April 20, 2026, PREPA filed its PIMs proposal, recommending using the same performance metrics originally established for its T&D System Operation and Maintenance Agreement with LUMA in 2022: energy savings as a percentage of total energy sales and peak demand savings as a percentage of total peak demand. On May 29, 2026, NEPR issued an order temporarily approving the Energy Efficiency and Demand Response Three Year Plan, while the Energy Bureau finishes reviewing the plan in anticipation of a final order.

R.C.C. 243, as passed by the House in November 2025, is a joint resolution imposing a 24-month moratorium during which the Puerto Rico Energy Bureau (NEPR) cannot consider increases to PREPA's rates. During the moratorium, all ongoing tariff proceedings will be suspended. NEPR can still evaluate or authorize tariff revisions that result in adjustments or reductions that favor consumers, along with adjustments to fuel or energy costs in response to market prices. After the moratorium ends, NEPR will perform a public and independent audit of the electric tariff system that must include: (1) revisions to PREPA's reports on operational and administrative costs, (2) an evaluation of the reasonability of automatic adjustments for fuel and energy costs, (3) a verification of operator compliance with performance metrics, and (4) the identification of corrective or structural measures that reduce tariff impact on consumers. NEPR must provide an interim report to the legislature after the first 12 months of the moratorium and a final report after the second 12 months with their discoveries, conclusions, and recommendations for public policy.

Executive Order 26-05, signed on July 23, 2026, orders the Rhode Island Office of Energy Resources to allocate $28 million from Regional Greenhouse Gas Initiative (RGGI) auction reserves to provide bill credits to residential electric customers during the 2027 winter heating season. The Office filed its application with the Rhode Island Public Utilities Commission on August 6, 2026. RI Energy filed a proposed tariff to implement the bill credit on August 13, 2026; the tariff provides a $20.45 monthly bill credit to Rate A-16 (standard residential) and Rate A-60 (low-income residential) customers in January, February, and March 2027. In September 2026, the Commission filed notices of public comment and evidentiary hearings to allow for input on RI Energy's proposed rates and tariff advice.

subtopics: Cost Shift Prevention (Large Load); Low-Income Discount Rates
description: As part of a general rate case filed on November 26, 2025, RI Energy proposed lexical changes to its Low Income Rate A-60. The changes add clarifying information and reorganize the tariff for ease of understanding. During the proceeding, the utility and other participants agreed to review the structure of the rate and make revisions to improve its impact. Rate A-60 is currently two-tiered, with customers enrolled in Supplemental Security Income, LIHEAP, or SNAP receiving a 25% bill discount, and customers enrolled in Medicaid, General Public Assistance, or the Rhode Island Works Program receiving a 30% bill discount. On June 3, 2026, RI Energy filed a settlement agreement specifically for Rate A-60. Rate A-60 would shift from two tiers to five tiers: a 75% bill discount for households at 0-50% of the federal poverty limit, a 66% bill discount for households at 50-75% of the federal poverty limit, a 56% bill discount for households at 75-100% of the federal poverty limit, a 38% bill discount for households at 100-150% of the federal poverty limit, and a 10% bill discount for households at 150-250% of the federal poverty limit. There would be no changes to the eligibility criteria or participation requirements, but all budget-billing eligible customers must be offered budget billing when (re-)enrolling in Rate A-60. At an open meeting on August 21, 2026, the Rhode Island Public Utilities Commission voted on various issues. The Commission ordered the utility to file an extra-large load tariff by the end of the year, for customers 20 MW or higher. The open meeting did not discuss the Rate A-60 settlement agreement. Compliance tariffs filed a few days later kept Rate A-60's existing two-tier structure, however a supplemental record request filed at the same time outlines a timeline to implement the settlement's version of Rate A-60. The revised Rate A-60 should go live in mid-December 2026.
sources: Docket No. 25-45-GE; Settlement Agreement (June 2026); Meeting Minutes (Aug. 2026)

categories: Customer Cost Allocation; Studies and Investigations; Utility Oversight and Cost Recovery
description: Executive Order 1, signed by the Governor in early February 2026, is titled Reducing Energy Costs and Improving Transparency. The executive order requires the Rhode Island Office of Energy Resources to conduct a comprehensive review of the state's net metering program (behind-the-meter and virtual) and the Renewable Energy Growth Program; the goal of the review is to control costs to ratepayers and ensure the programs do not impose and undue financial burden on households and businesses while remaining aligned with the state's emission reduction policies. The review should evaluate ratepayer impacts, state fiscal implications, and energy-system effects, assessing potential program modifications when appropriate. As part of this review, the Office must submit proposed budget changes regarding virtual net metering program to the Governor and the Office of Management and Budget by April 24, 2026; the changes should maintain ratepayer savings while updating the structure of the program, avoiding adverse impacts on existing solar projects and considering approaches used by other states to maintain cost-effective solar incentives. In addition, the Office must complete a longer-term review of behind-the-meter net metering and the Renewable Energy Growth Program, providing key findings and potential policy and legislative options to the Governor and the Office of Management and Budget by October 2026. The executive order also directs the Rhode Island Department of Public Utilities and Carriers to evaluate and communicate the anticipated ratepayer impacts of all significant energy legislation under consideration by the General Assembly to ensure that policymakers, stakeholders, and the public have a clear and timely understanding of the potential effects on utility rates, customer bills, and overall energy affordability. As part of the process, the Department must determine which proposed legislation is sufficiently broad in scope, material in ratepayer impact, or sufficiently advanced in the legislative process to warrant an official Ratepayer Impact Note. The Department must: (1) develop an internal framework for Ratepayer Impact Notes, (2) establish a legislative notification and coordination process to ensure Ratepayer Impact Notes are available to legislators, and (3) establish a process to provide plain-language impact summaries of relevant legislative proposals on its website.

Background: In October 2025, RI Energy filed an application to issue bill credits to hold customers harmless from an acquisition-related increase in rates; specifically, the credits will ensure customers are held harmless from any changes to accumulated deferred income taxes as a result of PPL Corporation's acquisition of RI Energy from National Grid in 2022. The utility withdrew its application in November 2025 due to concerns that arose during the pre-hearing process. Recent Action: On April 16, 2026, RI Energy re-filed its application with a revised tariff. All customers - gas and electric - would receive credits in January, February, and March of 2027 and 2028. The total amount of credits RI Energy issues would be based on the net present value of the hold harmless commitment; within that total amount, each customer would receive the same bill credit value within a month. RI Energy would reconcile any leftover total credit in the March 2028 bill. On the same day, the Rhode Island Public Utilities Commission consolidated this docket into RI Energy's ongoing general rate case. At an open meeting on August 21, 2026, the Rhode Island Public Utilities Commission voted on various issues, including authorizing RI Energy to implement the bill credits with the following conditions: (1) the utility must used revised assumptions and methodologies; (2) it must the distribute the credit via a uniform fixed monthly bill credit to all electric accounts from October 2026 through September 2027; (3) after September 2027, the utility must reconcile the calculated vs actual credits; (4) any leftover credits must go towards the utility's storm fund, while any overdrawn credits could be recovered; (5) RI Energy must notify the Commission by August 25, 2026, whether it will accept these terms or withdraw its proposal; and 6) if it decides to withdraw the proposal, then it must apply an annual Hold Harmless credit related to federal transmission rates in each subsequent rate filing. On August 25, 2026, RI Energy filed a letter accepting revised program. Under its compliance filing a few days later, the credit for electric customers will be $14.51/month.
sources: Docket No. 25-33-GE; Docket No. 25-45-GE; Meeting Minutes (Aug. 2026)

description: H.B. 7127, an appropriations bill enacted in June 2026, requires utilities to participate in ISO-New England in order to own, operate, or control transmission facilities in the state. Because current utility participation is voluntary, utilities are eligible for a 0.5% adder on their return on equity for transmission assets. By mandating participation, utilities are no longer eligible for the adder.

On July 15, 2026, Dominion Energy South Carolina and NextEra Energy filed a joint petition with the South Carolina Public Service Commission requesting approval for NextEra to acquire Dominion. The petition proposes a variety of merger benefits, including $2.25 billion in shareholder-funded bill credits over a two-year period for Dominion's customers across Virginia, North Carolina, and South Carolina. South Carolina will receive approximately $387 million in merger benefits, resulting in about a $10 bill credit per customer with some variation according to actual energy usage.

On May 27, 2026, Duke Energy Progress and Duke Energy Carolinas filed a petition with the South Carolina Public Service Commission to open a docket allowing comment and investigation into the creation of a large load tariff. This petition comes in response to stipulations in Docket No. 2025-154-E providing that the parties to the stipulation (the utilities and intervenors) would work together to file a “Petition with the Commission requesting that the Commission open a generic docket for the purpose of evaluating issues associated with new large load (50 MW or greater) additions including existing rate schedules, service regulations, line extension policies, and interconnection rules,” and requesting “that the Commission allow interested parties to file or otherwise present comments on topics related to new large load customers.” The topics to be covered in this docket include: (1) minimum contract period and contract demand for billing purposes; (2) collateral requirements; (3) exit policies and restrictions on customer capacity reduction; (4) treatment of generation, transmission, and administrative costs; (5) interconnection costs, including opportunities to support grid-enhancing technologies to manage such costs; (6) optional tariff provisions for flexible interconnections; and (7) optional tariff provisions for the management of clean behind-the-meter resources, and optional clean transition tariffs to enable direct selection of new clean energy resources. The Commission held a status conference on June 17, 2026, and scheduled a generic large load workshop for October 26-27, 2026.

categories: Customer Cost Allocation; Customer Cost-Saving Programs
subtopics: Cost Shift Prevention (Large Load); Tariffed On-Bill Financing
description: On May 8, 2026, as part of a general rate case proceeding, Dominion Energy South Carolina, the South Carolina Office of Regulatory Staff, and other parties filed a settlement agreement related to the revenue requirement and related issues, which included a provision that requires Dominion Energy to facilitate a discussion of on-bill financing programs through its established Energy Efficiency Advisory Group. Parties also filed a large load stipulation in May 2026, in which Dominion Energy agrees to participate in the large load generic docket (Docket No. 2026-138-E) along with Duke Energy. The South Carolina Public Service Commission issued an order on July 2, 2026, approving both the large load stipulation and the settlement provision related to on-bill financing.
sources: Docket No. 2025-325-E; Settlement Agreement (May 2026); Large Load Stipulation (May 2026); Order (July 2026)

description: H.B. 5126, as enacted in September 2026, is South Carolina's primary budget bill for fiscal years 2026-2027. It includes a requirement for the Electricity Market Reform Measures Study Committee to issue a report on its work to the South Carolina General Assembly by January 31, 2027.

On July 27, 2026, Otter Tail Power filed a petition to create a new class for very large customers, as well as revise several existing tariffs. The revisions would allow the utility to divide the Large General Service class into tiers, provide a new schedule for high power comput (HPC) customers, enhance cost accuracy, and ensure alignment between customer billing and the costs incurred to serve them. The HPC rate is designed as a long-term, take-or-pay service constructor that assigns the data center all costs attributable to serving their load. To take service under the HPC, customers must have a new load and intend to take firm electric service of at least 75 MW. Additionally, the customer must post and maintain credit support and will be charged and exit fee for early termination.

On April 7, 2026, El Paso Electric (EPE) filed an application for a new High Load Factor Large Power Service Rate for very large data center or advanced manufacturing customers with an annual peak demand of 75 MW or larger and an annual load factor of at least 85%. The rate is based on EPE's existing Economic Development Service Rates (Schedules 33A and 33B), approved last year; if this new rate is approved, then EPE requests Schedule 33A for larger customers be terminated. The tariff includes a provision for cost recovery associated with "dedicated" facilities via a facility charge, which would likely be transmission facilities only used by the participating customer; the value of the facility charge would be determined in the service agreement. Customers can also participate in the Green Energy Plus Tariff, which allows them to enter procurement agreements with EPE or a third party for renewable resources, with all costs associated with the resources borne by the customer. Energy from these systems would either offset the customer's load requirements (using a 15-minute netting interval) or be supplied to other customers at EPE's avoided cost. The customer would retain any RECs or environmental attributes.

On June 12, 2026, the Public Utility Commission of Texas Staff filed proposed rule changes to implement S.B. 6 (enacted in 2025). The rule changes focus on transmission cost recovery from large load customers, with the technical changes designed to ensure that wholesale transmission charges appropriately allocate costs for transmission investment based on the costs caused by each customer class. The proposal requires the use of a minimum billing demand for large load customers and requires investor-owned distribution service providers to update class allocation factor values annually. The rules also require non-opt-in-entity distribution service providers to provide ERCOT with access to settlement-quality meter data for each large load customer in its service territory.

On July 13, 2026, Entergy Texas filed a request for a waiver from certain rate case requirements. Entergy plans to file its next rate case in August 2027, and it has requested a waiver from filing an independent review of its application and the performance of the review. As Entergy's financial statements are already audited by an independent auditor, this filing would be an unnecessary expense. On August 24, 2026, Public Utility Commission of Texas Staff recommended approval of the application.

On May 9, 2025, the Utah Public Service Commission initiated a rulemaking proceeding as ordered by S.B. 132 (enacted in 2025), which created requirements for providing electrical service to large-scale electrical loads. The Commission filed proposed rules in October 2025. The rules describe the allocation of transmission costs between large load customers and retail customers for large load contracts, the Commission's review process for large load contracts, and a large-scale generation provider’s registration and registration status with the Commission. In December 2025, numerous stakeholders filed additional comments either supporting implementation of the rules or recommending certain revisions to the rules. While S.B. 132 required the Commission to make the rules effective January 1, 2026, the Commission believes the comments it received warrant additional consideration. Therefore, the Commission will continue the rulemaking to consider potential amendments. The Commission consolidated this proceeding with Docket No. 24-035-43 and held a technical conference on April 2, 2026.

On July 15, 2026, Dominion Energy and NextEra Energy filed a petition with the State Corporation Commission to allow NextEra to acquire Dominion. The merger petition proposes to provide nearly $2.25 billion in bill credits to all customers in the Dominion-NextEra service territory, including Virginia, North Carolina, and South Carolina customers.
sources: Docket No. PUR-2026-00112; Petition for Acquisition (July 2026)

description: On March 24, 2025, Appalachian Power Company filed a petition to update its Rate Schedule Large Power Service (L.P.S.), a large load tariff. The utility is proposing to add additional requirements to Schedule L.P.S. that will be applicable to new large load additions greater than or equal to 150 MW on an aggregated basis or 100 MW at an individual site (“large load customers”). Specifically, Appalachian seeks to add the following additional terms and conditions applicable to these customers: (1) a contract term for an initial period of 12 years; (2) a minimum five-year notice to discontinue or modify service; (3) an 80% monthly minimum billing demand; and (4) an increased minimum amount of collateral to be provided by the customer. On November 10, 2025, the parties in the case proposed the following stipulation terms: (1) the new terms of Schedule L.P.S. will not apply to existing large loads and only new loads or newly expanded loads of at least 100 MW or 150 MW in aggregate will be subject to the new terms; (2) the initial contract term will be 14 years, inclusive of the load ramp period; (3) the monthly billing demand is the highest 30-minute peak; (4) customers are subject to a monthly minimum charge; (5) the collateral requirement is as proposed in the petition; and (6) the customers have increased contractual flexibility, such as no fee for reducing load in the first five years and a minimum of 42 months notice for ending the contract. On June 1, 2026, the Virginia State Corporation Commission filed an order approving the changes to Schedule L.P.S. outlined in the stipulation.

As part of its rate case filed on February 27, 2026, Old Dominion Power Company proposed a number of changes to its rates. Significantly, these changes include a proposed Extremely High Load Factor rate schedule (a large load tariff). Rate EHLF has the following characteristics: (1) customers with a contract capacity greater than 50 MVA and an average monthly load factor above 85% would take service under Rate EHLF. Because extremely high load factor customers’ demands would not change appreciably across various times of day or seasons by definition, Rate EHLF has a single, non-time-differentiated demand charge to recover all demand-related costs of service; (2) rate EHLF requires the monthly billing demand to be the greater of (a) the maximum measured load in the billing period, (b) the highest measured load in the preceding 11 billing periods, or (c) 80% of the maximum contract capacity; (3) rate EHLF requires a minimum initial contract term of 15 years; (4) each Rate EHLF customer or its guarantor must provide collateral in the form of cash or a letter of credit equal to 24 months of the minimum billed amounts at the largest contract capacity value. Rate EHLF will not apply to existing customers.

In a final order in Docket No. PUR-2026-00056, the State Corporation Commission created parameters regarding direct assignment of certain transmission costs to large load customers and agreed that supplemental proceedings would be necessary for that purpose. The order also directed Dominion Energy to file proposed amendments to its line extension policy. The Commission opened this docket on August 25, 2026 to receive those filings and to continue addressing the matter of transmission cost allocation to large load customers.

The State Corporation Commission opened a new proceeding on August 25, 2026 to amend the regulations for shared solar, as required by legislation enacted earlier in the year. H.B. 807 increased the program capacity limit for part two of Dominion Energy's community solar program from 150 MW to 525 MW. Of this total, 450 MW must serve no more than 51% low-income customers, and 75 MW may serve more than 51% low-income customers.

On December 1, 2025, Dominion Energy filed an application for approval of updates to its Demand Side Management (DSM) programs. As a result, the utility is requesting additional program funds for a three-year extension period for its residential and non-residential Income and Age Qualifying (IAQ) DSM programs. The proposed Residential Home Energy Services (EE) Program offers a comprehensive and unified residential home energy evaluation program offering, consisting of a no-cost introductory in-home energy audit, no-cost virtual audit, no-cost welcome kits, and an optional comprehensive Building Performance Institute audit. The proposed program will also be available for qualifying residential customers residing in manufactured housing and multifamily dwellings. The Residential Home Energy Services Program also consolidates five previously standalone program offerings, including Welcome Kits, Virtual Audit, Retrofit, Multifamily, and Manufactured Housing. Beyond these two extensions, the filing also proposes several new pilot programs specifically targeting IAQ customers: Residential IAQ Battery Storage Pilot, which incentivizes IAQ customers to discharge home battery systems during peak demand events to support grid reliability; and the Residential IAQ Battery Purchase Pilot, which provides IAQ customers with a no-cost battery storage system installation. It specifically targets IAQ customers who previously had solar panels installed through the utility's DSM IX H.B. 2789 Solar Pilot. On August 3, 2026, the State Corporation Commission filed an order approving Dominion Energy's proposed extensions to existing DSM programs and the new IAQ battery pilot programs.

To comply with H.B. 1062, enacted in April 2026, the State Corporation Commission scheduled a technical conference for October 30, 2026 to evaluate a "Pay as You Save" (PAYS) program in Virginia. The technical conference will examine: (1) how customers may be impacted by implementation of a PAYS Program, including any potential for customer protections and impacts on non-participating customers; (2) eligibility requirements; (3) what requirements could be placed on measures that may be incorporated into a PAYS Program; (4) feasibility of establishing standards for evaluation, measurement & verification of any measures included in a PAYS Program; (5) ratemaking considerations for costs associated with a potential PAYS Program; (6) ensuring compliance with the standards developed and maintained by the Energy Efficiency Institute, Inc.; and (7) details with respect to the administration of a potential PAYS Program.

In July 2026, Solar United Neighbors and Governor Spanberger announced the creation of Switch Together, a bulk solar procurement program that provides lower cost solar installations to residential customers. Switch Together organizes a reverse auction with installers who compete to offer service, ensuring customers receive a discount on their solar installation. Participants can also receive discounts on battery storage systems and heat pumps. Customers may save an average of 23% on home and business solar installations, equivalent to $6,300 on a typical system, which is estimated to save the average household approximately $2,200 a year on electricity costs.

In October 2024, the Virginia State Corporation Commission opened a new proceeding to explore the state's projected load growth from new data centers in a comprehensive manner. The proceeding will explore one or more potential frameworks that could be utilized by electric cooperatives and investor-owned utilities to serve potential new large use customer load in a manner that reasonably addresses the risks and issues attendant to this new load type, is just and reasonable to both current and future customers, and is permissible under current Virginia statutory law. It will also explore a tariff framework specific for these customers, and whether certain generation and transmission costs should be directly assigned to them. Commissioner-led technical conferences were held on December 16, 2024 and December 12, 2025.

H.B. 903 and S.B. 251, signed into law in April 2026, direct the State Corporation Commission to consider whether a performance-based regulatory framework, which would evaluate electric utility performance and cost control incentives, is in the public interest of the Commonwealth. The bills also direct the Commission to develop related legislative recommendations and include its findings and recommendations in a report due July 1, 2027.

On July 25, 2025, the Vermont Public Utility Commission opened a docket to evaluate Vermont's three energy efficiency utilities' Demand Resources Plans (DRP) for the 2027-2029 triennium. The three energy efficiency utilities, Efficiency Vermont (EVT), Vermont Gas Systems (VGS), and Burlington Electric Department (BED) submitted proposed plans for consideration by the Commission. EVT's plan makes five major changes from the previous triennium, four of which impact customer affordability: discontinuation of Energy Efficiency Modernization Act (EEMA) programs, recognition of savings attributable to new construction, enhancements to the Weatherization Assistance Program (WAP), and flat flexible load management spending. The changes to WAP are significant in that, beginning in 2027, they will be paid for out of EVT's thermal energy budgets rather than its electric efficiency budgets, while still maintaining the size and level of service for customers. One of EVT's discontinued EEMA programs is $1 million for low-income fuel switching; EVT is proposing to continue this program with a focus on heat pumps as part of its ongoing electric resource acquisition programming in order to improve cost-effectiveness. EVT proposes to spend around $1.7 million each year on residential energy efficiency programs. According to EVT's analysis, while residential rates are expected to increase by 2% due to energy efficiency programs, bills will decrease by around 3.8%. VGS' plan includes expanded incentives and tailored offerings for LMI households, renters, and small businesses; stronger geographic equity considerations; and improved engagement with historically underserved communities. The plan introduces higher weatherization incentives for income-qualified households, streamlined intake and income-verification processes, and direct-to-contractor rebates to remove upfront cost barriers. VGS proposes to spend around $1.6-1.8 million each year on residential energy efficiency programs. BED is proposing possible reductions in services in its DRP, due to potential statutory changes in Vermont that will make natural gas more readily available. As a result, BED expects to have a surplus in its thermal energy budgets, which should be reinvested to continue delivering energy efficiency services to customers, such as a newly proposed electric panel retrofit for income-qualified customers. Overall, BED is proposing around $1 million in residential incentives over the triennium, and predicts rate increases of 2.6% and bill decreases of 0.31% for residential customers.
sources: Docket No. 25-1203; VT Gas Systems Demand Resources Plan (Dec. 2025)

description: On August 28, 2026, the Vermont Public Utility Commission issued an order in Green Mountain Power (GMP)'s rate case and Multi-Year Regulation Plan (MYRP) directing GMP to develop a new affordability metric for its MYRP reporting. The utility initially defined this metric in its application as the number of customers enrolled in the Energy Assistance Program as a percentage of estimated total eligible customers as of December 31 of each year. The Commission further directed GMP to work with the Vermont Department of Public Service and make a filing elaborating on any proposed metrics within 90 days of this order in the respective compliance docket, which is Docket No. 25-1955-PET.

subtopics: Arrearage Management; Bill Assistance; Payment Plans
description: On July 1, 2026, Avista Utilities filed a request to revise its Low-Income Rate Assistance Program (LIRAP) (Schedule 92), to incorporate various program design changes established in collaboration with the utility's Energy Assistance Advisory Group (EAAG) as part of the company's 2026 LIRAP re-calibration. The revisions include: (1) shifting from a single year-round discount to separate winter and non-winter discounts; (2) incorporating Comfort Level Billing, an optional billing program designed to mitigate seasonal variability in bills by aligning monthly payments with average annual usage, into the seasonal discounts; (3) reducing its arrearage maximum eligible past due balance from $2,500 to $1,000; (4) changing the frequency customers may use the Arrearage Management Program (AMP) and Arrearage Forgiveness Program (AFP) from twice every seven years and once over the lifetime of the customer's account, respectively, to once per program year for both programs; and (5) making several updates to LIRAP eligibility and verification guidelines. The utility is also introducing an Arrearage Relief Program for customers with incomes equal to the greater of 51% - 200% of the Federal Poverty Level or 80% of Area Median Income. This program would be available to customers who would qualify for the AMP but can pay the portion of their arrearage balance required by the AMP in full at the time of enrollment. These customers may opt to receive immediate forgiveness of the remaining balance rather than entering the 12-month AMP repayment period. On August 27, 2026, the revisions were allowed to become effective via the No Action agenda.

On March 20, 2026, as part of a general rate case, Puget Sound Energy (PSE) filed testimony that included proposals to address affordability for low-income high energy-burdened customers and named communities. The proposals are based on key insights and takeaways from PSE's 2024 Energy Burden Analysis findings. The Energy Burden Analysis allows PSE to estimate the number of low-income customers, respective energy burdens, and the energy assistance need. PSE proposes two recommendations to reduce energy burden for customers: (1) reduce energy burden on low-income customers through reduced customer charges; and (2) prioritize low-income customers who are energy-burdened customers for energy assistance. PSE is proposing that low-income residential electric service (Schedule 7) customers pay 60% of the standard monthly customer charge, before any application of bill discount rates, reducing the impact of the utility's proposed increase of this charge. Additionally, the utility's proposed time-of-use rate expansion was designed to remain compatible with affordability programs. PSE also proposes to prioritize energy assistance for low-income, energy-burdened customers to the maximum extent possible as offering significant energy assistance to all low-income customers, regardless of energy burden, appears unsustainable. Through the Energy Burden Analysis, PSE determined the reach of energy assistance for low-income, highly energy-burdened customers, and its effectiveness in reducing energy assistance need, can be improved as there are a significant number of low-income, highly energy-burdened customers who are either not receiving sufficient levels of energy assistance or are not receiving assistance at all. The utility plans on consulting with interested parties and advisory groups to help identify feasible ways to redesign some of its energy assistance programs to increase the efficacy of energy assistance funds such that they better assist low-income, highly energy-burdened households. Public comment hearings will be held on September 29 and October 7, 2026.

On July 7, 2026, Pacific Power filed an application to revise its Residential Energy Efficiency Rider - Optional for Qualifying Low Income Customers (Schedule 114) to implement a Weatherization Repair Readiness Pilot program. This program would last for 12 months and would assist in funding essential home repairs that prepare residences for weatherization, prevent deferrals, or address issues that have delayed existing projects. The repairs would resolve structural, mechanical, or other conditions. The utility will reimburse between 50% - 100% of project costs and will work in conjunction with the state's Weatherization Plus Health Program.

On March 16, 2026, the Washington Utilities and Transportation Commission opened a new proceeding for the facilitation of a Commission-led workshop series on large load interconnections and tariffs. The first conference was held on April 27, 2026 and discussed topics such as cost tracking, load forecasting and resource adequacy, and ratepayer protections. A large loads technical workshop was held on August 12, 2026.

The Washington Utilities and Transportation Commission opened a new proceeding in October 2021 to implement S.B. 5295, enacted in May 2021. The bill directed the Commission to develop a policy statement addressing alternatives to traditional cost-of-service ratemaking, including performance measures or goals, targets, performance incentives, and penalty mechanisms. The bill further directed the Commission to consider a number of factors in the proceeding, including lowest reasonable cost planning, affordability, increases in energy burden, cost of service, customer satisfaction and engagement, service reliability, clean energy or renewable procurement, conservation acquisition, demand side management expansion, rate stability, timely execution of competitive procurement practices, attainment of state energy and emissions reduction policies, rapid integration of renewable energy resources, and fair compensation of utility employees. In Phase 1 of the proceeding, the Commission intended to gather stakeholder input on the development of utility performance metrics. Phase 2A would cover reporting and review, and Phase 2B would examine multi-year rate plan revenue adjustment mechanisms. Phase 3 would establish performance incentive mechanisms, Phase 4 would explore other alternative forms of regulation, and Phase 5 would be an ongoing process for re-evaluating and improving the policy. In April 2024, the Commission issued a Policy Statement containing interim guidance related to performance-based measures or goals, targets, performance incentives, and penalty mechanisms. This Policy Statement is not an enforceable rule. The policy statement focused on performance measures metrics and stated the Commission's preferred metrics under four goals. These goals include metrics (1) to demonstrate resilient, reliable, and customer-focused utility distribution systems; (2) related to customer affordability; (3) to evaluate equity in utility operations; and (4) related to environmental improvements. In August 2024, the Commission issued a policy statement to finalize the initial reported metrics for regulated energy companies to file with the Commission on an annual basis as published in April 2024. At this time, the Commission declined to include additional metrics, stating a comprehensive performance-based regulation (PBR) framework cannot be established with finality at this juncture. On June 17, 2025, the Commission held a workshop to discuss the docket's current status, the needs and priorities for Phases 3-5, and best practices for developing the performance incentive mechanisms (PIMs). On January 26, 2026, the Commission issued a Policy Statement clarifying reported performance metrics and addressing PIM principles. It should be noted that this statement only addressed performance metrics with requested clarification. Additionally, the statement included guiding principles for PIMs which the Commission will apply on a case-by-case basis. These principles included: (1) alignment with policy goals and outcomes; (2) clarity, measurability, and verifiability; (3) utility control and achievability; (4) balance of risk, reward, and customer benefits; (5) integration with the broader regulatory framework; (6) incentive structure and calibration; and (7) adaptability, review, and safeguards. On June 30, 2026, the Commission issued a regulatory assessment on the current regulatory environment, mechanisms, and incentives to understand how such tools interact and help balance utility risk and finances with customer affordability and benefits. The assessment found that the current framework generally provides an appropriate balance and has already implemented many of the foundational elements commonly associated with PBR. The assessment does not identify a need for a fundamental redesign, but instead suggests targeted improvements to existing mechanisms. Generally, the assessment supports maintaining mechanisms that advance statutory requirements, customer affordability, safety, reliability, and public policy objectives, while certain existing trackers and adjustment mechanisms should be modified, incorporated back into base rates, or periodically reevaluated. On July 8, 2026, the Commission filed a revised regulatory assessment. On August 5, 2026, the Commission published a policy statement regarding return on PPAs. According to the statement, to qualify for a return, PPAs must be determined as prudent via the Commission on a case-by-case basis and must have a duration of at least 12 months. Additionally all prudent PPAs sourced from Clean Energy Transformation Act-compliant resources qualify for a return.

description: On June 22, 2026, Xcel Energy proposed a new Very Large General Time of Day Service tariff (Cg-13) that would be mandatory for new large loads. Proposed changes include creating a new customer class for cost allocation purposes, with pricing set within the new Large Load Tariff. Pricing structures utilize existing cost allocation and pricing for commercial and industrial customers, plus incremental demand charges unique to large load customers that would be set through a new production cost allocation method established and revisited in regular biennial rate cases. The proposal also includes an application fee to offset development, legal, planning and regulatory costs associated with onboarding a new large customer; a non-binding load forecast requirement; and provisions designed to support innovative generation and transmission partnerships, optional interruptible rates, and other new terms and conditions to mitigate unique risks of serving new large loads. The proposed 100 MW applicability threshold is defined in terms of retail transmission interconnection capacity, not a measure of billed demand. Xcel Energy noted that it has no current customers that would be impacted by the proposed tariff or modifications to existing tariffs.

On July 15, 2026, Madison Gas & Electric (MGE) filed an application to implement a Very Large Customer Service Tariff (Schedule Cp-VLC) and a Bespoke Resource Service (BRS) tariff. The VLC tariff is mandatory for customers eligible to be served at 24,900 volts or higher from dedicated facilities and which have an aggregated load forecast of over 100 MW of new load. The VLC Tariff requires a minimum 15-year term; renewing annually for one-year terms and specifies cancellation notice requirements and cost responsibilities after termination. Load curtailments may be made to maintain reliability and system integrity with no limit to the number or length of occurrences. Rates include a minimum monthly bill and various administrative and market-based charges. Eligible customers must execute related payment and cancellation agreements or VLC service agreements to reliably serve the firm service level with firm resources. The BRS would enable Cp-VLC customers to subscribe to specific generation resources and pay for their proportional share of those resources, preventing generation costs from being shifted to general ratepayers. Bespoke resources include any MGE-owned, contracted, or managed assets that can provide accredited capacity and qualify as Planning Resources in MISO’s Planning Resource Auction (PRA). VLC customers must pay for any remaining balance on bespoke resources in the event of early termination of their contracts.

On September 4, 2026, Alliant Energy's Wisconsin utility proposed a new Large Load Power Service Tariff (Schedule Cp-3) to standardize service for large load customers. It is mandatory for customers forecasted to reach 100 MW or more in monthly maximum demand. Two optional riders are included: the Marginal Capacity Rider, allowing customers to supplement Baseline Firm Demand with shorter-term capacity from Alliant Energy's fleet, customer-owned resources, third parties, or the MISO market; and the Resource Subscription Rider, allowing customers to subscribe to a share of a carbon-free resource for energy, capacity, or sustainability needs, paying associated costs for bill credits, subject to the utility's review for resource adequacy impacts. Customers bear all construction-work-in-progress financing charges for any transmission project, and a new Grid Access Charge recovers the utility's costs under transmission owner agreements for infrastructure serving the customer's load. Internally, service may be curtailed for emergencies, reliability needs, or NERC/MISO requirements, with advance notice when practical.

On June 19, 2026, Cheyenne Light, Fuel & Power (Black Hills Energy) filed a petition to implement a new Large Customer Transmission Cost Adjustment Mechanism (LCTCAM). The tariff assigns LCTCAM customers the costs associated with new transmission system upgrades that are driven by the needs of the LCTCAM customers. Additionally, certain costs that are shared and cannot be assigned to a particular investment, as well as administrative and general and operations and maintenance expenses will be allocated between the Base Transmission Cost Adjustment Mechanism Tariff and the LCTCAM.
